doi:10.5194/acp-26-16203-2026.title: Photochemical mechanism–dependent ozone formation and precursor sensitivity under varying NOx conditions
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16203-2026.summary: Photochemical mechanisms are core components of air quality models, yet differences among them can introduce substantial uncertainty in tropospheric ozone (O 3 ) simulations. We compared three mechanisms (CB06, SAPRC07, and RACM2) using CMAQ during an O 3 pollution episode in Chengdu, China. A customized volatile organic compound (VOC) emission inventory was developed for RACM2. RACM2 and SAPRC07 produced comparable O 3 levels (94.8–96.1 ppbv) with better performance at high-NO x urban site, whereas CB06 simulated lower O 3 (∼80 ppbv) and performed better at low-NO x site. Inter-mechanistic differences in O 3 formation were mainly associated with RO 2 +NO reactions, consistent with larger variability in RO 2 than in HO 2 , while O 3 loss differences mainly arose from OH+NO 2 and O 3 +alkene reactions. Differences in primary RO x production were most evident in carbonyl photolysis, whereas termination differences mainly involved RONO 2 formation and peroxy-radical self- and cross-reactions. Mechanism-dependent discrepancies were more pronounced at high-NO x urban site. Despite these discrepancies, the three mechanisms exhibited a broadly consistent photochemical framework, with O 3 formation dominated by RO 2 +NO and RO x termination shifting from NO x -dependent pathways at high-NO x urban site toward peroxy-radical reactions at low-NO x suburban site. Sensitivity analysis showed O 3 was most sensitive to anthropogenic aromatics and alkenes at urban site and relatively more sensitive to biogenic VOCs at suburban site, although response magnitudes remained mechanism dependent. These findings demonstrate that mechanism choice substantially affects O 3 formation and precursor sensitivities, emphasizing the need for multi-mechanism approaches to improve model reliability and support emission control strategies.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16247-2026.title: A climatological description of atmospheric CO2 concentrations
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16247-2026.summary: At regional scales, atmospheric CO 2 concentrations show (i) a global trend, (ii) a seasonal cycle that varies with location and altitude and (iii) inter-annual and synoptic variability. The CO 2 atmospheric inversion of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) constrained by surface measurements of the gas concentration provides a 4D (spatial+time) description of the CO 2 mixing ratio. A comparison of the CAMS modelling against AirCore profiles acquired over France and the USA indicates an accuracy on the order of 1 ppm (CO 2 ) at most levels in the atmosphere with larger errors close to the surface. Evaluation of the total column against the Total Carbon Column Observing Network (TCCON) observations shows a standard deviation of less than 1 ppm over most sites. In this paper, we attempt a simple description of the concentration time series where the trend is provided by the Mauna Loa measurement dataset and the seasonal cycle is adjusted using annual and semi-annual harmonics. Most of the atmospheric concentration variability is captured by this simple modelling. Over France, the differences between simulated concentrations and in-situ (AirCore) measurements are on the order of 1.5 ppm over the free troposphere and higher. The evaluation against column concentration retrievals from TCCON indicates typical errors on the order of 1 ppm for the climatological fit. The climatological product is updated in near-real time with the Mauna Loa measurements and may therefore be used as prior information for ground-based and satellite-based remote sensing of the CO 2 profile or the column-averaged dry air mole fraction of CO 2 (XCO 2 ). Besides, the deviations between the full CAMS modelling and the climatological fit are used to compute realistic vertical variance-covariance matrices for each of the model grid cells.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16173-2026.title: Mineral dust concentration controlling convective cirrus structure and persistence: a large-eddy simulation study with observational constraints
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16173-2026.summary: Dusty cirrus clouds are optically thick, convectively organized ice clouds that occur during intense mineral dust outbreaks. Previous modeling studies have found a link between mineral dust and convectively generated cirrus, but have been unable to explicitly resolve the associated convective dynamics due to limited spatial resolution. Here, we investigate the evolution and persistence of dusty cirrus using large-eddy simulations constrained by in-situ aircraft observations from the ML-CIRRUS 2014 campaign and complementary remote sensing data. The simulations indicate that sustained convective cirrus requires mineral dust concentrations exceeding climatological values by approximately one to two orders of magnitude, corresponding to number concentrations on the order of N D ∼1 cm −3 . Under these conditions, heterogeneous freezing on mineral dust dominates ice formation and maintains sufficiently high ice crystal number concentrations to sustain strong longwave cooling at cloud top and preserve convective overturning under shortwave radiative warming. In contrast, homogeneous freezing remains largely suppressed across a wide range of simulated conditions. The direct radiative effect of mineral dust is comparatively weak relative to cloud radiative feedbacks and does not significantly influence cirrus evolution. The simulated cirrus is also highly sensitive to the choice of deposition ice nucleation parameterization, highlighting a major source of uncertainty in representing dust–ice interactions. Overall, the results identify mineral dust availability as the primary control on dusty cirrus persistence and emphasize the need for improved representation of heterogeneous ice nucleation in atmospheric models.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16151-2026.title: Vertically stratified long-range transport of biomass-burning aerosol over Reunion Island during September 2017
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16151-2026.summary: Biomass-burning (BB) aerosols seasonally perturb the otherwise relatively clean atmosphere of the South-West Indian Ocean (SWIO), but vertically resolved observations remain sparse in its eastern sector. We examine an enhanced aerosol episode over Reunion Island (21° S, 55° E) in September 2017 by combining AERONET sun-photometer measurements, ground-based Raman and elastic lidar retrievals, FTIR CO observations, MODIS and CALIOP products, CAMS EAC4 reanalysis, and FLEXPART simulations. AERONET aerosol optical depth at 550 nm reached unusually high values (0.16–0.42) during the second half of September. CAMS provided temporally continuous total and species-resolved model AOD and simulated organic matter as the largest aerosol contribution. MODIS and CALIOP provided regional context, showing elongated enhanced-AOD corridors and elevated aerosol layers frequently classified as smoke-related over the western SWIO. On 19 September, lidar observations identified one layer between 2.8 and 4.7 km with Å355/532 = 1.32 ± 0.23. On 25 September, two vertically separated layers with distinct optical properties were observed: a lower layer (3.3–5 km, Å = 1.45 ± 0.12) and a drier upper layer (5–9 km, Å = 1.60 ± 0.06). FLEXPART simulations for two selected source regions, evaluated against vertically smoothed FTIR CO observations, support Southern African influence on both cases and an additional South American contribution to the lower layer on 25 September. The observations demonstrate that column-integrated measurements alone cannot resolve the layered aerosol structure over Reunion; the combined evidence provides an illustrative case of vertically distinct long-range transport pathways in the eastern SWIO.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16261-2026.title: Constraining the hydrogen soil sink and photochemical source: insights from atmospheric H2 inversions (2003–2023)
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16261-2026.summary: Hydrogen (H 2 ) is expected to become an increasingly important energy carrier during the energy transition, likely leading to higher atmospheric H 2 levels due to losses during production, transport, storage and usage of hydrogen. Multiple studies have shown this could impact atmospheric composition through interactions with the hydroxyl radical. However, the magnitude of this impact remains uncertain due to large uncertainties in the global H 2 budget, particularly in the soil sink and photochemical source. To address this, we present a spatiotemporally resolved H 2 budget derived using atmospheric inversions with the TM5 chemical transport model. With this approach, we infer a global mean soil sink of 52.8 [47.8–56.7] Tg yr −1 and a photochemical source of 34.6 [29.2–38.2] Tg yr −1 over 2003–2023. Relative to Ouyang et al. (2025), we estimate a soil sink that is 45 % and 35 % weaker in the Middle East and Oceania, and 45 % and 70 % stronger in South America and Russia, respectively. Our results further suggest that variability in the observed H 2 growth rate between 2003–2023 was primarily driven by changes in the photochemical source from CH 4 oxidation, together with a declining global soil sink at a mean rate of 0.23 Tg yr −2 . Finally, we infer a sensitivity of the soil sink to the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, strongest over diffusion-limited soils in tropical South America, with increased uptake during drier El Niño conditions and reduced uptake during wetter La Niña conditions.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16125-2026.title: Physics-constrained inverse neural estimation (PINE) of NOx emission spatial patterns from TROPOMI NO2 columns over the North China Plain
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16125-2026.summary: Satellite NO 2 columns constrain where nitrogen oxides (NO x ) are emitted, but conventional inversions are costly or depend on existing emission products. We present physics-constrained inverse neural estimation (PINE), applied to NO x as PINE-NO x : a neural encoder maps Sentinel-5P/TROPOMI NO 2 columns to emissions, and a fixed, differentiable two-dimensional transport–chemistry decoder maps them back. We retrieve annual, monthly and overpass-time daily emission patterns over the North China Plain at 0.1° for 2023, with the annual total normalized to the EDGAR inventory; the observations adjust the daily relative pattern around this prior, which still sets the magnitude and large-scale structure. On 54 validation days used only to select the training epoch, the retrieved emissions raise the log-space spatial correlation between simulated and observed columns from 0.332 (EDGAR) to 0.856 (observation reconstruction, not emission accuracy). PINE-NO x places less emission than EDGAR in the strongest-emitting cells, but a synthetic test with known emissions gives a similar decrease, so this shift is primarily a structural artefact, most likely of this decoder, not an observed signal. Relative to MEIC, which the inversion does not use, 13.5 % of July emissions are placed in different 0.5° cells, against 18.5 % in the synthetic test and 20.5 % for EDGAR; January shows no clear gain. The 1 σ uncertainty of annual 0.5° emission shares is at least 17.5 % (structural error excluded), mostly from the prior inventory. In a one-month WRF-Chem simulation, the retrieved emissions bring simulated columns closer to TROPOMI but do not improve agreement with surface NO 2 stations.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16225-2026.title: Meteorological conditions and aerosol-meteorology feedback drive divergent responses of co-occurring PM2.5 and O3 pollution to NOx–VOC perturbations in Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei–Shandong
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16225-2026.summary: Co-occurring PM 2.5 and O 3 pollution (Double High Pollution, DHP) is a growing concern, yet its response to emission controls under different meteorological conditions is poorly quantified. Previous studies focused on synoptic-scale classifications or single meteorological variables, largely neglecting aerosol-meteorology feedback. This study investigated the PM 2.5 / O 3 response to NO x –VOC precursor perturbations, which jointly control O 3 and nitrate, and the impact of aerosol-meteorology feedback on PM 2.5 / O 3 response in Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei–Shandong in July 2020 using WRF-Chem. DHP occurred under warm (23–31 °C), moderately humid (45 %–80 %), and shallow boundary layer (0.5–1.1 km) conditions that were classified into five types: Convective, Stable, WarmHumid, DryHot, and Moderate based on boundary layer height, temperature and humidity. PM 2.5 was highest under Stable and WarmHumid (∼ 46 µg m −3 ) and lowest under DryHot (∼ 40 µg m −3 ); O 3 was highest under DryHot and Moderate (∼ 163 µg m −3 ) and lowest under WarmHumid (∼ 149 µg m −3 ). O 3 responded most strongly under WarmHumid and weakest under DryHot at all joint reduction levels (−25.2 % and −23.3 % at 50%/50% NO x / VOC) with stronger NO x sensitivity under WarmHumid and Convective; PM 2.5 reductions were largest under Stable and WarmHumid (−20.6 % and −20.9 %) and smallest under DryHot (−15.2 %). Aerosol-meteorology feedback enhanced PM 2.5 reduction most under Stable and WarmHumid but weakened O 3 reduction under Stable for large NO x -only cuts, driven by the most lasting PBLH increase and strong OH amplification. These results demonstrate that meteorological condition-specific strategies, particularly coordinated NO x –VOC control under stagnant and humid summer conditions, are essential for effective DHP mitigation.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16295-2026.title: Temperature-dependent evaporation emission and gas/particle partitioning drive the seasonal dynamics of primary intermediate-volatility organic compounds
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16295-2026.summary: Intermediate-volatility organic compounds (IVOCs) serve as crucial precursors to secondary organic aerosol (SOA), yet their seasonal variations remain insufficiently characterized, impeding a comprehensive understanding of their atmospheric processing and impacts on air quality. To capture the seasonal dynamics of primary IVOCs and identify the key drivers governing their variability, four-season field campaigns were conducted at an urban site in Yangtze River Delta region. The total concentration of measured IVOCs was 1228.2±132.7 ng m −3 (average ±95 % confidence interval), dominated by long-chain alkanes. A distinctive summer-maximum and winter-minimum pattern was identified for measured IVOCs, contrasting sharply with typical seasonal trends of most primarily-emitted air pollutants. This pattern was driven by enhanced temperature-dependent evaporative emissions and efficient particle-to-gas partitioning of low-volatility IVOCs during warm seasons. Petroleum-related sources were confirmed as the dominant contributors to the measured IVOCs. Positive matrix factorization (PMF) model further revealed evaporative emissions as the largest contributor (38.9 %), followed by vehicle exhaust (37.7 %), gas/particle partitioning (14.8 %), and industrial emissions (8.6 %). Our findings elucidate the critical roles of temperature-dependent emissions and gas/particle partitioning in shaping the seasonal cycle of IVOCs, and highlight the potentially expanding contribution of evaporative sources to urban IVOC loads under future climate change scenarios.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2611874123.title: Global lake synchrony signals rising planetary-scale ecological coupling
doi:10.1073/pnas.2611874123.summary: Understanding how localized ecosystem dynamics scale up to influence Earth-system stability remains a major challenge. Lakes, though covering less than 2% of Earth’s surface, play a disproportionate role in regulating global carbon, nutrient, and biodiversity dynamics, making them a critical nexus for assessing emerging large-scale environmental coupling. By integrating satellite observations with century-scale sedimentary archives from ~2,000 lakes, we reveal a marked acceleration in global lake synchrony since 2000. This synchronization, coinciding with converging climatic and socioeconomic pressures, signals a widespread erosion of the spatial heterogeneity and regional distinctiveness that historically characterized inland waters. We propose that increasing lake synchrony represents an emergent property of the Anthropocene, transforming lakes from regionally structured, asynchronous waterscapes into dynamically coupled planetary commons. By temporally aligning carbon and nutrient dynamics across broad spatial scales, this synchronization modifies the timing and amplitude of aggregate biophysical fluxes, altering how inland waters interact with larger-scale environmental cycles. Ultimately, this finding motivates a macroscale monitoring framework that jointly tracks synchrony, modularity, and their functional consequences, demanding a shift in governance toward preserving the ecological heterogeneity essential for maintaining long-term environmental stability.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2612873123.title: Impact pathways of a jurisdictional approach to slowing deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon
doi:10.1073/pnas.2612873123.summary: Governance of many of the world’s largest remaining tropical forests is shared across multiple levels of government, giving subnational jurisdictions a central role in forest management. This has motivated growing interest in jurisdictional approaches (JAs) to control deforestation. For JAs to deliver on national and international conservation priorities, those priorities must be translated into incentives that reduce deforestation at the jurisdictional level. Brazil’s Priority List (PL), launched in 2008, creates such incentives by identifying high-deforestation municipalities, subjecting them to intensified monitoring, enforcement, and credit restrictions, and establishing jurisdiction-wide criteria for exit that make municipalities accountable for deforestation within their borders. While prior studies show that the PL reduces deforestation, it remains unclear where these reductions occur and whether there is displacement across land tenure types or into neighboring municipalities. We assemble a municipality-level panel dataset for the Brazilian Legal Amazon (2000–2024) that combines PL designations with annual deforestation disaggregated by land tenure. Using a heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences estimator, we estimate effects within and across municipalities. We find large and statistically significant reductions concentrated on private lands, including agrarian reform settlements and other private properties. Within listed municipalities, we find no evidence of decreased or increased clearing in Protected Areas, Indigenous Territories, or undesignated public lands. Total deforestation also declines in neighboring municipalities, with reductions concentrated on private lands. These findings are consistent with the PL translating national conservation priorities into local land-use change while limiting displacement, offering insights for the design of jurisdictional approaches aimed at forest conservation.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2615294123.title: A decadal record of isotopic trends in martian atmospheric CO 2
doi:10.1073/pnas.2615294123.summary: This work represents the first long-term record of the isotopic composition of martian atmospheric CO 2 , acquired in situ by the Curiosity rover at Gale crater during Mars Years (MY) 31–38 (2012–2025). Measurement campaigns were designed to investigate possibilities of both diurnal and seasonal effects on CO 2 isotopes. Coordinated pairs of analyses during MY 31 and 38 revealed no significant differences in isotopic composition of CO 2 acquired during daytime and nighttime hours. However, here we show evidence for modest enrichment in heavy isotopes of oxygen in both northern and southern hemisphere spring-summer seasons. We assessed several processes, including precipitation/sublimation and adsorption/desorption of CO 2 , CO 2 photolysis, and oxygen isotope exchange as potential candidates for producing the observed fractionations. We find that while sublimation of CO 2 from polar caps, sublimation and desorption of CO 2 from lower latitude reservoirs, and CO 2 photolysis are insufficient alone, we can reproduce the measured enrichment through modeling of isotope exchange between CO 2 and 18 O-enriched H 2 O in thin liquid-like films at Mars’ surface or adsorbed within the regolith as Mars approaches and transits through perihelion. Lesser 18 O enrichment near aphelion may reflect less favorable conditions for oxygen isotope exchange at lower temperatures. Observed seasonal variations in CO 2 carbon isotopic composition are less pronounced, consistent with less carbon isotope exchange with surface reservoirs than seen for oxygen. Since our measurements were obtained at a single near-equatorial location on Mars, the relative contributions from global, regional, and local processes cannot be well-constrained by the available data.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2620213123.title: A hybrid ultrafast phase transition in a chemically complex alloy under extreme conditions
doi:10.1073/pnas.2620213123.summary: The face-centered cubic to hexagonal close-packed (FCC–HCP) phase transition is ubiquitous in static high-pressure experiments of conventional FCC metals and alloys, yet its conspicuous absence under laser shock compression (LSC) has remained a puzzle. Here we show that this transition can be realized and directly observed in the prototypical CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy under LSC at pressures exceeding ~114 GPa and Hugoniot temperatures above ~1,800 K. Time-resolved X-ray diffraction reveals that the transformation occurs on a timescale at least as fast as 1 to 2 ns, orders of magnitude faster than diffusion-controlled nucleation-growth processes, yet reversible upon pressure release, unlike classical FCC–HCP martensitic transformations. We hypothesize that the high Hugoniot temperature may provide the atomic mobility for reversibility, while the extreme deviatoric stress likely promotes rapid, displacive atomic motion. This fusion of athermal speed and thermal reversibility is difficult to classify within the classical dichotomy of phase transitions as either purely martensitic or purely thermally activated and may represent a class of stress-assisted, thermally reversible transformation accessible only under extreme pressure–temperature ( P-T ) conditions. First-principles Gibbs free-energy calculations show that the HCP phase is thermodynamically favored at low temperature over the pressure range 50 to 142 GPa, and that the computed FCC–HCP phase boundary places the laser-shock P-T state on the HCP-stable side, making it accessible to the transient LSC path. Our findings are consistent with chemical complexity acting as a powerful parameter for controlling phase transformation pathways under extreme P-T conditions, and reveal a distinct class of ultrafast, reversible transformations.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2525610123.title: Vessel noise pollution offsets marine mammal energy budgets
doi:10.1073/pnas.2525610123.summary: Shipping is a major global source of underwater noise pollution and is frequently reported to alter the behavior of marine mammals. However, the energetic consequences of these noise-induced behavioral disruptions and their implications for population fitness remain poorly quantified. Using behavioral proxies of energy acquisition and expenditure derived from high-resolution sound and movement tags on 28 wild harbor porpoises, we estimate that porpoises decrease energy acquisition by 20% (range: 1 to 36%) during high-noise vessel exposures, while maintaining constant energy expenditure. With a median of 11 high-noise vessel exposures per day, these disruptions may result in an average daily shortfall of 4.6% of their net energy budget. Sustained over time, such noise-induced energetic deficits have the potential to compromise individual fitness, ultimately affecting the dynamics of harbor porpoise populations in industrialized coastal areas worldwide and reducing their functional carrying capacity. This framework establishes a direct mechanistic link between behavioral disruption and fitness-relevant impacts, providing a biologically grounded metric for predicting population-level outcomes of noise pollution and an objective basis for defining acceptable exposure levels of vessel noise for wild marine mammal populations. Moreover, it is scalable across species and ecosystems and offers a common currency for assessing the cumulative effects of multiple stressors in the Anthropocene oceans. As vessel traffic and its associated noise outputs continue to increase globally, our results offer timely insights for evidence-based management, and support efforts to balance the societal demand for low-cost maritime transport with the responsibility to ensure the sustainable use and conservation of marine biodiversity.

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-.title: How does ocean carbon sequestration change under different glacial conditions?
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-.summary: Over the past 800,000 years, Earth's history has been marked by dramatic shifts in climate, swinging from warm periods to cold, when large ice sheets covered much of the Northern Hemisphere and sea ice greatly expanded. The transition between the two climates is paced by the Earth's orbit with respect to the sun, but changes in the amount of carbon dioxide (CO2), a greenhouse gas, also affect global temperatures. By understanding how CO2 is exchanged between the atmosphere and the ocean, scientists hope to apply that knowledge to future climate scenarios. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-small-.title: Small life, big job: Enlisting microbes to fight climate change
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-small-.summary: A working quarry isn't a pretty sight. Dust and bare rock, deep cuts into a hillside that appear like steps made for a giant. Nothing grows here, or so you would assume. Earth Sciences

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-prehis.title: Prehistoric ecosystems could hold clues to preventing future wildfires
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-prehis.summary: Could bringing back large herbivores help preserve Europe's rural landscapes and reduce wildfire risk? This is one of the key questions explored by an international study involving the University of Zaragoza, recently published in the journal Ecosystem Services. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sea-is.title: Watch: Sea level rise isn't just waves—how groundwater threatens coastal cities from below
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sea-is.summary: With El Niño winter storms rolling in, coastal communities will naturally brace for the obvious: surging high tides, pounding waves and seawater spilling over seawalls. Decades of storm coverage have encouraged us to measure climate risk by what crashes onto the shoreline. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-indone.title: Indonesia may need 350 years to recover land burned in 2026 wildfires
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-indone.summary: Throughout most of 2026, fires have been burning across Indonesia, from savannas on Papua Island to peatlands on Sumatra and Borneo. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-climat.title: Climate change can worsen income inequality
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-climat.summary: A study published in Sustainable Development that analyzed the relationship between climate change and income inequality for 23 emerging market economies from 2002 to 2022 found that greater climate pressure is positively associated with income inequality across three different inequality indicators (the Gini coefficient, the Palma ratio and the Theil index). Per capita income and institutional quality were negatively associated with inequality, whereas unemployment was positively associated with it. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-atlas-.title: An atlas of vanished places: How climate change is rewriting the books on our shelves
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-atlas-.summary: On Aug. 26, 2026, a huge mass of rock and ice broke away at an altitude of around 5,200 meters (17,100 feet) in the Himalayas. Within minutes, it became an avalanche of debris and water that hurtled down toward the Nepal-Tibet border, with such force that the seismic signals were initially mistaken for an earthquake. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cop31-.title: COP31: How to make carbon markets more effective
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cop31-.summary: At the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, a key question for negotiators is how to get more money to developing countries so they can adapt to a warming world. For the past 30 years, climate talks focused on cutting greenhouse gas emissions and preventing future global warming. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-stay-t.title: How much CO₂ will stay? New study estimates long-term residual emissions under the EU Emissions Trading System
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-stay-t.summary: Current CO₂ emissions covered by the EU Emissions Trading System (EU-ETS1) could be substantially reduced by 2040. A new study by the Oeko-Institut, commissioned by Carbon Market Watch, examines the level of emissions that could remain in 2040 and 2050. In 2040, installations covered by the EU-ETS1—including waste incineration—could still emit between 159 and 231 million metric tons of CO₂. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-rapid-.title: Rapid-scan satellite data offer clues to typhoon intensity
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-rapid-.summary: Between 1970 and 2019, tropical cyclones killed nearly 780,000 people worldwide and caused approximately $1.4 trillion in economic losses. As coastal populations continue to grow and climate continues to change, accurate forecasting is essential for saving lives and reducing economic damage. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-large-.title: Large companies can still fall short on their climate commitments. Here's what must change
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-large-.summary: International climate conferences like the COP31 climate summit, now in its second week, tend to focus on the role of individual countries. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-lava-c.title: Lava flows studied for their carbon dioxide storage potential
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-lava-c.summary: As global warming intensifies, scientists are exploring ways to reduce carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions. One emerging approach being explored in environmental research is carbon capture and storage (CCS), which involves capturing CO₂ and storing it deep underground, away from the atmosphere. In this context, researchers at the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar (IITGN) have investigated ancient volcanic rocks in Maharashtra to assess their suitability for this purpose. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-carbon.title: The carbon bubble question: How much are fossil-fuel companies really at risk?
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-carbon.summary: The global shift toward cleaner energy raises a difficult financial question: Are fossil-fuel companies worth more than they should be because investors have not fully accounted for the risks of climate change and stronger climate policies? Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cookin.title: Cooking Thanksgiving dinner could create an indoor air quality problem inside your home, expert says
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-cookin.summary: The Thanksgiving turkey may be the centerpiece of the holiday meal, but cooking it, along with all the sides and other dishes, can invite an unexpected guest: indoor air pollution. Environment

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-scient.title: Scientists take global fight against pharmaceutical pollution to landmark UN summit
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-scient.summary: Researchers from the University of York will urge global action to tackle the growing threat of pharmaceuticals contaminating rivers and seas at a major United Nations conference in Geneva. Environment

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: This remarkable new material could solve a major carbon capture problem
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists have developed a new carbon capture material that turns moisture from an obstacle into an advantage, potentially solving a major problem with removing CO2 from industrial emissions. The material works even in extremely humid conditions and can be reused repeatedly, offering a promising path toward cheaper, more effective carbon capture.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists discover a mysterious silicone pollutant that may be everywhere
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Researchers have uncovered unexpectedly high levels of silicone-based pollutants called methylsiloxanes floating through the atmosphere across cities, rural regions, and even forests. Much of the pollution appears to come from vehicle emissions, likely linked to engine oil additives that survive combustion and escape into the air. Scientists say humans may inhale more of these compounds daily than other notorious pollutants like PFAS or microplastics.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists say this algae could remove microplastics from drinking water
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Researchers created a special kind of algae that can grab microscopic plastic pollution out of water almost like a magnet. The algae produce limonene, an orange-scented oil that helps them bind to water-repelling microplastics, forming easy-to-remove clumps. As a bonus, the algae also clean wastewater while growing.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists just found where airborne microplastics really come from
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Microplastics are floating through the atmosphere and spreading across the globe, but their true origins have been misunderstood. New research shows land sources emit over 20 times more microplastic particles into the air than the ocean, challenging earlier beliefs. Scientists also discovered that previous models dramatically overestimated how much plastic is in the atmosphere.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: MIT scientists just found a hidden problem slowing the ozone comeback
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: The ozone layer has been on track to recover thanks to the Montreal Protocol—but a loophole may be holding it back. Chemicals still permitted for industrial use are leaking into the atmosphere at higher rates than expected. Scientists now estimate this could delay ozone recovery by up to seven years. Closing this gap could speed up healing and reduce harmful UV exposure worldwide.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Unusual airborne toxin detected in the U.S. for the first time
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists searching for air pollution clues stumbled onto something unexpected: toxic MCCPs drifting through the air for the first time in the Western Hemisphere. The likely source—fertilizer made from sewage sludge—points to a hidden route for contamination.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists shocked to find lab gloves may be skewing microplastics data
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists may have been unknowingly inflating microplastics pollution estimates, and the surprising source could be their own lab gloves. A University of Michigan study found that common nitrile and latex gloves release tiny particles called stearates, which closely resemble microplastics and can contaminate samples during testing. In some cases, this led to wildly exaggerated results, forcing researchers to track down the unexpected culprit.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Microplastics are falling from the sky and polluting forests
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Tiny plastic particles aren’t just choking oceans and cities—they’re quietly infiltrating forests too. Scientists discovered that most microplastics arrive through the air, settling onto treetops before being washed or dropped to the forest floor in rain and falling leaves. Once there, natural processes like leaf decay help bury and store these particles deep in the soil. The findings reveal forests as hidden reservoirs of airborne pollution—and potentially a new frontline in the growing microplastics crisis.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: A massive freshwater reservoir is hiding under the Great Salt Lake
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: A hidden freshwater system deep beneath the Great Salt Lake has been revealed using airborne electromagnetic surveys. Scientists found that freshwater extends much farther under the lake than expected, reaching depths of up to 4 kilometers. The discovery began with mysterious reed-covered mounds formed by pressurized groundwater pushing upward. Researchers are now investigating whether this underground water could help control hazardous dust from the drying lakebed.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: An invisible chemical rain is falling across the planet
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: A new study reveals that chemicals used to replace ozone-damaging CFCs are now driving a surge in a persistent “forever chemical” worldwide. The pollutant, called trifluoroacetic acid, is falling out of the atmosphere into water, land, and ice, including in remote regions like the Arctic. Even as older chemicals are phased out, their long lifetimes mean pollution is still rising.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: A shocking amount of plastic is floating in city air
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Plastic pollution is not just in oceans and soil. Scientists have now found enormous amounts of microscopic plastic floating through urban air, far exceeding earlier estimates. Road dust and rainfall play a major role in moving these particles through the atmosphere. The findings suggest the air may be one of the most important pathways for plastic pollution.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists found a dangerous feedback loop accelerating Arctic warming
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: The Arctic is changing rapidly, and scientists have uncovered a powerful mix of natural and human-driven processes fueling that change. Cracks in sea ice release heat and pollutants that form clouds and speed up melting, while emissions from nearby oil fields alter the chemistry of the air. These interactions trigger feedback loops that let in more sunlight, generate smog, and push warming even further. Together, they paint a troubling picture of how fragile the Arctic system has become.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Microplastics are leaking invisible chemical clouds into water
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Microplastics in rivers, lakes, and oceans aren’t just drifting debris—they’re constantly leaking invisible clouds of chemicals into the water. New research shows that sunlight drives this process, causing different plastics to release distinct and evolving mixtures of dissolved organic compounds as they weather. These chemical plumes are surprisingly complex, often richer and more biologically active than natural organic matter, and include additives, broken polymer fragments, and oxidized molecules.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: New data reveals one of the smallest ozone holes in decades
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: This year’s ozone hole over Antarctica ranked among the smallest since the early 1990s, reflecting steady progress from decades of global action under the Montreal Protocol. Declining chlorine levels and warmer stratospheric temperatures helped limit ozone destruction. Scientists say the layer remains on track to recover later this century.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Polluted air quietly erases the benefits of exercise
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Long-term inhalation of toxic air appears to dull the protective power of regular workouts, according to a massive global study spanning more than a decade and over a million adults. While exercise still helps people live longer, its benefits shrink dramatically in regions with heavy fine particle pollution—especially above key PM2.5 thresholds common in many parts of the world. The researchers emphasize that outdoor activity shouldn’t stop, but better air quality could unlock far greater health gains.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: A global shipping detour just revealed a hidden climate twist
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Rerouted shipping during Red Sea conflicts accidentally created a massive real-world experiment, letting scientists study how new low-sulfur marine fuels affect cloud formation. The sudden surge of ships around the Cape of Good Hope revealed that cleaner fuels dramatically weaken the ability of ship emissions to seed bright, reflective clouds—cutting this cloud-boosting effect by about two-thirds.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: This glowing particle in a laser trap may reveal how lightning begins
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Using a precisely aligned pair of laser beams, scientists can now hold a single aerosol particle in place and monitor how it charges up. The particle’s glow signals each step in its changing electrical state, revealing how electrons are kicked away and how the particle sometimes releases sudden bursts of charge. These behaviors mirror what may be happening inside storm clouds. The technique could help explain how lightning gets its initial spark.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: New report reveals major risks in turning oceans into carbon sinks
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Experts say the ocean could help absorb carbon dioxide, but today’s technologies are too uncertain to be scaled up safely. New findings released during COP30 highlight the risks of rushing into marine carbon removal without proper monitoring and verification. With the 1.5°C threshold approaching, researchers stress that emissions cuts must remain the top priority. Ocean-based methods may play a role later, but they need careful oversight first.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Your pumpkin might be hiding a toxic secret
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Researchers in Japan have revealed how some gourds draw pollutants into their fruits. The secret lies in a protein that carries contaminants through the plant sap. By manipulating this protein’s structure, scientists hope to breed crops that resist contamination or serve as natural soil purifiers. This finding bridges food safety and environmental cleanup.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists say dimming the sun could spark global chaos
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists are taking the once-radical concept of dimming the sun through stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) seriously, but a Columbia University team warns that reality is far messier than models suggest. Their study reveals how physical, geopolitical, and economic constraints could derail even the best-intentioned attempts to cool the planet. From unpredictable monsoon disruptions to material shortages and optical inefficiencies, every step introduces new risks.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: A clue to ancient life? What scientists found inside Mars’ frozen vortex
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Mars’ north polar vortex locks its atmosphere in extreme cold and darkness, freezing out water vapor and triggering a dramatic rise in ozone. Scientists found that the lack of sunlight and moisture lets ozone build up unchecked. This discovery, made with data from ESA’s and NASA’s orbiters, could reveal clues about Mars’ past atmospheric chemistry and potential for life.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Ocean heatwaves are breaking Earth’s hidden climate engine
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Marine heatwaves can jam the ocean’s natural carbon conveyor belt, preventing carbon from reaching the deep sea. Researchers studying two major heatwaves in the Gulf of Alaska found that plankton shifts caused carbon to build up near the surface instead of sinking. This disrupted the ocean’s ability to store carbon for millennia and intensified climate feedbacks. The study highlights the urgent need for continuous, collaborative ocean observation.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists made plastic that eats carbon
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: A team of chemists has discovered how to transform PET plastic waste into BAETA, a material that captures CO2 with remarkable efficiency. Instead of ending up as microplastics in the environment, discarded bottles and textiles could become tools to combat climate change. The method is energy-friendly, scalable, and potentially lucrative, offering industries both sustainability and practicality.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Rapid rocket growth raises alarm over Earth’s fragile ozone layer
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: The booming space industry has filled the skies with rockets and satellites, but this rapid expansion comes with a hidden danger: slowing the recovery of the ozone layer. Rocket launches and burning space debris release chlorine, soot, and metals high in the atmosphere, where they linger for years, damaging Earth’s protective shield against UV radiation. Scientists warn that if annual launches surge to projected levels by 2030, ozone recovery—already not expected until mid-century—could be delayed for decades.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Ozone recovery could trigger 40% more global warming than predicted
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: As the ozone layer recovers, it’s also intensifying global warming. Researchers predict that by 2050, ozone will rank just behind carbon dioxide as a driver of heating, offsetting many of the benefits from banning CFCs.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Protected seas help kelp forests bounce back from heatwaves
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Kelp forests bounce back faster from marine heatwaves when shielded inside Marine Protected Areas. UCLA researchers found that fishing restrictions and predator protection strengthen ecosystem resilience, though results vary by location.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: The surprising way rising CO2 could supercharge space storms
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Rising CO₂ levels will make the upper atmosphere colder and thinner, altering how geomagnetic storms impact satellites. Future storms could cause sharper density spikes despite lower overall density, increasing drag-related challenges.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists discover the strange way CO2 cools part of Earth’s atmosphere
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists have finally cracked the mystery behind one of climate change’s strangest fingerprints: while Earth’s surface heats up, the upper atmosphere is rapidly cooling. Researchers at Columbia University discovered that carbon dioxide acts very differently high above the planet, where it actually helps radiate heat into space instead of trapping it. The team found that certain infrared wavelengths fall into a “Goldilocks zone” that becomes increasingly effective as CO2 levels rise, accelerating cooling in the stratosphere.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists stunned as volcano cloud destroys methane in the atmosphere
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: A colossal underwater volcano in the South Pacific may have revealed a surprising new weapon against climate change. After the 2022 eruption of Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha’apai, scientists detected enormous amounts of formaldehyde in the atmosphere — a telltale sign that methane, one of the planet’s most powerful greenhouse gases, was being destroyed. Researchers now believe volcanic ash mixed with salty seawater and sunlight created reactive chlorine particles that effectively “cleaned up” some of the methane released by the eruption itself.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists develop dirt-powered fuel cell that could replace batteries
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists have developed a fuel cell that uses microbes in soil to produce electricity. The device can power underground sensors for tasks like monitoring moisture or detecting touch, without needing batteries or solar panels. It works in both dry and wet conditions and even lasts longer than similar technologies. This could pave the way for sustainable, low-maintenance sensors in farming and environmental monitoring.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Scientists solve 12,800-year-old climate mystery hidden in Greenland ice
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: A mysterious spike of platinum buried deep in Greenland’s ice has long fueled theories of a catastrophic comet or asteroid strike 12,800 years ago—possibly triggering a sudden return to icy conditions known as the Younger Dryas. But new research points to a far less dramatic, yet still powerful culprit: volcanic eruptions. Scientists found the platinum signal doesn’t match space debris and actually appeared decades after the cooling began, ruling out an impact as the trigger.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Congo basin blackwater lakes are releasing ancient carbon into the atmosphere
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Deep in the Congo Basin, vast peatlands quietly store enormous amounts of Earth’s carbon — but new research suggests this ancient vault may be leaking. Scientists studying Africa’s largest blackwater lakes discovered that significant amounts of carbon dioxide bubbling into the atmosphere come not just from recent plant life, but from peat that has been locked away for thousands of years.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: A simple water shift could turn Arctic farmland into a carbon sink
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Deep in the Arctic north, drained peatlands—once massive carbon vaults built over thousands of years—are quietly leaking greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. But new field research from northern Norway suggests there’s a powerful way to slow that loss: raise the water level. In a two-year study, scientists found that restoring higher groundwater levels in cultivated Arctic peatlands dramatically cut carbon dioxide emissions, and in some cases even tipped the balance so the land absorbed more CO₂ than it released.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: New catalyst turns carbon dioxide into clean fuel source
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Researchers have found that manganese, an abundant and inexpensive metal, can be used to efficiently convert carbon dioxide into formate, a potential hydrogen source for fuel cells. The key was a clever redesign that made the catalyst last far longer than similar low-cost materials. Surprisingly, the improved manganese catalyst even beat many expensive precious-metal options. The discovery could help turn greenhouse gas into clean energy ingredients.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: A breakthrough that turns exhaust CO2 into useful materials
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Scientists have created a device that captures carbon dioxide and transforms it into a useful chemical in a single step. The new electrode works with realistic exhaust gases rather than requiring purified CO2. It converts the captured gas into formic acid, which is used in energy and manufacturing. The system even functions at CO2 levels found in normal air.

url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.title: Microplastics are undermining the ocean’s power to absorb carbon
url:https://www.sciencedaily.com/release.summary: Tiny plastic particles drifting through the oceans may be quietly weakening one of Earth’s most powerful climate defenses. New research suggests microplastics are disrupting marine life that helps oceans absorb carbon dioxide, while also releasing greenhouse gases as they break down. By interfering with plankton, microbes, and natural carbon cycles, these pollutants reduce the ocean’s ability to regulate global temperatures.

url:https://www.scientificamerican.com/a.title: How bad would SpaceX’s million AI satellites be for Earth’s atmosphere?
url:https://www.scientificamerican.com/a.summary: A new study estimates that the company’s plans to launch a million orbital data centers could increase Earth’s upper atmospheric pollution by more than a 100-fold
