url:https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-b.title: How Voyager 1 became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day
url:https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-b.summary: As of November 18, 2026, if you send a signal out at the speed of light in the direction of Voyager 1 — humanity’s most distant spacecraft — it will now take more than a full day for that signal to arrive . At that impressive distance, more than three times the distance to Pluto, over 16 billion miles, and over 25.9 billion kilometers away, the Sun appears 30,000 times fainter than it does from Earth. (That’s still brighter than the full Moon, but only by a factor of 14, or under three astronomical magnitudes.) It’s moving away from the Sun at a current speed of 60,770 km/hr (37,760 mph), and has reached that one light-day milestone after a cumulative journey of 49 years and 72 days. In all the years since 1977, we’ve never launched another spacecraft that has rivaled Voyager 1. No other spacecraft has traveled as far; no other spacecraft is leaving the Solar System with as rapid a velocity; no current or even planned spacecraft is on track to ever overtake it. Voyager 1, the first spacecraft to exit the Solar System, is still the most distant, and looks to remain so for the foreseeable future. There’s a remarkable story behind this mission and how it achieved its record-breaking properties, and there’s an equally interesting story behind how we could someday catch or even surpass Voyager 1: if only we invested in doing so. This image shows Voyager 1 lifting off aboard the Titan III/Centaur rocket on September 5, 1977: joining its sister spacecraft, Voyager 2, which was launched 16 days prior. Voyager 1 was not the fastest spacecraft upon launch, but now on a trajectory out of the Solar System, has become the fastest-moving spacecraft away from the Sun: showcasing that initial speed is not everything when it comes to how far a craft can ultimately make it into the Universe. Credit : NASA Anytime you want to send anything to any place in space, you have two options for how to get it there once you launch it above Earth’s atmosphere. The first option is to use some sort of engine — something that provides thrust, like rocket fuel — to propel your spacecraft to the needed speed in the proper direction, i.e., with the right trajectory, to get there. The second option is to take advantage of the natural gravity of other objects that you’ll encounter, such as planets that orbit the Sun or moons that orbit planets, in order to provide an “assist” to your spacecraft. This gravity assist maneuver can, depending on how it’s leveraged, provide either an increase or a decrease in speed, and can also alter your trajectory significantly in the process. Of course, it’s possible to combine these two effects as well, in what’s known as either a powered flyby or the Oberth effect , to either gain or lose even more speed than using thrusters and gravity assists separately. When an object has a gravitational encounter with a planet within our Solar System, from the planet’s perspective, the object comes in and goes out in a speed-conserving interaction. However, since the planet is in motion relative to the Sun, its gravitational influence redirects the spacecraft in such a way that the planet’s motion, depending on whether it’s “with” or “against” the spacecraft’s relative motion, can either boost or de-boost the spacecraft relative to the Sun. This type of maneuver is known as a gravity assist. Credit : David Shortt, Rachelz9999/Wikimedia Commons In the case of Voyager 1, it was launched on September 5, 1977, with an initial speed of around 40 km/s: the equivalent of 89,500 miles-per-hour or 144,000 km/hr. Interestingly, that launch date and launch speed were both later and slower than its twin: Voyager 2. However, they were designed for different purposes. Voyager 2 was planned to fly by Jupiter and Saturn in a way that could potentially take it to Uranus and Neptune afterward (performing a “grand tour” of the Solar System), while Voyager 1 was designed to fly by Jupiter, Saturn, and then to get a choice between heading all the way out to Pluto or to fly close to Saturn’s giant moon Titan. Because of these differences, different initial speeds and trajectories were required for each of the Voyagers. Although Voyager 2 launched first and started out faster, it was passed by Voyager 1 on December 19th of 1977, as Voyager 1 headed on a more direct course toward Jupiter. On March 5, 1979, it arrived: Voyager 1 made a close approach of Jupiter , coming within 279,000 km of the edge of Jupiter’s atmosphere. It also flew by its moons Amalthea, Io (at a distance of just 20,570 km), Europa, and on March 6, by Ganymede and Callisto as well. Its views of Io, Ganymede, and Callisto, plus Jupiter, were the highest-resolution photos of those worlds ever taken. Its approach video to Jupiter remains one of the most iconic sequences in space history. This animation sequence shows Voyager 1’s approach of Jupiter in March of 1979. Its swirling winds, moving bands, and hurricane-like storm raging in its Great Red Spot were all revealed in detail that had never been seen before. During Voyager 1’s 1979 flyby encounter with Jupiter, a brief “point” of light was seen on Jupiter’s surface, representing the first observed bolide event in Jupiter’s atmosphere. Credit : NASA/JPL/Voyager 1 Another big surprise was the discovery of active volcanic activity on Io: now known to be the most volcanically active world in the Solar System. As Jupiter’s tidal forces continuously open cracks in Io’s crust and trigger massive volcanic eruptions, the entire world gets resurfaced on timescales of mere thousands of years, giving it the youngest surface in the entire Solar System. Io is the innermost of Jupiter’s four major Galilean moons, with the closest, tightest orbit around Jupiter of them all. Voyager 1 actually flew interior to Io’s orbit, passing just behind it mere hours after departing from its closest approach to Jupiter. However, there was another purpose to flying so close to Jupiter on the specific trajectory that was chosen: to boost Voyager 1’s speed and alter its trajectory to send it on to Saturn. When choosing how to direct the spacecraft, the decision was made to go after an extremely close approach to Saturn’s Titan, rather than to go on an extended mission to Pluto. The reason was scientifically motivated: because Titan was known to have an atmosphere, and a substantial one at that. Therefore, the thinking was, more science value could be extracted by flying by Titan than by eschewing that to go after Pluto. As a result of the close flyby to Jupiter, Voyager 1’s speed — which had dropped down to 13 km/s owing to the gravitational pull of the Sun as it sped away from it — shot back up to 23 km/s after receiving a near-maximal gravity assist. This animation shows the trajectory of Voyager 1, launched in 1977, as it received a gravity assist from Jupiter during its flyby and then another one from Saturn (and Titan) when it encountered that planet and its lunar system. Those two gravitational interactions boosted Voyager 1 to the highest escape speed of any human-made object ever, and after overtaking Pioneer 10 in 1998, it has remained our most distant spacecraft ever since. Credit : Phoenix7777/Wikimedia Commons A year and a half later, In November of 1980, Voyager 1 arrived at Saturn: double the distance from the Sun compared to Jupiter. Although its speed had slowed down to about 20 km/s owing to the continued, energy-draining climb out of the Sun’s gravitational potential well, it managed to pass incredibly close to Titan: passing within just 3915 km of its surface. Although the surface remained obscure, it was able to study Titan’s nitrogen-rich atmosphere along with the cloudy methane hazes present within it, paving the way for the later Cassini-Huygens mission . (Carolyn Porco, who became the Principal Investigator of Cassini-Huygens, was a Voyager imaging scientist prior to that.) From November 12 through November 14, 1980, Voyager 1 also experienced close flybys of Saturn’s moons Tethys, Mimas, Enceladus, Rhea, and Hyperion, and came within 125,000 km of the edge of Saturn’s atmosphere. After experiencing a gravity assist from the Saturnian system by traveling extremely close to Titan and below Saturn’s south pole, it received both a speed boost and a trajectory change: boosting it back up to almost 22 km/s but taking it far out of the plane of the ecliptic. Because of this, it was unable to travel to other worlds within the Solar System, but the high-priority observations of Titan meant that the later-arriving Voyager 2 would be free to do exactly that. Voyager 2’s grand tour of the Solar System, which included visits to Uranus and Neptune, remain our most informative photos of both the Uranian and Neptunian systems even more than a quarter of the way through the 21st century. After receiving gravity assists from the Jovian and Saturnian systems in 1979 and 1980, respectively, Voyager 1’s encounter with Saturn and Titan gave it a speed boost but also a redirect: knocking it onto a trajectory 35 degrees above the ecliptic plane of our Solar System. From its perspective in 1990, it created a now-iconic Family Portrait of our Solar System, and continues to follow that same trajectory while being gradually slowed down by the Sun’s gravity. Credit : Joe Haythornthwaite and Tom Ruen/Wikimedia Commons Voyager 1’s boosted speed and new trajectory out of the ecliptic plane set it up for another set of amazing milestones, which it experienced as part of its still-ongoing extended mission. As it rises above the ecliptic plane at approximately a 35 degree angle, it heads, from our perspective, toward the constellation of Ophiuchus . From above the Solar System’s planets, it has the opportunity to look “down” on the planets orbiting the Sun, and to image them from a perspective that could never be acquired from within the Solar System’s plane itself. In 1984, Voyager 1 crossed the orbit of Uranus: achieving an in-plane distance that exceeded the distance from the Sun to our Solar System’s 7th planet. In late 1988, it crossed outside the orbit of Neptune as well. That led to, in 1990, an interesting idea: Voyager 1, from its unique perch, could image each of the planets in the Solar System, one after the other, creating an iconic “family portrait” from an unprecedented perspective. Although Mercury was too dim and too close to the Sun to be imaged as part of it, and Mars was undetectable in the camera’s optics, the Voyager 1 images of Neptune, Uranus, Saturn, Jupiter, Earth, and Venus remain iconic. That view of Earth — the last picture of our home taken by Voyager 1 before its imaging camera was switched off — was immortalized as the Pale Blue Dot . The gray panels show data taken by Voyager 1’s imaging camera in early 1990, in its last scientific set of observations before switching off. It attempted to image all of the Solar System’s eight major planets, succeeding for six of them: Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. The image of Earth, famously, was acquired on February 14, 1990, and is known as the iconic “Pale Blue Dot” image. Credit : NASA/JPL-Caltech As Voyager 1 continued to recede from the Sun, its speed continued to gradually fall, yet remained higher than all other spacecraft at a comparable distance from the Sun. (Interestingly, if Voyager 2 had visited only Uranus and had skipped Neptune, it would have wound up going faster than Voyager 1.) As various milestones were reached, its speed gradually dropped even as its distance continued to increase, and to increase faster than all other spacecraft on their way out of the Solar System. On February 17, 1998, Voyager 1 overtook Pioneer 10 — launched 5 years earlier than Voyager 1 back in 1972 — as the most distant spacecraft. It continues to extend its distance record over Pioneer 10’s reach as time goes on: by more than 150,000,000 km per year. On December 17, 2004, at a distance of 94 AU from the Sun (where 1 AU is the Earth-Sun distance), it passed the termination shock of our Solar System, entering the heliosheath region. On December 13, 2010, Voyager 1 confirmed the lack of detection of the outward flow of solar wind particles from the Sun, thought to arise when the solar wind encounters the interstellar wind that pushes against the heliosphere, turning solar wind particles sideways. The solar wind flux dropped to zero back in June of 2010, but the Low Energy Charged Particle device provided confirmation of this fact six months afterward. And on August 25, 2012, at a distance of 121 AU, it crossed over the boundary of the heliopause : officially becoming humanity’s first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. (Voyager 2 did it afterward in 2018, and later, in 2023, overtook Pioneer 10 for second place in distance from the Sun.) In July and August of 2012, abrupt changes began to be detected by Voyager 1 in low-energy ions from inside the heliosphere (top, purple) and cosmic rays from outside the Solar System (bottom, blue), with the flux of low energy ions from the Sun dropping all the way down to zero in late August of 2012. That correlates with when Voyager 1 can officially be said to have departed from the Solar System: at a distance of 121 AU. Credit : NASA/JPL-Caltech/GSFC Over all that time, its velocity away from the Sun continued to drop: down to a current value 16.88 km/s as of November 18, 2026. It won’t decrease much more than that; at its current distance of 1 light-day, the gravitational influence of the Sun is extremely small. Overall, the Sun will “steal” about another 1000 km/hr (620 mph) of recession speed from Voyager 1, meaning that it will wind up slowing down to a recession speed of 16.6 km/s and then will remain there. This is well above the Sun’s escape velocity at the distance of Voyager 1 (which is only 3.2 km/s), and so the final stage of its voyage — to the stars — has already commenced. Voyager 2, Pioneer 10, Pioneer 11, Ulysseys, and New Horizons are the only other spacecraft ever launched by humans that will also escape (or have escaped) from the Solar System’s pull, and the gravitational influence of the Sun. New Horizons was launched most recently, in 2006, but despite its greater initial launch velocity, it only ever received a meaningful gravity assist from Jupiter, and as of today , is only receding from the Sun at 13.6 km/s: not enough to ever catch or surpass Voyager 1. Ulysses was a Sun-observing spacecraft never intended to exit the Solar System, but a gravitational encounter with Jupiter in 2098 will put it on an escape course as well. All five of these spacecraft are already behind Voyager 1 in terms of distance, and Voyager 1 will continue to put more distance between them far into the future as well. This graph shows the change in speed and distance of the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft as a function of the year since their 1977 launch. Various spikes in the data correspond to gravity assists and close planetary encounters. For two intervals of time, immediately following its launch and after its encounter with Uranus but before its encounter with Neptune, Voyager 2 briefly moved faster away from the Sun than Voyager 1. Voyager 1, however, is now and, for the foreseeable future, the most distant human-made spacecraft from the Sun. Credit : Phoenix7777/Wikimedia Commons; Data: HORIZONS System, JPL, NASA It will take a little under 18,000 years for Voyager 1 to reach a further milestone of 1 light-year from Earth: something that should happen around the 199th century. After approximately 75,000 years, it will be more distant from the Sun than the next-nearest star presently is, although the positions of the stars will change substantially over tens of thousands of years, too. Although Voyager 1 doesn’t have enough power or fuel on board to be redirected to eventually encounter a star, that remains a possibility for New Horizons , albeit one that’s not favored by the current science team. Even without the development of new space travel technologies, however, the “alignment” that enabled the historic Voyager missions to take place was rare, but not unique. A combination of: a high launch velocity, the proper alignment of the planets and planned gravity assists, and the implementation of Oberth maneuvers, as appropriate, could lead to several profound advances. A planetary alignment occurring in 2034 could enable a spacecraft that was properly designed, like the Origins, Dynamics, and Interiors of the Neptunian and Uranian Systems (ODINUS) mission, to reach Uranus in 2047 and Neptune in 2050, leaving orbiters at both of them. A new close-up view of the outer worlds of our Solar System remains plausible, with new windows opening up roughly every 12 years with alignments between Earth, Jupiter, Uranus, and Neptune. This graph shows the trajectory and distance of Voyager 1, the most distant and fastest-departing spacecraft from the Solar System, compared to the distances to several of the closest stars, or stars that will become quite close in the near future. Proxima Centauri is presently 4.24 light-years away, but will come within 3 light-years roughly 20,000 years from now. Voyager 1, on the other hand, will reach a distance of 1 light-year after just under another 18,000 years. About 26,000 years from now, Voyager 1 will become closer to Proxima Centauri than it is to our Sun. Credit : SternFuchs/Wikimedia Commons If the goal was instead to leave the Solar System at maximum speed, there are several options for going much faster than Voyager 1 went at. A series of unpowered gravity assist maneuvers using the outer planets could create a “velocity at infinity,” which is 16.6 km/s for Voyager 1, of up to 40 km/s. A series of Oberth maneuvers, using the combination of on-board thrusters to enhance gravity assists, could lead to realistic speeds that reach up to 60 km/s. And the most severe option, to steal most of a spacecraft’s velocity to bring it within just a few solar radii of the Sun and then use powered gravity assists (Oberth maneuvers), could lead to “velocity at infinity” of up to 100 km/s: about 6 times the speed of Voyager 1. It’s vital to remember that the distances between stars is vast , so even though Voyager 1 has nearly a half-century head start on anything we’d send out to attempt to catch it, it could easily be surpassed within centuries, and that a nearby star system, such as the Alpha/Proxima Centauri system — if we were inclined to design such a mission — could be reached with current technology before Voyager 1 were even one light-year away. We can actually explore the Universe if we so choose; all it takes is a commitment to put the resources and the right people in the right places to make it happen. Voyager 1’s latest milestone is a reminder of how far we can go; we just have to collectively choose to do it. This article How Voyager 1 became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day is featured on Big Think .

url:https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-b.title: 8 size and distance comparisons: from subatomic to cosmic
url:https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-b.summary: Here in this Universe, there are multiple different ways to look at all that exists in terms of size. You can look at the physical size, or volumes, that the objects occupy, and you can do that in a variety of ways. For humans, we can measure our dimensions — things like our height, width, and depth — or the amount of volume we displace when placed in a bath of water. Whichever method we choose, we get a proxy for our size. For planets, we can look at the edges of their solid surfaces or atmospheres; for stars, we can look at the boundary of their photospheres; for atoms, we probe them through techniques like force microscopy or scattering experiments. But in addition to these physical sizes, we can also examine such objects relative to other objects of the same type as found in nature. We can look at the distance from one human to another, for example, under a variety of common conditions. We can examine the distances between atoms, or stars, or planets, or galaxies, or anything else that we choose. And if we like, one interesting comparison that we can make, on any scale we choose, is the ratio between the physical size of the object itself to the distance from it to the next similar object. If we were to do this, which scale would be the most extreme, and how does that relate to human scales that we’re familiar with? Let’s examine eight different scales, from the quantum to the cosmic, to find out. Although, by volume, an atom is mostly empty space, dominated by the electron cloud, the dense atomic nucleus, responsible for only 1 part in 10^15 of an atom’s volume, contains ~99.95% of an atom’s mass. Reactions between internal components of a nucleus can be more precise and occur on shorter timescales, as well as at different energies, than transitions restricted to an atom’s electrons. Credit : Yzmo and Mpfiz/Wikimedia Commons 1.) Subatomic scales On scales smaller than an atom, we run into things like atomic nuclei, electrons, individual protons or neutrons within the nucleus, and quarks and gluons. Of these particles, it’s not necessarily fair to talk about “size” for most of them: quarks, gluons, and electrons are consistent with being what we call point particles, or particles consistent with having an actual size of 0. From scattering experiments, we’ve determined that if they do have a size, that size is no larger than about 10 -19 meters, or a tenth of an attometer. Protons, neutrons, and atomic nuclei, however, do have an actual size: about that of a femtometer, or 10 -15 meters. Within this context, you might consider looking at the distance from one subatomic particle — like a proton or the nucleus — to an electron as a measure of distance on subatomic scales. (If you went to look between two protons in the same nucleus, you’d find that they were practically adjacent: a distance-to-size ratio of around 1-to-1.) Since electrons are typically around a tenth of a nanometer, or 10 -10 meters, away from the nucleus, that results in a ratio of around 100,000-to-1. If the atomic nucleus were the size of a basketball located at Pepperdine University in Malibu, the electron would be roughly 24 kilometers (15 miles) away on the Santa Monica Pier. The K-4 crystal consists exclusively of carbon atoms arranged in a lattice, but with an unconventional bond angle compared to either graphite, diamond, or graphene. These inter-atomic properties can lead to drastically different physical, chemical, and material properties even with identical chemical formulas for a variety of structures. The average separation between two atoms in a lattice-like structure is only marginally larger than the size of one atom itself. Credit : Workbit/Wikimedia Commons 2.) Atomic scales Atoms are the building block of nearly everything we find on Earth, with enormous numbers of these very, very small entities combining together to compose the entire world and so much more. Atoms make up the atmosphere, the seas, the rocks and soil, every living creature on our planet, and the entire world itself, as well as pretty much every other known world in the Universe and much more. Atoms are generally the same physical size everywhere in the Universe — with the smallest atom, helium, having a diameter of 0.06 nanometers and the largest well-measured one, cesium, having a diameter of between 0.520 and 0.596 nanometers — with a typical atom’s size being around 10 -10 meters. But atoms can come in a huge variety of configurations, with some configurations placing atoms almost perfectly adjacent to one another and others creating great separations between them. Some examples include: in a water molecule, hydrogen and oxygen atoms are separated by 0.1 nanometers, in a diamond, two carbon atoms are separated by 0.15 nanometers, in the Earth’s crust, silicon and oxygen atoms are separated by 0.16 nanometers, and in a helium balloon, gaseous, monatomic helium atoms are typically separated by 3.4 nanometers. In solids and liquids, or wherever atoms are bound together into molecules, the next atom over is approximately only one or two atomic diameters away, while in a gas composed of atoms, the next atomic particle (at Earth’s standard pressure and temperature) is only a few dozen atom diameters away. If an atom again were a basketball on a basketball court, the next atom over for solids and liquids would be at the distance of a very tight defender, while for gases, the next atom over would be standing over by the 3-point line. Whereas ice requires water molecules to take on a relatively inefficient bond angle structure, even warm water achieves greater densities than ice does. At lower temperatures and higher pressures, liquid water is the densest form of water of all. The separation between water molecules in ocean water is approximately the same scale as the diameter of a water molecule itself. Credit : World Ocean Review 3.) Molecular scales This is an interesting one, because the separation distance between molecules depends tremendously on which type of molecules we’re talking about and the environment that they’re found in. Sure, when we think of molecules we typically think of something like water, which is a small molecule just 0.28 nanometers across: barely larger than an atom. But human DNA is also a molecule, albeit one that’s about three billion base pairs in length, spanning over a micron in length when coiled up (over 1000 nanometers) or extending for more than two meters if stretched out end-to-end. The protein Titin , found in striated muscle, is similarly large when coiled. But what about the distances between molecules? Again, the distance depends on the environment, and it varies tremendously. In red blood cells, the distance between hemoglobin molecules is about 7 nanometers, compared with the size of hemoglobin at about 5 nanometers. In the ocean, water molecules are separated by about 0.31 nanometers, compared to a size of 0.28 nanometers. Nitrogen molecules in Earth’s atmosphere at sea level are separated by 3.4 nanometers, while a nitrogen molecule is just 0.3 nanometers in size. In Mars’s carbon dioxide-rich but thin atmosphere, however, the average separation distance is more like 17 nanometers, compared to a molecular size of 0.3 nanometers. Although gases can be very sparse indeed, for most applications, if a molecule was the size of a basketball, the next molecule over would still be on the same basketball court, and in many cases, just around one basketball-diameter away. This crowd in Mauerpark, Berlin, is an excellent example of large numbers of people gathered together in one place: where the average separation distances between humans is small even compared to the scale of a single human. However, humans are spread out across a large area of the planet, heavily clustered together in urban areas. As such, the minimum separation distance between two humans varies tremendously dependent on location. Credit : Loozrboy/flickr 4.) Human scales At last, something we’re familiar with: the scales at which we live. A human being ranges in size from about 45 centimeters (18 inches) at birth to 2 meters (6’7″) for a very tall human. (There are greater extremes, but most of us fall somewhere in the middle.) For a full-grown adult human, most of us are somewhere between 150 cm and 190 cm: a narrower range that encompasses nearly 90% of the population over 18 years old. However, how well-separated we are varies tremendously depending on where we live. If all 8.3 billion humans were evenly distributed across the Earth, we’d be spaced approximately 270 meters apart. (Including uninhabitable places like oceans or ice sheets.) In the densest Tokyo wards (like Toshima), the average distance between the two closest people is just 3.25 meters apart. In a Tokyo subway car during rush hour, the average spacing between humans is just 40 cm. But in a rural area like northern Siberia, Russia, the average distance between any two people can rise to several kilometers. And outside of the capital city of Nuuk, there are 17 towns and 56 small settlements along Greenland’s coastline; the average spacing between two nearest-neighbors outside of this rises to between 3 and 7 kilometers: the largest human-spacing on Earth. Even in the sparsest, least population-dense places on Earth, humans are more closely packed together than subatomic particles are within an atom: with a maximum ratio of just a few thousand-to-1 in terms of distance-to-size. If a human were a basketball, those of us in cities would make a court that looked like the fans had just rushed it, but those of us in the most rural areas would still have other humans in the arena, but not necessarily on the court. The TRAPPIST-1 system contains the most terrestrial-like planets of any stellar system presently known, and is shown scaled to temperature equivalents to our own Solar System. These seven known worlds, however, exist around a low-mass, consistently flaring red dwarf star. It’s plausible that exactly none of them have atmospheres any longer, although JWST will have more to say about that in future years. Credit : NASA/JPL-Caltech 5.) Planetary scales But as we turn to planetary scales, things suddenly get very, very large in terms of both sizes and distances, with distances far exceeding the size scales. A planet like the Earth is large: about 12,700 km in diameter. Rocky planets can be significantly smaller, of course: Mercury is the smallest major planet in our Solar System with a diameter of 4880 km, but planets could, in theory, be just a few hundred kilometers in diameter and still meet all of the necessary criteria for being classified as a planet. On the largest end, Jupiter is 143,000 km in diameter, and several super-Jupiter exoplanets up to double Jupiter’s size are known. Nonetheless, as impressive as those numbers are, they’re absolutely paltry compared to the distances between planets. Relative to Earth, our nearest-neighbor planet at closest approach is Venus: 38 million km away, or about a factor of 3000 greater than Earth’s diameter. For an outer planet like Uranus, its diameter of 51,000 km is peanuts compared to its separation from Saturn or Neptune: 1.43-1.45 billion km away, or a factor of 28,000. Even in a close-packed planetary system like the TRAPPIST-1 system, the average spacing between planets is 1.26 million km, or more than a factor of 100 larger than the average TRAPPIST-1 planet diameter, at 12,100 km. If a typical planet were a basketball, the most closely-spaced planetary systems would put the next-nearest planet somewhere still in the arena. If Earth were a basketball, the nearest planets would still be in the same town, while the outer distant planets would be quite a way down the highway. Still, the distance ratios are less extreme than inside an atom, but that all changes when we go to the next scale up. In the early 21st-century, we’ve successfully mapped out practically all the stars in our neighborhood in three-dimensional space. The closest stars to us don’t always align with the stars we can see, as what’s visible is determined by a combination of distance and intrinsic brightness, but all stars beyond the Sun are at a much, much greater distance than anything within our Solar System. The Alpha/Proxima Centauri system is a trinary, and has the three closest stars to our Sun at present; Barnard’s star is the fourth closest, and is the nearest singlet star system to our own. Stars themselves are millions of times smaller than the distances separating different star systems. Credit : Andrew Z. Colvin 6.) Stellar scales Even compared to the sizes of and distances between planets, the scales of stars are far more impressive. Our own Sun is a whopping 1.4 million km in diameter. Even the smallest red dwarf stars are significantly bigger than Jupiter, with Proxima Centauri coming in at 200,000 km across. On the other end of the spectrum, a blue giant like the brightest star in the Beta Centauri system is over 13 million km across. An evolved red giant like Arcturus is closer to 35 million km in diameter, while a massive, evolved red supergiant like Betelgeuse is closer to a whopping 900 million km across. Some stars even cross the billion kilometers mark in terms of physical size! But the distances between stars are in a whole other league. From the Sun to Proxima Centauri, our closest star, it’s 4.24 light-years, or 40 trillion km: a distance-to-size ratio of 28 million-to-1 for the Sun. Stars in globular clusters can be closer together: separated by as little as 0.15 light-years in the cluster core, but that still yields a distance-to-size ratio of a million-to-1 for most stars. And in the sparser places — like the ultra-diffuse galaxies of the Universe — average stellar separations can rise to 20 light-years, while the average star is even smaller than the Sun: exceeding a 100,000,000-to-1 distance-to-size ratio. The distances between stars, even relative to the massive size of a star itself, provide the most extreme distance-to-size ratios of any object on any scale in the Universe. If our Sun were a basketball, the next-nearest star would be located on the opposite side of the Earth from our gym! Composite of galaxies from the smallest to the largest, shown (approximately) actual size. The giant elliptical galaxy at the heart of cluster Abell 2029, IC 1101, is the largest known galaxy in the Universe, at least in terms of stellar extent. It is much, much larger than the Milky Way or Andromeda (or any spiral galaxy), but also towers over even other typical giant ellipticals. Credit: E. Siegel 7.) Galactic scales Stars aren’t completely isolated, however. They’re bound together in extremely large-magnitude collections of their own: galaxies. The distances between galaxies absolutely outscales the distances between stars in impressive fashion. Therefore, you might wonder about the scale of a galaxy compared to the distances between galaxies; perhaps it’s even more impressive. Our own Milky Way contains approximately 400 billion stars, largely confined to a disk 100,000 light-years across. Smaller galaxies, like a variety of dwarf galaxies , are often only a few thousand light-years in diameter. Meanwhile, the largest known single galaxy of all, IC 1101 , has a diffuse halo of starlight that extends for over 4 million light-years (and maybe up to 6 million light-years) across. Galaxies can be tiny or enormous, with Milky Way-like galaxies sitting squarely between them. The nearest Milky Way-like galaxy to our own is Andromeda, which is the only other galaxy in the Local Group with as much mass as our Milky Way possesses. It’s quite distant, too: 2.5 million light-years away. However, that means we have a distance-to-size ratio of just 25-to-1! If the Milky Way were a basketball located at the basket itself, Andromeda would be roughly at the free-throw line. Galaxies are often grouped together, and even isolated galaxies — or field galaxies — are usually between 10-15 million light-years from another major galaxy. Because galaxies themselves are so big, the distance-to-size ratios for these objects aren’t nearly as impressive as we find on even planetary scales. The Coma Cluster of galaxies, as seen with a composite of modern space and ground-based telescopes. The infrared data comes from the Spitzer Space Telescope, while ground-based data comes from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. The Coma Cluster is dominated by two giant elliptical galaxies, with over 1000 other spirals and ellipticals inside. Gas-free, red-and-dead elliptical galaxies are very common, especially toward the cluster center, in large galaxy clusters such as this one. The cluster spans over 20 million light-years across, but is separated by nearby clusters by around 100 million light-years. Credit : NASA / JPL-Caltech / L. Jenkins (GSFC) 8.) Super-galactic (galaxy group/cluster) scales You might think, then, to look to the largest scales of all: the scales at which galaxies collect together into groups and clusters. We’re a part of the Local Group: a collection of galaxies that includes Andromeda, our Milky Way, and a few hundred smaller galaxies all bound together. We’re not all that big of a group, as many galaxy clusters contain thousands of large galaxies all bound together, but we still extend for between 3-5 million light-years in total span. The largest galaxy clusters, like the Coma Cluster, can span more than 20 million light-years from end-to-end. Sure, space is vast and mostly empty, but the separations between galaxy groups and clusters is even less severe than it is for galaxies when compared to their sizes. We have other galaxy groups relatively close to our own: the M81 group , for example, is less than 12 million light-years away, for a 4-to-1 distance-to-size ratio at most. For bigger structures, like galaxy clusters, the separation distances are greater, but the sizes are also greater. The Virgo cluster and the Fornax cluster are two of the nearest galaxy clusters to Earth, separated by around 100 million light-years in space from each other. But with a diameter of 15 million light-years, the Virgo cluster has only about a 7-to-1 distance-to-size ratio. If galaxy groups and clusters were basketballs, their neighboring groups and clusters would be able to make up a “starting 5” as well as an opposing team, and fit them all on the same half of the basketball court. It’s a fairly crowded place when you consider such large structures, after all. The isolated galaxy MCG+01-02-015, all by its lonesome for over 100,000,000 light-years in all directions, is presently thought to be the loneliest galaxy in the Universe. The features seen in this galaxy are consistent with it being a massive spiral that formed from a long series of minor mergers, but that has never experienced a major merger, and where star-forming activity has been relatively quiet for the past several billion years. It’s the size of a galaxy, but as isolated as a typical galaxy cluster. Credit : ESA/Hubble & NASA and N. Grogin (STScI); Acknowledgement: Judy Schmidt This means, in terms of a distance-to-size ratio, it’s the stellar scales that are the most impressive. Compared to even the size of the largest stars, the cosmic distances separating them are absolutely tremendous, typically reaching ratios of several million-to-1. As big as a star is, the distance separating the stars gives us the most extreme ratios. In second place is the separation between subatomic particles within an atom: electrons within an atom or the separation between the atomic nuclei and an electron. That ratio of 100,000-to-1 outclasses all scales except the stellar, putting it in a strong second place on this list. In third place are planetary scales, which are less extreme than subatomic particles, but which have more extreme separations than humans do on planet Earth, which (perhaps surprisingly) comes in fourth on this list. Galactic scales typically follow next in fifth, with atomic separations (at least, in gases) coming in sixth. It’s fairly remarkable that the two most extreme examples of a distance-to-size ratio occur on such different scales than one another: one of them on interstellar scales and one on tiny, subatomic scales. The reason for it is the same in both cases: the objects are simply physically much, much smaller than the distances separating them from the next-nearest such object. From the quantum to the cosmic, the Universe is full of delights and surprises. This article 8 size and distance comparisons: from subatomic to cosmic is featured on Big Think .

doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02139-2.title: Kuroshio Extension warming shaped by Gulf Stream variability via the Arctic atmosphere
doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02139-2.summary: Abstract Recent unprecedented ocean warming has produced coherent sea surface temperature anomalies across the Northern Hemisphere extratropics. While the tropical Pacific is a natural source of North Pacific variability, the influence of the mid-latitude North Atlantic has remained poorly understood. Here we investigate whether Gulf Stream variability modulates Kuroshio Extension variability using 100-year idealized model simulations. We find that Gulf Stream variability remotely modulates Kuroshio Extension variability, explaining 13% of its internal sea surface temperature variance, whereas we find no evidence that Kuroshio variability similarly modulates the Gulf Stream. Positive Gulf Stream sea surface temperature anomalies excite a Northern Annular Mode-like atmospheric circulation response that weakens the Aleutian Low over the North Pacific. The resulting northward shift of the Kuroshio Extension enhances northward warm-water transport and promotes warming in the western mid-latitude North Pacific. We further show that a high-resolution ocean model is required to properly capture this coupling between Gulf Stream variability and atmospheric circulation, highlighting the importance of western boundary currents and associated oceanic fronts for this interbasin pathway. These findings indicate that North Atlantic variability contributed to the exceptional North Pacific warming during 2020–2024 and may provide a source of decadal predictability for Northern Hemisphere climate.

doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11297-7.title: Injury-induced signalling coordinates immunity and cannibalism in locusts
doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11297-7.summary: Abstract Cannibalism, the consumption of conspecifics, is widespread across the animal kingdom and can profoundly influence individual fitness and population dynamics 1,2 . Although the ecological and social conditions that favour cannibalism have been well documented 2 , the molecular signals that trigger cannibalistic attacks have remained poorly understood. Here we show that in Locusta migratoria , guaiacol, a volatile compound with augmented release after injury, attracts gregarious nymphs and induces cannibalistic behaviour. Guaiacol is detected by olfactory receptors LmOR36 and LmOR34, and disruption of either receptor abolishes attraction, thereby impairing induction of cannibalism. Guaiacol is synthesized by haemolymph symbiont Enterobacter hormaechei . Injury promotes bacterial congregation at the wound site, leading to elevated guaiacol production through a clustered set of vanillic acid decarboxylase genes; deletion of this gene cluster abolishes guaiacol production and its behavioural effects. Notably, guaiacol initially functions as a beneficial signal after injury. Guaiacol activates immune-related pathways in wounded locusts, enhancing pathogen resistance and increasing survival following minor injury. However, when guaiacol emission exceeds a threshold determined by injury severity, it functions as an external cue that attracts cannibals. Cannibalistic locusts exploit this immune-related odour to locate severely injured conspecifics, gaining both nutritional resources and immune system benefits. Together, our findings identify a microbial–chemical mechanism that links immune defence with cannibalistic behaviour and provide potential molecular targets for manipulation of cannibalism-dependent population dynamics.

doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11298-6.title: Tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity
doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11298-6.summary: Abstract Tropical land-use intensification threatens global biodiversity, yet most assessments of tropical agricultural landscapes focus on local-scale biodiversity, overlooking how land use restructures biodiversity across space and multiple taxa. Here we provide an ecosystem-wide assessment of 24 taxonomic groups across all domains of life—encompassing 40,049 species—along a land-use intensification gradient from lowland forests to intensively managed smallholder cash-crop monocultures in Indonesian landscapes. Despite widespread losses of landscape and local multidiversity 1 in monocultures (approximately 78% and 50%, respectively), we found no evidence for consistent community homogenization with land-use intensification. Instead, monocultures exhibit a systematic shift from turnover to nestedness for aboveground taxa. Such patterns of differentiation may mask trajectories towards biotic homogenization via early stages of assemblage simplification. Biotic differentiation has the potential to partly mitigate biodiversity losses by positively affecting γ-diversity. This opens management options, including the conservation of existing remnants of traditional agriculture and the implementation of sustainable management practices 2–4 . Our results demonstrate that tropical land-use intensification restructures biodiversity not only through species loss, but also via a pervasive reorganization of community composition across trophic levels. Conserving tropical biodiversity, therefore, requires a multi-taxon, landscape-scale perspective that explicitly integrates agricultural land uses with the protection of natural and semi-natural habitats to reconcile agricultural production and conservation.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh3524.title: Engineering interfacial nucleation and growth for long-life, ultrahigh-rate anode-free sodium batteries
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh3524.summary: The practical application of anode-free sodium batteries (AFSBs) is limited by the poor reversibility of sodium plating and stripping on current collectors. Here, we show that conventional graphite unexpectedly regulates sodium plating and stripping through a dynamic, interactive interface that enables multidimensional charge transport. This behavior arises from the combination of ultrafast mixed ion-electron transport, reversible ether solvent cointercalation, and the anisotropic flake architecture of graphite, which together promote efficient charge exchange and edge-dominant nucleation. The resulting adaptive interface forms an ultrathin, mechanically robust SEI that stabilizes sodium plating and stripping across a wide current density range (1C to 10C). Ampere hour–level anode-free pouch cells based on this design exhibit an initial Coulombic efficiency of 92.3%, retain 84.9% capacity after 1100 cycles at 3C, and display exceptional safety characteristics, including minimal temperature rise at high rates and no thermal runaway during nail penetration. These results establish a platform for controlling interfacial metal nucleation and growth in AFSBs.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aej5212.title: Interband connectivity and climate shaped Neanderthal extinction and Homo sapiens’ dispersal
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aej5212.summary: To what extent Neanderthal extinction was triggered by climate change or the arrival of Homo sapiens , and by which mechanisms, remains unresolved. Here, on the basis of climate-driven changes in habitat favorability for primary and secondary consumers and in net primary productivity, we estimate carrying capacity, herbivore biomass, and intraguild predation pressure during the time Neanderthals and H. sapiens lived in Europe. These spatially explicit estimates were incorporated into an agent-based model simulating human demographic dynamics under various scenarios. Results indicate that carrying capacity changes cannot explain Neanderthal extinction at a continental scale, though they are essential to understanding spatiotemporal distribution patterns of both human species. Conversely, the arrival of H. sapiens remarkably increased Neanderthal extinction likelihood. Because of the successive demographic expansions and contractions, group connectivity emerges as the key factor shaping population stability in both species. These findings support that Neanderthal disappearance and H. sapiens dispersals were interconnected demographic processes.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aek3182.title: Environment-adaptive molecular neural networks enabled by heterogeneous threshold DNA neuron
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aek3182.summary: Molecular neural networks enable autonomous information processing in biochemical environments, yet most existing DNA-based implementations operate with fixed connectivity after assembly, limiting their ability to adapt network topology to changing environments. Here, we report an environment-adaptive molecular neural network enabled by DNA neurons with sequence-programmed, heterogeneous activation thresholds. These neurons incorporate triplex-based proton-gated DNA switches with tunable pH-response windows, which regulate the accessibility of toehold and recognition domains to switch pre-encoded weighted connections between inactive and signal-propagating states, thereby reconfiguring network connectivity without changing molecular composition. We demonstrate this principle in a DNA neural network that processes 64-bit inputs, where environmental acidification activates dormant neurons and reconfigures the computational topology from a sparse convolutional neural network for coarse two-class categorization into a fully connected neural network for fine-grained discrimination among four distinct patterns. Our results establish DNA-based neural circuits capable of adapting their computational architecture to environmental cues, offering a framework for molecular information processing in fluctuating biochemical environments.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh9812.title: Nanoparticle-enabled gene delivery for pediatric brain tumors
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh9812.summary: Pediatric brain tumors are the leading cause of disease-related death in children, yet effective treatment remains a major clinical challenge. These aggressive tumors have limited therapeutic options capable of crossing the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and frequently recur due to genetic or epigenetic alterations and treatment resistance. Gene therapy offers a promising strategy to address these limitations by modifying gene expression, correcting mutations, or introducing functional genes. Nanoparticle (NP) delivery systems facilitate this approach by protecting genetic cargo and enabling BBB penetration and tumor-specific uptake. This review summarizes current genetic engineering strategies and NP-based delivery systems for pediatric brain tumors, including their design principles and delivery mechanisms, highlights key therapeutic approaches under preclinical and clinical investigations, and discusses the major challenges and future directions in NP-mediated gene therapy for pediatric neuro-oncology. By critically evaluating these developments, we aim to underscore the transformative potential of NP-mediated gene therapies in reshaping treatment paradigms and improving outcomes and quality of life for children.

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sand-g.title: Bouncing sand grains may explain planet-wide dust storms on Mars
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-sand-g.summary: When a storm hits Earth, it is always a regional event. A storm might hit northern Europe, but it never expands to cover the entire continent. That is not the case on Mars. Every three or four years, a storm of such immense scale breaks out on Mars that it swallows the entire planet. Dust blocks out the sunlight, plunging the surface into darkness. That darkness spells trouble if humans are to settle on the Red Planet in the future. Space Exploration

url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-decade.title: Over a decade of atmospheric data from NASA's Curiosity rover hints at small amounts of surface water on Mars
url:https://phys.org/news/2026-11-decade.summary: NASA's Curiosity rover has been collecting data about Mars' thin, carbon dioxide–rich atmosphere since 2012. Now, a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences has analyzed over a decade of this data to determine whether the daily and seasonal changes in Mars' atmosphere could be explained by known processes, including the freezing and release of carbon dioxide at its poles. What they found suggests a process involving water either attached to soil grains or in extremely thin, liquid-like films at the surface. Astrobiology

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16389-2026.title: Measurement report: Differences in cloud optical and microphysical properties in the Arctic and Antarctic derived using thermal infrared spectroscopy
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16389-2026.summary: Climate models struggle to accurately represent polar regions, largely due to the difficulty in modeling clouds. The uncertainty budget of polar radiation is dominated by cloud and cloud-aerosol interactions, but challenges in maintaining robust field observations mean that even basic knowledge such as cloud occurrence is not well known. Measurements of the thermal emission of Earth's atmosphere can help close this knowledge gap due to the sensitivity of this spectral region to radiative properties of clouds. Measurements of the downwelling atmospheric emission (400 to 3000 cm −1 ) have been collected at two polar field sites using Atmospheric Emitted Radiance Interferometer (AERI) instruments, two at the Polar Environment Atmospheric Research Laboratory (PEARL) in Eureka, Canada (80° N), for which we use data from 2006 to 2022, and another at McMurdo Station (77° S) in Antarctica as part of the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) West Antarctica Radiation Experiment (AWARE) project in 2016. We analyze these spectra, with supplementary data from other instruments and models, to compare optical and microphysical properties of moderately thick clouds at Eureka and McMurdo Station, including optical depth, thermodynamic phase, liquid droplet and ice crystal effective scattering radii, and cloud boundaries. We find that the clouds sampled at McMurdo generally feature lower temperatures, smaller liquid droplets, a more concentrated distribution of ice effective radii, less seasonal variability in optical depth, and lower optical thickness because they consist of a higher proportion of ice than those at Eureka. Additionally, both locations have high occurrence rates of supercooled liquid and mixed-phase clouds and exhibit differences between single-phase and mixed-phase microphysical properties.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16441-2026.title: Cloud occurrence, properties, and ice crystal effective dimension parameterization from 9 years of far-infrared observations on the Antarctic Plateau
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16441-2026.summary: Clouds over the Antarctic Plateau exert a strong influence on the regional radiation budget, yet observations and modelling of their properties remain scarce. Here, 9 years (2012–2020) of ground-based high-resolution spectral radiance measurements from the REFIR-PAD spectroradiometer at Concordia Station (Dome C, Antarctica) are analyzed in synergy with co-located lidar observations. A machine-learning Cloud Identification and Classification (CIC) algorithm is applied to discriminate clear sky, ice cloud, and mixed-phase cloud conditions, enabling the construction of a long-term cloud climatology. Cloud optical and microphysical properties are subsequently retrieved using a simultaneous atmospheric and cloud retrieval framework, for cases with reliable cloud boundaries and cloud base heights above 500 m. Results confirm that cloud occurrence over Dome C is dominated by optically thin ice clouds, with approximately 95 % of cases exhibiting optical depths below 1. Median optical depth ranges from 0.11 in summer to 0.32 in winter. The median temperature of the ice layers is approximately 237 K. Mixed-phase clouds are rare and mainly confined to the austral summer, but exhibit larger optical depths (median 1.7) and warmer temperatures (approximately 246 K). Based on the retrieved dataset, a new parameterization of ice crystal effective dimension is derived. Compared with commonly used parameterizations developed for tropical and midlatitude conditions, the proposed scheme predicts systematically smaller particle sizes, highlighting the inadequacy of existing formulations for the Antarctic environments. These results provide new observational constraints on Antarctic cloud microphysics and support improved cloud representation in climate and numerical weather prediction models.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16415-2026.title: Lightning in global chemistry-climate models: a review of parameterizations, evaluations, and future projections
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16415-2026.summary: Climate models are our main tool to project how global lightning activity may change in a warmer world. However, the spatial and temporal scales involved in cloud electrification are too small to be explicitly resolved, so lightning is typically simulated using empirical relationships with proxy variables such as cloud top height (CTH), convective precipitation, the product of convective available potential energy and precipitation, or upward ice flux. This review summarizes existing global lightning parameterizations, their skill in reproducing observed lightning patterns, and their projected future changes. We identify 19 parameterizations (including some variants) that have been applied in global modelling studies, with CTH – the earliest developed – remaining the most widely used. Most parameterizations predict total lightning, while cloud-to-ground lightning is rarely computed directly. Several parameterizations, including CTH, reproduce observed spatial lightning patterns reasonably well ( r > 0.7), whereas precipitation-based methods perform worse ( r often < 0.6). Most approaches underestimate lightning over central Africa and in mid-to-high latitudes, while overestimating activity over the Amazon and Maritime Continent. They also struggle to capture the observed land–ocean contrast in lightning activity and tend to underestimate temporal variability from diurnal to inter-annual scales. Future projections show large uncertainty, ranging from an 11 % decrease to a 44 % increase in global lightning frequency per degree global warming. The mean across all parameterizations is +5.5 ± 8.7 % K −1 (one value per parameterization), while the mean across all individual projections (which are strongly biased towards CTH) is +7.7 ± 8.3% K −1 . Although there is a broad agreement that lightning activity will increase in high latitudes, the tropical response remains highly uncertain.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16373-2026.title: Addressing systematic underestimation in a global ship emission inventory through improved fleet representation and fuel compliance characterization
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16373-2026.summary: As a sector with high energy demand, long-lived assets, and limited near-term low-carbon alternatives, global shipping is considered difficult to decarbonize and is subject to stringent emission controls. To evaluate emission control effects and conduct rapid response air quality simulations, accurate and timely ship emission inventories are indispensable. However, existing inventories face challenges from incomplete fleet representation and large uncertainties in PM 2.5 emissions after the global sulfur regulation. Here, we updated the Ship Emission Inventory Model to SEIMv2.3 by introducing an improved representation of post-2020 fuel sulfur compliance pathways and enabling near-real-time emission calculation within 3 d of AIS data acquisition. Ship activity and technical database are updated daily instead of yearly to obtain a more complete and rapid description of the global ship fleet. Fleet's multiple choices to comply with fuel sulfur regulation were considered, including switching to very low sulfur fuel and utilizing scrubbers to keep consuming heavy fuel oil. The daily expansion of ship technical database uncovered 8 % and 6.2 % of the total gross tonnage of active bulk carrier and container fleets, unveiling up to 5.4 % of global ship CO 2 emissions. The resulting emission discrepancies gradually accumulated over 2024, indicating that delayed fleet information updates remain an important source of uncertainty in ship emission estimates. Meanwhile, assuming that all ships switch to low-sulfur fuels after 2020 would lead to underestimation of PM 2.5 and BC emissions by approximately 43 % and 15 %. Although South China Ocean had the most absolute underestimation, the Indian Ocean had the highest underestimated portion, reaching 56 % and 15 % of its total PM 2.5 and BC emissions.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16309-2026.title: Isolating the influence of aerosols on Arctic cloud radiative effects during a polluted warm air mass intrusion
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16309-2026.summary: Arctic warm air mass intrusions are key to the region's energy balance because they transport large amounts of heat and moisture from lower latitudes. The resulting changes in heat and moisture content influences cloud properties, the thermodynamic structure of the boundary layer, and surface radiation. Warm air mass intrusions can also carry significant amounts of aerosols into the Arctic, including aerosols from anthropogenic sources at lower latitudes, which could influence the radiative impacts of such events. In this study, we examine the role of aerosol transport during a warm air mass intrusion that occurred in the central Arctic in April 2020. We use a version of the regional chemistry-climate model WRF-Chem adapted for Arctic conditions (WRF-Chem-Polar), to investigate the radiative impact of aerosol-cloud interactions associated with the event. We isolate the effects of the high aerosol burden by running the model with and without anthropogenic emissions. Anthropogenic emissions increase cloud droplet number concentration by 117 % and liquid water content by 52 %. However, the net surface radiative impact of these aerosol-cloud interactions is limited over sea ice. The high albedo of the underlying sea ice limits shortwave cloud cooling, while the longwave effects of cloud perturbations are small. Over open ocean regions, the surface radiative impacts of the aerosols are stronger. Overall, these results suggest that the net effect of an extreme aerosol transport event is sensitive to the season in which the event takes place, due to strong dependence on the surface state and the background Arctic haze conditions.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16341-2026.title: Airborne and marine microplastics in the Northern Indian Ocean: decoupled pathways traced by black carbon
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16341-2026.summary: Microplastics (MPs) have been detected in both marine and atmospheric particulate matter, but their sources, transport, and air–sea exchange remain poorly constrained in remote marine regions. We investigated airborne microplastics (AMPs) and marine microplastics (MMPs) during a 1-month campaign at the Maldives Climate Observatory Hanimaadhoo and in adjacent coastal waters. Airborne particles were collected with a deposition box, and seawater was sampled at coastal sites. Particle morphology, size, and polymer composition were determined by optical microscopy and μ -Raman spectroscopy and evaluated alongside aerosol scattering and equivalent black carbon (eBC). AMP concentrations ranged from 0 to 10.3 MP m −3 (mean: 3.1 ± 2.8 MP m −3 ). MMP concentrations ranged from 120 to 2656 MP m −3 (mean: 876 ± 804 MP m −3 ), exceeding typical open-ocean values and indicating substantial local influence from inhabited islands and maritime activity. Significant differences in size distributions and pronounced compositional differences of AMPs and MMPs suggest weak coupling between the atmospheric and marine reservoirs. Low dry-season wind speeds probably suppressed wave breaking, bubble bursting, and sea-spray-mediated transfer from ocean to atmosphere. Instead, AMP variability coincided with polluted air-mass advection, elevated eBC, and enhanced aerosol scattering, indicating stronger control by regional atmospheric transport than by local marine emissions. These results show that remote island atmospheres are exposed to anthropogenic plastic aerosol transport and demonstrate the value of combining MP observations with established aerosol tracers to resolve plastic-particle pathways in marine environments.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16325-2026.title: Vertical structure and controlling factors of cloud condensation nuclei activation over eastern China: Insights from aircraft measurements and interpretable machine learning
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16325-2026.summary: Cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) play a critical role in cloud droplet formation and microphysical processes. Based on aircraft observations, this study investigated the factors controlling CCN number concentrations (NCCN) under different aerosol vertical structures (Decrease, Increase, and Stable, representing decreasing, increasing, and relatively stable aerosol concentrations with altitude, respectively) and supersaturation (SS) conditions using generalized additive models (GAM) combined with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP).NCCN reached up to 10 3 cm −3 near the surface and generally decreased with altitude, while aerosol vertical structures modulated its abundance, with the Increase structure showing higher NCCN than Stable and Decrease structures. CCN activation ratios increased with SS and exhibited a non-monotonic vertical variation, with no consistent ranking among aerosol structures, indicating that supersaturation dominates CCN activation. Activated CCN droplet spectra showed unimodal distributions, with peak diameters increasing from ∼2 µm at SS=0.2 to ∼5 µm at SS=1.0. Although spectral shapes were similar among different structures, higher small-size aerosol concentrations (SA, 0.1–1 µm) were associated with higher CCN peak concentrations. GAM results identified several important explanatory variables for NCCN variations, with relative SHAP contributions of 19 %–57 % for temperature ( T ), 9 %–45 % for SA, 9 %–40 % for relative humidity (RH), and 3 %–32 % for horizontal wind speed (WS). SHAP analysis revealed that the contributions of T varied among different aerosol vertical structures, showing positive associations under Decrease and Increase structures but negative associations under Stable conditions, whereas SA consistently exhibited positive contributions. RH showed nonlinear relationships with NCCN, with an inflection point near 60 %.

doi:10.5194/ar-2026-44.title: Anthropogenic Particles in the Urban Atmosphere: Evidence of microplastics and textile fibers in the air of Rionegro, Colombia
doi:10.5194/ar-2026-44.summary: Anthropogenic Particles in the Urban Atmosphere: Evidence of microplastics and textile fibers in the air of Rionegro, Colombia James Londoño-Valencia, Maria Isabel Ríos-Pulgarín, Mariana Botero Flórez, Jaime Andrés Gutiérrez-Monsalve, and Felipe Amezcua Martínez Aerosol Research Discuss., https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-2026-44,2026 Preprint under review for AR (discussion: open, 0 comments) Anthropogenic particles (APs), including microplastics and textile fibers, were studied in indoor and outdoor environments of Rionegro, an Andean city in Colombia. Passive sampling (42 samples, 7761 APs) showed mean deposition of 2,358 particles m⁻² d⁻¹ indoors versus 271 outdoors (p < 0.001). Fibers predominated; spectroscopy identified PET, PP, acrylic and cellulosic materials. These contrasting patterns highlight the need to assess human exposure to airborne APs.

doi:10.5194/ar-2026-45.title: Understanding distribution patterns of secondary inorganic aerosols in two distinct environments through statistical learning
doi:10.5194/ar-2026-45.summary: Understanding distribution patterns of secondary inorganic aerosols in two distinct environments through statistical learning Zehao Zou, Wei Du, Giancarlo Ciarelli, Yongchun Liu, Chao Yan, Jing Cai, Qiaozhi Zha, Kaspar Rudolf Daellenbach, Men Xia, Xinran Zhang, Qi Yuan, Tinghan Zhang, Feixue Zheng, Yuzheng Wang, Chenjie Hua, Zongcheng Wang, Hongyu Pang, Boying Song, Li Ma, Wenshuo Zhou, Junlei Zhan, Wei Ma, Tuukka Petäjä, Nina Sarnela, Ilona Jaakkola, Lauri Ahonen, Veli-Matti Kerminen, Markku Kulmala, and Tom Kokkonen Aerosol Research Discuss., https://doi.org/10.5194/ar-2026-45,2026 Preprint under review for AR (discussion: open, 0 comments) We used statistical methods to compare two major components of air pollution in Beijing and a Finnish forest. Their levels were analyzed in the forest and formed several groups in Beijing. In Beijing, gases that can form particles were more important at lower levels, while humidity and air arriving from other regions mattered more at higher levels. These findings could help identify conditions linked to high particle pollution and inform efforts to improve air quality.

url:https://www.universetoday.com/articl.title: Are Uranus and Neptune Secretly "Rock Giants"? A Noble Gas Might Hold the Answer
url:https://www.universetoday.com/articl.summary: For decades, astronomers have divided the planets in the outer solar system into two distinct camps. Jupiter and Saturn were the “gas giants” made up primarily of hydrogen and helium. Uranus and Neptune were the “ice giants”, and were much smaller but were packed with heavier elements. A new paper from Olivier Mousis of the Southwest Research Institute and his co-authors, available in The Planetary Science Journal, explores whether we can use an isotope of a noble gas - argon-40 - to determine whether there are hidden mountains of rock under the ice giant’s thick atmospheres.

url:https://www.universetoday.com/articl.title: Microscopic Space Dust Reveals A Hidden Reservoir Of "Heavy Water" Beyond Neptune
url:https://www.universetoday.com/articl.summary: Astronomers can find valuable information in even the tiniest objects. That was certainly the case recently when twelve dust grains collected by a high-altitude aircraft helped solve a mystery about the birth of our Solar System. Or at least that is the argument in a new paper published in Science Advances by researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center and UCLA. According to the paper, the region beyond Neptune once had a massive isolated reservoir of “heavy water” that never mixed in with the inner planets.

doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11299-5.title: Fully integrated perovskite active polaritonic circuits
doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11299-5.summary: Abstract Photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a key technology for compact, analogue and energy-efficient optical information processing 1 . Yet, their practical implementation remains limited by the intrinsically weak optical nonlinearities of conventional materials, which demand high power and large device footprints to achieve substantial nonlinear responses 2 . Exciton–polaritons, hybrid light–matter excitations of semiconducting materials, offer a promising route to overcome these limitations by combining strong optical nonlinearities with the high speed and scalability typical of photonic platforms 3–5 . However, despite their potential, fully integrated on-chip polaritonic systems simultaneously delivering room-temperature waveguide lasing, controllable optical routing and amplification have remained elusive. Here we demonstrate a fully integrated perovskite polaritonic circuit that brings these functionalities together in a single-step-grown platform. We realize precise and scalable polariton circuits with integrated gratings that act as both couplers and reflectors, enabling in-plane Fabry–Pérot cavities. These structures support robust in-plane polariton lasing with coherent guided emission at a geometry-defined wavelength, optical amplification of propagating polaritons and nonlinear optical phase control exceeding π, all within the same on-chip architecture. Our results establish perovskite polariton circuits as a scalable platform for active and interferometric integrated photonics.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aef6804.title: Seasonal effects of simulated marine heatwaves on temperature-dependent growth performance
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aef6804.summary: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) are increasingly longer and more frequent globally, but the cumulative impacts of multiple events on organism performance remain poorly understood. Using thermal performance models, we simulate the effects of simple seasonal MHW scenarios on the predicted growth of 36 mariculture species across the western Pacific Ocean. Simulations suggested that winter MHWs could generally benefit growth, while summer MHWs produced generally negative impacts, especially at higher latitudes where species experience summer growth periods. When combined, winter and summer MHW scenarios indicated a cumulative negative effect for most species. Vulnerability was highest at the warm- and cold-range edges of species’ distributions. These simulations suggest that temperature-dependent growth may be closely linked to the seasonal timing and frequency of extreme events, with multi-season MHWs posing potential challenges for mariculture species in the future. Our simulations highlight the importance of considering multi-season impacts in climate adaptation strategies.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh6253.title: Spheroid-laden hydrogels with dual biomimetic intra- and perispheroidal niches for enhanced bone healing
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeh6253.summary: Stem cell spheroid–hydrogel platforms offer promise for bone defect repair, but implantation-associated oxidative stress, poor vascular ingrowth, and insufficient osteogenic cues limit their clinical translation. Here, we developed dual-NICHE (dual niche-instructive construct for bone healing and engraftment), a gelatin methacryloyl hydrogel containing human adipose–derived stem cell spheroids with spatially distinct intra-/perispheroidal niches. Within a single construct, these two niches provide complementary functions to simultaneously address the key bottlenecks in bone regeneration. The intraspheroidal niche incorporated bone morphogenetic protein-2–immobilized fibers to promote osteogenic differentiation, whereas the perispheroidal matrix contained Sr 2+ –tannic acid nanoparticles (NPs). Upon implantation, the NPs mitigated oxidative stress and supported vascular infiltration. Concurrently, the osteogenic cue promoted differentiation, while the NPs facilitated mineral nucleation and growth, as further supported by molecular dynamics simulations. Together, this spatial integration enhanced vascularized bone formation with a bone volume fraction of ∼13.5% using only 5208 cells per defect in a mouse calvarial model, providing a potentially translatable framework for bone regeneration.
