doi:10.1029/2026je009985.title: Laboratory Experiments Identify Meteoritic Organic Precursors for Chlorinated Compounds Detected by the Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) Instrument at Gale Crater
doi:10.1029/2026je009985.summary: Abstract The Viking missions landed two spacecraft on Mars each equipped with a pyrolysis‐gas chromatograph‐mass spectrometer system capable of detecting signs of life. Although working as intended, detections of chloromethane and dichloromethane were initially attributed to terrestrial contamination. Decades later, the Phoenix Mars Lander identified perchlorate salts in the Martian regolith that are known to catalyze the oxidation and chlorination reactions of organics. Subsequent analyses by the Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument suite aboard the Curiosity rover have since confirmed a variety of syngenetic chlorinated hydrocarbons in Gale crater samples. However, the nature of the parent organic matter (exogenous, abiotic endogenous, or biological) remains unresolved. Here we evaluate the Murchison (CM2) carbonaceous chondrite as a proxy for organic matter delivered to the surface of Mars by meteoritic and interplanetary dust particle infall over geologic timescales. We characterize the generation of chlorinated hydrocarbons during the pyrolysis of Murchison in the presence of 1 and 5 wt.% calcium perchlorate. Experiments produced a suite of C 1 ‐C 7 chlorinated hydrocarbons dominated by aromatic species, including compounds detected by both Viking and SAM. Increasing the perchlorate content from 1 to 5 wt.% did not amplify the relative abundances or diversity of chlorinated products but rather preferentially oxidized parent organics. Results suggest that organics detected at Gale crater represent a fraction of molecules liberated from a macromolecular source that is compositionally consistent with meteoritic organic matter. Unambiguously resolving the origin and diversity of Martian organic matter may ultimately require the coordinated laboratory analysis of samples returned to Earth.

doi:10.1029/2026je009887.title: Magnetopause Surface Waves at Jupiter and Their Potential Link to Polar Auroral Pulsations
doi:10.1029/2026je009887.summary: Abstract A surface wave is a mechanical wave propagating along the interface between two media, such as the magnetopause. Planetary magnetopause surface waves influence mass and energy circulation in interplanetary space, magnetospheres, and coupled ionospheres and atmospheres. Although surface waves have been extensively investigated on Earth and Saturn, their characteristics on Jupiter require further investigation. Our analysis of Juno in situ data reveals periodic magnetopause crossings consistent with a large‐scale surface‐wave interpretation. The Doppler‐shifted source‐period range overlaps a 13.7‐min auroral periodicity observed by the Hubble Space Telescope on the same day. This correspondence motivates a hypothesized link between magnetopause surface waves and polar auroral pulsations that remains to be tested with simultaneous observations, field‐line mapping, and precipitation diagnostics. The occurrence of surface waves in Jupiter’s rapidly rotating, strongly magnetized environment further suggests that such waves are a broadly shared feature of planetary magnetospheres and may contribute to energy coupling under diverse conditions.

doi:10.1029/2026je009971.title: 3D Radiative Transfer Simulations for Characterization of the Optically Thick DART Ejecta Plume
doi:10.1029/2026je009971.summary: Abstract The Hyperion package is a three‐dimensional Monte‐Carlo radiative transfer approach to modeling dust ejecta. Because it has proven to be a powerful tool for simulating optically thick environments with complicated structure, we are applying the routines to observations of the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) impact on asteroid Dimorphos. Our analysis focuses on the LICIACube LUKE red‐filter image acquired 175 s after impact, when the near‐surface plume remained dense and not strongly structured. The model incorporates the updated Dimorphos shape model, spacecraft and solar geometry derived, and size‐dependent scattering properties of realistic dust particles. We adopt an axisymmetric conical ejecta geometry and iteratively adjust the particle size distribution (PSD) and vertical number density profile to reproduce observed brightness profiles extracted from the LUKE image. We find that a power‐law PSD with slope and a number density peak located at approximately 120 m above the surface best reproduces the brightness contrast between the illuminated surface, the bright ejecta plume, and the adjacent dark band produced by shadowing within the optically thick material. The resulting best‐fit model implies a total ejecta mass of kg within 500 m of the impact site.

doi:10.1029/2026je010064.title: Climatology of the Martian Northern Dayside Ionosphere Across Different Phases of Solar Cycles 24–25 Using MAVEN Spacecraft
doi:10.1029/2026je010064.summary: Abstract The Martian ambient plasma environment varies with solar activity; however, the evolution of the topside ionosphere across different phases of solar cycles (SC) 24–25 remains a key research gap in planetary space research. This study uses NASA's Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN (MAVEN) mission data (150–500 km) from Martian Years 32–37 (2015–2024) during solar quiet‐time conditions to characterize the northern daytime topside ionosphere (e − , CO 2 + , O 2 + , NO + , OH + , O + , N + , and C + ) across SC 24–25 phases. The ionosphere shows a significant seasonal and latitudinal variation, with higher densities at low latitudes (0–30°N) than at mid‐latitudes (31–60°N) throughout the SC. The topside ionosphere dependence on solar zenith angles (SZAs; 10–60°) is not significant below 350 km; however, ionosphere shows little variability above 400 km at higher SZA across SC phases. Additionally, the dayside ionosphere densities vary strongly with SC phases, with the highest densities during solar maximum than during weaker phases. Electron and molecular ion densities increased by factors of ∼1–5 and 1–13, respectively, while O + density enhances by ∼ 2–2.5 times, along with an upliftment of ∼40–50 km in peak height. The enhanced dayside plasma densities during the solar maximum are attributed to elevated EUV/SXR irradiance (∼1.4–6 times) compared to other phases. An increase of 33%–66% in solar wind electron flux, along with enhanced magnetic fields during SC maximum, likely also contributes to the enhanced dayside ionization. This study, for the first time, uses long‐term MAVEN observations across the descending‐to‐maximum phases of SC 24–25 to reveal the climatology of the Martian daytime topside ionosphere.

doi:10.1029/2025je009488.title: Spatio‐Temporal Variability of Topside Layers in Mars’ Dayside Ionosphere Using Near‐Simultaneous Mars Express and MAVEN Conjunctions
doi:10.1029/2025je009488.summary: Abstract This study investigates the spatio‐temporal variability of topside ionospheric layers over the strong crustal magnetic fields and an unmagnetized region in the southern hemisphere of Mars with multipoint observations between Mars Express (MEX) and Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN (MAVEN) very close in time and space. We identified 79 events between 2014 and 2021 when both spacecraft trajectories nearly overlapped. Four of these events, all from 2015 and in the dayside ionosphere, are selected: three occur over crustal field regions and one over an unmagnetized region. We analyze the ionosphere using radar sounding observations from the Mars Advanced Radar for Subsurface and Ionospheric Sounding (MARSIS) on MEX and compare them to in situ ionospheric measurements by the Langmuir Probe and Waves instrument on MAVEN. From across the four events of this study, a comparison of observations from both spacecraft shows the potential motion of topside ionospheric layers, which exhibited maximum displacements of ° in latitude (149.4 km), 5.4° in east longitude (337.6 km), and up to 28 km in altitude over a span of 8–43 min. The electron densities of some of these structures increase by up to a factor of 2.6 during the same period of time. In this study, we demonstrate small and rapid variability occurring in the topside ionosphere of Mars, which was only possible to observe thanks to multispacecraft and near‐simultaneous observations.

doi:10.1029/2026je009716.title: Sediment‐Rich Flow Morphology and Stratigraphy as Records of Emplacement Pressures on Mars
doi:10.1029/2026je009716.summary: Abstract Abundant geologic evidence suggests that sediment transport by liquid water on Mars took place across a wide range of atmospheric pressures, from at least ∼100 mbar in the Noachian‐Hesperian to ∼7 mbar average of today. Because these low pressures do not occur naturally on Earth, experimental studies in Mars pressure chambers are required to understand and interpret sediment flows and their deposits. Previous experimental studies show that low surface pressures (∼5–13 mbar) affect the transport and deposition of sediments by liquid water. Building on these studies, we conducted experiments to explore how pressure affects the morphology and stratigraphy of warm‐temperature (>293 K) basaltic sediment‐rich flows under varying Mars‐like pressures (7–1,013 mbar), representative of warmer conditions in the Noachian, Hesperian, and Amazonian epochs. At low pressures, over a warm surface, vaporization‐related processes dominate, resulting in deposits with numerous lobes and surface features like vugs, levees, and high surface roughness and slope. Their stratigraphy is characterized by wavy to convoluted bedding that is laterally discontinuous, consistent with burial and entrainment. In contrast, at higher pressures, deposits have sub‐planar bedding, fewer lobes, and surfaces lacking vugs and levees. Our results suggest that sedimentary deposits formed under periods of low atmospheric pressure may be distinguished from deposits formed under the denser and wetter conditions of early Mars and on Earth based on differences in morphology and stratigraphy. Identifying pressure‐dependent differences could help constrain the atmospheric conditions under which sedimentary deposits formed, providing insights into the climatic evolution of Mars.

url:https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-b.title: Ask Ethan: Do polonium radiohalos support a young Earth?
url:https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-b.summary: One of the most beautiful things about science is that if even one single piece of robust evidence comes along that contradicts even our most deeply held ideas about reality, it means that our current way of thinking about things must be revised. The observations of Mercury’s orbit in the late 1800s led to the overthrow of Newtonian gravity; the observation that energy was quantized into discrete entities led to the birth of quantum physics; the observation of ultra-faint, variable stars in Andromeda led to the discovery of extragalactic objects and, soon after, to the expanding Universe. Wherever a seemingly contradictory observation occurs, there’s a chance for advancing our best scientific picture of how the Universe works. We have to take immense care to make sure we don’t fool ourselves, but that applies in both directions. We have to make sure we don’t fool ourselves when it comes to accepting the established picture, but we must also make sure we don’t fool ourselves by believing flawed evidence that claims to undermine it. How is one to know what’s going on when different people who claim to be experts make inconsistent, contradictory assertions? That’s what Bob Brown wants to know, writing in to ask: “I received this article — ‘Polonium Radiohalos: Strong Evidence Against Millions of Years’ — from a friend… I’m at a loss as to how anyone should explain to him how this scenario just isn’t possible. Any insights you can provide will be greatly appreciated.” One of the hallmarks of the scientific enterprise is to be able to consider an idea, even an “out there” alternative idea, and subject it to rigorous scrutiny. If it holds up, it cannot be discarded, no matter how absurd it sounds. However, if it crumbles beneath the weight of evidence, it cannot be viable. Let’s take a good look at what’s going on with this new claim. The Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary layer is very distinct in sedimentary rock, but it’s the thin layer of ash, and its elemental composition (especially its severe iridium enhancement), that teaches us about the extraterrestrial origin of the impactor that caused the mass extinction event, enabling us to conclude that it was a carbonaceous asteroid of likely either the CM or CR type. Earth has hundreds of meters worth of sedimentary rock covering its surface practically everywhere, with limestone making up about 10% of the sedimentary rock in total. Credit : James van Gundy The conventional view of planet Earth is that it is, indeed, approximately 4.5 billion years old. The Sun and the Solar System itself is slightly older, while the Earth-Moon system was formed by a collision between two large protoplanets: a proto-Earth and a Mars-sized body named Theia. While many lines of evidence support an old Earth, including: various layers of sedimentary rock with older metamorphic rock beneath them, a fossil record dating back more than 3 billion years, and our knowledge of solar physics, indicating the lifetime of the Sun, the strongest evidence comes from radiometric dating : the measurements of elements and isotopes that arise from the radioactive decay of precursor elements that were present initially on our world. By their very nature, minerals contain a wide variety of elements and isotopes: some of which are stable and others of which aren’t stable, with the unstable ones instead undergoing radioactive decay. Those decays often proceed in a chain: continuing until a final, stable product is reached. If you can know the initial concentration of the (parent) decaying element, the half-life of every element in the decay chain, and can measure the concentration of the (daughter) end product, you can calculate the age of the rock. Those are a lot of “ifs,” of course, but we’ve done that for Earth and for many other bodies in the Solar System, obtaining ages for Earth rocks in the billions of years and for several meteorites of around 4.55-4.56 billion years. That’s the conventional view. This animated version shows the lead isotope isochron that Clair Patterson first used to determine the age of the Solar System and of Earth back in 1956. The animation further shows progressive growth over 4550 million years of the lead isotope ratios within meteorites; the relationship between the lead 207-204 vs. lead 206-204 is key. Credit : Jmpalin/Wikimedia Commons However, there’s a new assertion out by Jake Hebert , claiming that the conventional age of billions of years for the Earth is wrong, and that even millions of years is too long. Instead, he claims that radioisotope dating supports an age that’s just thousands of years old for the Earth: an age that’s consistent with the claims of biblical creationism . This specific claim is that one should look at rocks known as Phanerozoic granites, and at features — or inclusions — within them known as polonium radiohalos. While Hebert notes that the conventional picture claims that these radiohaloes are typically under 541 million years old and that nuclear decay rates (like the laws of physics) are a constant over time, he instead puts forth the idea that the decay rates were accelerated a few thousand years ago, and that the radiohalos from decaying polonium survive as the evidence of that. To understand what he’s claiming, let’s go through what he states, but let’s do it in a way that compares what he’s asserting against the conventional story told by geologists, geophysicists, and nuclear physicists to see where there’s agreement and when there’s something he’s suggesting that’s outside of the realm of what’s generally accepted. New Zealand’s Split Apple Rock is composed of granite, and dates back to the Cretaceous period more than 65 million years ago. The cause of the split down the rock’s center was a naturally occurring joint, and was likely broken apart by a combination of rains and ocean waves. Granite is generally a product of magma or lava that has cooled, and often naturally contains fractures where minerals, veins, or inclusions frequently appear. Credit : Rosino/flickr First, Hebert talks about granites in general (and Phanerozoic granites in particular) as having formed like any igneous rock: when hot magma cools and solidifies. He notes that zirconium silicate crystals often form within these granites, and that sometimes there’s a chemical substitution of (radioactive) uranium for zircon in these crystals. This part is generally true. Granite is a common igneous rock, and it’s generally formed when magma comes to Earth’s surface and erupts (becoming lava, but that’s not an important detail), flows over the land, and cools, becoming solid rock. During the time that the rock is in the liquid state — as magma or lava — any radioactive decays that occur will produce daughter particles that don’t remain; alpha particles (or helium nuclei) become gas and escape, while only the ultimately stable daughter particle persists. It’s for this reason that measuring things like the uranium-to-lead ratio (or the potassium-to-argon ratio, among other radioactive tracers) allows you to date how long it’s been since a rock has formed: since it solidified. The part about this being a Phanerozoic granite just means that it comes from the geological Phanerozoic period : approximately dating from the beginning of the Cambrian period and extending to the present time. Therefore, by definition, it covers the time period of the past 539 million years or so, and Phanerozoic granites represent rocks formed during this time period. So far, this is in full agreement with what’s presently understood. This diagram shows an illustration of the decay chain of a uranium-238 nucleus: resulting in the ultimate production of the stable element lead-206. In total, 6 beta decays and 8 alpha decays occur, but several of the alpha decays are at very similar energies such that, when examined under microscopy, only five separate “rings” can be seen within any uranium halo. Credit : Tosaka/Wikimedia Commons Hebert then goes on to describe how — once a solid rock containing uranium is formed — a decay chain process occurs. This is indeed true. Overall, uranium’s most common isotope starts with 146 neutrons (U-238), and: after a half-life of 4.5 billion years, decays to thorium-234, which very quickly (after 24 days) decays to protactinium-234, which again very quickly (after 1.2 minutes) decays to uranium-234, which then (after 245,000 years) decays to thorium-230, which afterward (after 75,000 years) decays to radium-226, which in the next step (after 1600 years) decays to radon-222, which swiftly (after 3.8 days) decays to polonium-218, when very rapidly (after 3.1 minutes) either decays to astatine-218 (1.5 seconds) and then to bismuth-214, or to lead-214 (27 minutes) and then to bismuth-214, which after another 20 minutes, decays either to polonium-214 (0.16 milliseconds) and then to lead-210, or first to thallium-210 (1.3 minutes) and then to lead-210, and then, after 22 years, undergoes a decay either to bismuth-210 (5 days), polonium-210 (138 days), and then to lead-206, or a decay to mercury-206 (8.3 minutes), thallium-206 (4.2 minutes), and then to lead-206. At last, lead-206 is stable, and so when that product is reached, no further decays come about. Note how long the initial lifetime of uranium-238 is (4.5 billion years) compared to all of the intermediate products that come after. That’s why nearly 100% of the initial uranium-238 that begins in a sample will either still be uranium-238 or will have converted into lead-206. There will be tiny, trace amounts of the other elements/isotopes present at any given moment, where a total of eight alpha particles (helium-4 nuclei) and six beta particles (electrons) are emitted during the full decay chain process. This view of an Allanite mineral with a pleochroic halo consists of a thin, 30 micron section exhibiting defect-containing inclusions with dark halos around them: arising from alpha particles emitted from a radioactive decay chain occurring within the uranium (and uranium-descended) elements within them. Credit : Petr Hykš/flickr Hebert states that these eight alpha particles per parent uranium nucleus come in a spectrum of energies, and he’s right. He states that if you have enough uranium in one deposit, you’ll get a discolored halo from this radioactive material (a radiohalo) around it, where the higher-energy alpha particles produce longer-length tracks and the lower-energy particles produce shorter length tracks: again, correct. And then, the more uranium you start with and the more time that passes, the darker your radiohalo appears. All of this is in agreement with the consensus picture. Now, here’s where we get into the meat of the assertion. I’ll break it up into three chunks, so we can analyze each one separately. 1.) Hebert notes that, in some locations, you don’t see a large discolored halo with eight rings, indicative of a uranium-238 parent nucleus, but rather a smaller, less-discolored halo: sometimes with just three, two, or even one ring: indicative of polonium-218, polonium-214, or polonium-210 alone. 2.) And then, since you need hundreds of millions of alpha particles to form a radiohalo, that conventionally means you must have had hundreds of millions of years pass in order to create these radiohalos. But since polonium isotopes live only for days (or less), there’s no way to produce a radiohalo without starting from uranium, and therefore the standard picture is wrong. This diagram shows how a radioactive source (center) emits a spherical halo of alpha particles over time, and shows a series of pleochroic halos, or radiohalos, as viewed under microscopy. Some radiohalos are larger than others, with 5 rings for a typical uranium-based radiohalo, but with fewer rings (between 1 and 3) for polonium-based radiohalos, which are typically found embedded in or at the interface of a different mineral than the more common uranium radiohalos. Credit : Andrew Snelling/Institute for Creation Research 3.) Hebert then argues that in order to produce what he calls an “orphan” polonium radiohalo, you need to have produced a very large number of polonium atoms all at once, and then swiftly transport them a short distance away to a single, isolated location that’s nearby the original uranium halos. Therefore, the standard picture is wrong, and an alternative pathway — and Hebert proposed one that involves rapid, accelerated decays in the past, hydrothermal fluid flow, and rapid transport, allegedly occurring during the Biblical flood — is required to explain what we see. These are the three key statements that are at the core of what Hebert is asserting. But are they true? The first assertion is close. It’s true that, in theory, since there are eight steps to a typical radioactive decay of U-238, you’d expect eight concentric rings to appear. However, the energies of several steps in the radioactive decay chain are very close together; you can only discern up to five concentric rings under a lighted petrographic microscope. But if you have a polonium-218 halo (or a radon-222 halo), you indeed do see only three rings: one from Po-218, one from Po-214, and one from (the indistinguishable overlap of) Rn-222 and Po-210. (The immediate daughter products of U-238, which are U-234, Th-230, and Ra-226, also overlap to make one indistinguishable ring.) This image shows a magnified view of zircons enclosed in the mineral biotite: a common location where uranium pleochroic halos are found. Tiny crystals rich in radioactive material emit alpha particles, which causes discolorations in a halo-like configuration surrounding the inclusions themselves. Credit : Strekeisen/Wikimedia Commons For the second assertion, you do indeed need hundreds of millions of alpha particles to form a radiohalo in granite. If you start from U-238, you do indeed need hundreds of millions of years to pass for a radiohalo to form. And there’s plenty of uranium inside the Earth’s interior; it’s one of the heaviest elements abundantly produced in processes like supernovae that created the material that our pre-solar nebula formed from, and its radioactive decay generates a significant fraction of the Earth’s interior heat. However, uranium constantly decays inside the Earth, including in magma chambers. When it does, several of its immediate downstream products — thorium, protactinium, and radium — can be solid or liquid, depending on temperature. However, the next step in the decay chain after radium is radon: a gas. When you create a gas within a liquid, even if that liquid is magma, it rises until it gets trapped against a solid-bodied chamber: a crack, vein, or crevice of solid rock, for instance. Radon diffuses as a neutral gas along or through fractures. As was shown by Lorence and Barbara Collins many years ago , “daughter” atoms, including radon (which becomes polonium after its next decay) are continuously being produced within the Earth within magma chambers: a veritable “sea” of radon-producing (and hence, later on, polonium-producing) material. This image shows a fracture-rich section of coarse-grained igneous rock: syenite in this case. Fractures and other features are common in various forms of igneous rocks depending on the temperature that they cool and form at, and mineral-rich veins and inclusions can often be found where different types of igneous rocks form. Credit : James St. John/c.c.-by-2.0 And finally, the third key assertion is that polonium radiohalos are found nearby the uranium ones, and that an alternative scenario to the standard picture must be invoked in order to explain such a localized density of rapidly-decaying polonium atoms. But there’s a problem: polonium halos are not found in the same kind of granite where uranium halos are found . Granite that contains polonium halos occurs in rocks that have formed at temperatures above 700 ºC: rocks that have already crystallized and become solid by the time temperatures cool to 450 ºC, whereas granite that crystallizes from molten rock (which contains the uranium radiohalos) won’t have the necessary fractures within it so that the radon and polonium can collect at a particular, localized site. Only when the temperatures drop below about 150 ºC (300 ºF) do the alpha particles begin to leave trails in the (now-solid) rock, creating these radiohalos. Depending on how much time passes between when the radon gas collects in pockets and fractures and when enough cooling has occurred for the temperature to drop sufficiently for radiohalos to form is what determines whether: three-layered radiohalos (common for quick-cooling environments, if it cools in less than a week or so), two-layered radiohalos (very rare, if cooling takes about 1-2 weeks), or a one-layered radiohalo (common for slow-cooling environments that take months-to-years to cool) winds up forming. Instead of invoking an alternative scenario — one favored by creationists — to explain the presence of polonium radiohalos, you simply need to apply the actual geophysical conditions present in the Earth’s interior where these features ultimately originate. And again, this is in an environment that’s different, embedded in a different type of granite, from where the uranium radiohalos, with five observed layers, are typically found. This cross-section of pink granite showcases several dark, discolored inclusions: candidates for pleochroic halos, which are associated with the radioactive decay of either deposits of uranium-238 or the daughter decay particles arising from U-238 decays. Depending on where in the decay chain the radioactive atoms are concentrated and “frozen in,” a varying number of concentric rings can be found in these halos. Credit : Radioactive_Rocks/Reddit But there’s a more fundamental problem with this type of claim that’s very different from, “I’ve found something unusual that led someone to challenge the scientific consensus on an issue.” The point of this was not to claim that someone had found evidence that supported a conclusion other than the one accepted by the scientific mainstream. The point was to go out and find a line of reasoning that could, whether scrupulously or disingenuously, be used to convince people that mainstream science had our origin story wrong, and that the conclusion reached by Young Earth Creationists was correct instead. This is a hallmark tactic of pseudoscientists: to craft an argument that most legitimate scientists in the mainstream will be unfamiliar with, and that will require the general public to digest and process a large amount of information to understand it. Instead of a complex, nuanced story that involves synthesizing together a large suite of information to understand it properly, they tell a simple, disingenuous story that can be told quickly and simply, but that takes a mountain of evidence to debunk. From global warming deniers to those attempting to link vaccines and autism to the “alcohol is good for you, actually,” crowd to creationists and more, this technique of invoking Brandolini’s law — that the amount of energy needed to refute bullshit is an order of magnitude bigger than that needed to produce it — is as true today as it’s ever been. In this life, it’s important to be open and curious about ideas that are out of the mainstream, but if you care about getting things right, it’s even more important to be rigorous, honest, skeptical, and thoughtful. Without those traits, and without adhering to what the evidence actually states, we cannot have a constructive conversation. Send in your Ask Ethan questions to startswithabang at gmail dot com ! url:https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-b.title: NASA’s next flagship to answer the biggest question: “Are we alone?”
url:https://bigthink.com/starts-with-a-b.summary: There are a few questions that humanity has always pondered, yet scarcely could satisfactorily answer until the proper scientific advances came along. Questions like: What is the Universe? Where did it come from? How did it get to be this way? And what is its ultimate fate? These are questions that have been with us since time immemorial, yet remained unanswerable for nearly all of human history. Beginning in the 20th century and now into the 21st century, many of these questions are finally getting comprehensive answers thanks to incredible advances in physics and astronomy. However, perhaps the biggest question of all — the question of “Are we alone in the Universe?” — remains as perhaps the greatest existential unanswered question of all. While the current generation of ground-based and space-based telescopes can take us far into the Universe, this is a question that’s currently the reach of any observatory that presently exists. To get there, we’ll need to acquire direct images of Earth-like exoplanets: planets with sizes and temperatures similar to Earth, but that orbit Sun-like stars, not the more common red dwarf stars like Proxima Centauri or TRAPPIST-1. Those capabilities are precisely what NASA is aiming for with its next flagship mission: the Habitable Worlds Observatory . It’s an ambitious project, sure, but one that’s well worth it. After all, finding out we’re not alone in the Universe would quite possibly be the biggest revolution in all of science history. This animation shows the four super-Jupiter planets directly imaged in orbit around the star HR 8799, whose light is blocked by a coronagraph. The four exoplanets shown here are among the easiest to directly image owing to their large size and brightness, as well as their huge separation from their parent star. Our ability to directly image exoplanets is constrained to giant exoplanets at great distances from bright stars, but improvements in coronagraph technology will dramatically change that story. Credit : Jason Wang (Northwestern)/William Thompson (UVic)/Christian Marois (NRC Herzberg)/Quinn Konopacky (UCSD) At the present time, there are three main ways we’re actively searching for alien life . We’re exploring worlds in our Solar System, including Mars, Venus, Titan, Europa, and Pluto, remotely and in situ , with fly-by missions, orbiters, landers, and even rovers, searching for evidence of past life or even, potentially simple life that persists at the present time. We’re examining exoplanets, searching for evidence that there’s life on them, from the surface to the atmosphere and beyond, based on observable signatures of color, seasonal change, and atmospheric contents. And by looking for any signals that would reveal the presence of intelligent aliens: through efforts such as SETI and Breakthrough Listen. All three approaches have their advantages and disadvantages , and so it makes sense to invest in all three. As long as we don’t find anyone else, we’ll have no choice but to wonder whether we’re alone or not . However, once we have a successful example of life that originated outside of Earth, we’ll know for certain that we have company here in the cosmos. Given the sheer number of chances that are out there, most scientists believe that it’s the second option that’s most likely to deliver our first success. If life requires conditions similar to those found on Earth, we might well be the only world in the Solar System where life ever developed, survived, thrived, became technologically advanced, and still exists at the present time. Unless there are other intelligent, actively broadcasting civilizations nearby right now, endeavors like SETI won’t be able deliver any positive results. However, “life of any type” is a much lower bar than actively-transmitting intelligent, technologically advanced civilizations. If even a small fraction of worlds that exist with Earth-like properties have life of any type on them, exoplanet studies can deliver a success where the other two options won’t. And we’ve come a very long way in our studies of exoplanets: we have more than 6000 known, confirmed exoplanets within the Milky Way, where we know the mass, radius, and orbital period of nearly all of those confirmed worlds. Although more than 6,000 confirmed exoplanets are now known, with more than half of them uncovered by Kepler, there are no true analogues of the planets found in our Solar System. Jupiter-analogues, Earth-analogues, and Mercury-analogues all remain elusive with current technology. The overwhelming majority of planets found via the transit method are close to their parent star, are ~10% the radius (or, equivalently, ~1% the surface area) of their parent star or more, and are orbiting low-mass, small-sized stars. Credit : NASA/Ames/Jessie Dotson and Wendy Stenzel; annotated by E. Siegel Unfortunately, this isn’t enough to inform us about whether any of these worlds are inhabited. To make that determination, we need more than that. We’d need to be able to make the necessary measurements that could answer such questions as: Does the exoplanet have an atmosphere? Does it have clouds, precipitation, and weather cycles? Do its continents green-and-brown with the seasons, like they do on Earth? Does it have gases or gas combinations in its atmosphere that hint at biological activity, and do they show seasonal variations like Earth’s CO2 levels do? On the cutting edge of performing these measurements, today, are the space-based JWST and ground-based 10-meter class telescopes, performing direct exoplanet imaging and transit spectroscopy. But even those great observatories are not enough to reach the goal we’re truly after. JWST and 10-meter ground-based telescopes cannot measure the properties of Earth-sized planets in Earth-like orbits around Sun-like stars. For direct imaging studies, we can take pictures of planets that are the size of Jupiter and that are more than about Saturn’s distance from the Sun: good for gas giant worlds, but not so great for looking for life on rocky planets. For transit spectroscopy, we can see the light that filters through the atmospheres of super-Earth-sized worlds around red dwarf stars, but Earth-sized planets around Sun-like stars are well beyond the reach of current technology. When starlight passes through a transiting exoplanet’s atmosphere, signatures are imprinted. Depending on the wavelength and intensity of both emission and absorption features, the presence or absence of various atomic and molecular species within an exoplanet’s atmosphere can be revealed through the technique of transit spectroscopy. JWST cannot get spectra for Earth-sized planets around Sun-like stars, but Habitable Worlds Observatory finally will. Credit : ESA/David Sing/PLAnetary Transits and Oscillations of stars (PLATO) mission We have, however, come far enough to know that if we can scale up our technology, acquiring that data for the exoplanets we truly desire is possible. What we need to do is build on our current technology and enhance it further if we hope to find and characterize an actually inhabited planet. Currently, we’re building the next generation of ground-based telescopes, ushering in the era of 30-meter class telescopes with the GMTO , the ELT , and potentially Exo-Life Finder as well , and looking forward to the exquisite performance of the coronagraph aboard NASA’s next astrophysics flagship mission: the Nancy Roman Telescope. The Roman telescope will have the same capabilities as Hubble but with superior instrumentation, a field-of-view that’s 50-100 times as great as Hubble’s, and a coronagraph that allows us to image planets within the glare of their parent star’s light that are about 1000 times fainter than JWST can see. A critical test will arrive very soon, when Roman attempts to image a faint stellar companion that can sufficiently test its coronagraphic capabilities ; if it succeeds, it means we’re on track to directly image Earth-like worlds around Sun-like stars with the planned Habitable Worlds Observatory. Our technology does not remain stagnant, nor do our visions for discovery and exploration. Each decade, the National Academy of Sciences gets together to outline the highest priorities for astronomy and astrophysics, making recommendations as part of a decadal survey. Four flagship missions were proposed at the most recent (Astro2020) decadal: Lynx , a next-generation X-ray observatory, especially important given the reduced scope of the ESA’s upcoming Athena mission, Origins , a next-generation far-infrared observatory, filling a colossal gap in our wavelength coverage of the Universe, HabEx , a single-mirror telescope designed to directly image the very nearest Earth-like planets, and LUVOIR , an ambitious, giant segmented telescope that would be an astronomical all-purpose “dream” observatory. Ideally, the new space telescope Habitable Worlds Observatory, with capabilities between those of the previously-proposed HabEx and LUVOIR (shown here), will be large enough to image a large number of Earth-like exoplanets directly, while still having the desired properties to keep it on-budget and not require the development of wholly new, untested technologies. This observatory, known as Habitable Worlds Observatory, will be NASA’s next flagship mission after the Nancy Roman space telescope. Credit : NASA/GSFC, LUVOIR concept While the recommendation was that three of these four eventually be constructed, Lynx and Origins took a back seat to what was selected as the highest-priority mission: a scaled-up version of HabEx (or a scaled-down version of LUVOIR), taking features of both HabEx and LUVOIR into account to form the Habitable Worlds Observatory. In many ways, the proposed specification hit precisely in the “sweet spot” between feasibility given current technology, discovery potential given what we do and don’t know, and cost effectiveness, incorporating lessons learned from the problems and successes experienced along the way in the construction, design, and launch of JWST. The specifications proposed for Habitable Worlds Observatory are very encouraging. So far, the design includes: a segmented optical mirror design, similar to what’s already in use by JWST, an improved version of the coronagraph technology that’s presently equipped aboard the Roman Telescope, up-to-date sensors that can control the various mirror segments to achieve ~picometer-level stability (orders of magnitude better than JWST or current ground-based optical telescopes), planned compatibility with next-generation rockets that will be flying in the late 2030s/early 2040s, planned robotic servicing of components at the L2 Lagrange point, located ~1.5 million km from Earth, but, other than that, no wholly new technologies that haven’t been fully matured prior to the development/construction phase. The most expensive components of JWST were the all-new ones; with Habitable Worlds Observatory, there is nothing that’s all-new. This is extremely encouraging, as it presents an achievable plan that isn’t particularly susceptible to the delays and overruns that plagued JWST. Without the need to develop wholly new technologies, the path to getting a Habitable Worlds Observatory to the specifications we require is one of incremental improvement, rather than of wholesale invention. The prospect of detecting and characterizing the atmosphere of a true Earth-like planet, i.e., an Earth-sized planet in the habitable zone of its star, including both red dwarf and more Sun-like stars, is within our reach. With a next-generation coronagraph, a large ultraviolet-optical-infrared mission could find dozens, or even hundreds, of Earth-sized worlds to measure. Credit : National Academies/Astro2020 decadal survey With these capabilities, the Habitable Worlds Observatory will have an excellent chance to reach what’s perhaps the holy grail of astronomy: to reveal an actually inhabited planet to humanity for the very first time. With between a 6.0 and 6.5 meter primary mirror design, comparable to JWST in size and light-gathering power, it should be able to directly image Earth-sized planets around all of the stars within about ~14 light-years of Earth. Scientists on the design team will fight for every little bit of extra diameter they can get, because that’s what counts the most in this game; if you can double the radius you can see planets out to, you increase the search volume and the expected number of objects by a factor of eight. In the vicinity of the Sun, there are: 9 star systems within 10 light-years of Earth, 22 star systems within 12 light-years of Earth, 40 star systems within 15 light-years of Earth, and 95 star systems within 20 light-years of Earth. With its currently-planned design, somewhere between 20 and 30 Earth-like planets could be directly imaged by the Habitable Worlds Observatory. With a slightly scaled-up diameter, that number could easily be increased to around 100. If there’s even a ~few percent chance (or ~1%, in the upscaled scenario) of life taking hold on an Earth-like world, then this mission will likely bear the ultimate fruit: discovering our first inhabited planet beyond the Solar System. Perhaps, if nature is kind, we might even discover more than one. This graphic shows the location of the closest star systems beyond the Solar System, centered on the Sun. If you can double the radius out to what you can see and measure, you encompass eight times the volume, which is why the ability to see farther even by a little bit vastly increases your chances to find something remarkable, even if it’s a rare type of system you’re seeking. Roughly every few hundred thousand years, a star will pass within 120,000 AU (a little less than 2 light-years) of Earth: coming within the estimated size of the Oort cloud. Credit : Andrew Z. Colvin/Wikimedia Commons Because we’ve already gone through the pain of developing many of the precursor technologies, including: the 5-layer sunshield used with JWST, the folded/segmented mirror design used with JWST, and the deformable mirror used within the Roman coronagraph, there shouldn’t be anything wholly new or novel to trip up the Habitable Worlds Observatory like there was with JWST. However, all new developments come with risks. The idea of robotic servicing is encouraging, because we’ve done robotic servicing before, but only as far away as in low-Earth orbit. At the distance to L2, 1.5 million kilometers, even instructions sent at the speed-of-light have a 10 second round-trip delay. Upgrading the telescope and its instruments in orbit, i.e., the “servicing” component of the mission, will require both rocket technology and automated robotic technology that will need to be developed and matured. To achieve ~picometer level mirror alignments is a technical challenge that requires advances far beyond the ~nanometer-level alignments achievable today. Although this requires only an incremental improvement over existing technology, a substantial set of resources will need to be devoted to it, and are currently being devoted as part of the “technology maturation” process inherent in the design and pre-design phases. One big worry that hasn’t necessarily hit the right people’s radar is the suitability of the currently-designed Roman coronagraph for the Habitable Worlds Observatory. The JWST coronagraph is performing exactly as anticipated, enabling us to find and image planets that are just 1-part-in-100,000 as bright as their parent stars are. The Nancy Roman Telescope expects a factor of 1000 improvement over JWST, as their deformable coronagraph mirror is being optimized to deal with the interference patterns and stray light that emerges from a perfectly circular coronagraph shape. However, there’s a catch: one of the reasons that the Nancy Roman Telescope’s coronagraph can perform so much better than JWST’s is because JWST has a tiled mirror with a segmented design, while the Nancy Roman telescope will have a single, circular, monolithic mirror. The shape of the JWST mirror is why it has that “snowflake-like” diffraction pattern around all of its stars and bright point-sources of light: that’s just a mathematical consequence of the geometry of its optics. Since the architecture of the Habitable Worlds Observatory is slated to include a tiled primary mirror, this may pose a new set of compatibility difficulties. The point spread function for the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as predicted back in a 2007 document. The four factors of a hexagonal (not circular) primary mirror, composed out of a set of 18 tiled hexagons, each with ~4 mm gaps between them, and with three support struts to hold the secondary mirror in place, all work to create the inevitable series of spikes that appear around bright point sources imaged with JWST. This pattern has been affectionately called the “nightmare snowflake” by many of JWST’s instrument scientists. Credit : R. B. Makidon, S. Casertano, C. Cox & R. van der Marel, STScI/NASA/AURA After all, coronagraphs are circular in nature, and cannot easily “undo” the stray light that gets introduced from any sharp edges, including: the hexagonal tiles, the “corners” on the outer edges of the mirror, and the ~millimeter-sized “gaps” between the various segments. With a similar design to JWST, this seems like a very big problem for Habitable Worlds Observatory to reckon with, particularly since it needs coronagraphy that’s successful at the 1-part-in-10,000,000,000 (1-part-in-ten-billion) level to image Earth-like worlds around Sun-like stars: another factor of ~100 better than the Roman coronagraph will achieve. However, there’s still the possibility that a larger-bodied rocket, capable of launching a monolithic mirror of diameters of 6.0 meters or more (and perhaps even up 8.4 meters : the largest monolithic mirrors we can reliably produce), will be available by the time the Habitable Worlds Observatory moves to its final design stage. If that occurs, this problem evaporates, and the mission becomes much less dependent on overcoming a difficult, never-before-faced problem. This artist’s concept shows the geometry of a space telescope aligned with a starshade, a technology used to block starlight in order to reveal the presence of planets orbiting that star. From tens of thousands of kilometers away, the starshade and the telescope must achieve and maintain perfect alignment to enable direct exoplanet imaging. Compared to a coronagraph, a starshade’s optics are superior, but far fewer stellar systems can be probed in any given amount of time. Credit : NASA / JPL-Caltech A different potential solution is to launch a starshade either with the Habitable Worlds Observatory or even after-the-fact, to block the target star’s light before it ever reaches the Habitable Worlds Observatory’s primary mirror. Although this is technologically feasible, it’s both expensive and limited in its effectiveness; it has to travel some ~80,000 kilometers relative to the observatory every time it wants to switch targets. (However, there is evidence that such a starshade could be multi-purpose, and leveraged with ground-based observatories as well.) All told, the addition of a starshade can help the Habitable Worlds Observatory potentially image about one or two systems per year, meaning that it could allow for dozens or even scores of sufficiently imaged systems. An intermediate solution that perhaps should be considered is neither building a traditional segmented mirror nor a single monolithic mirror, but a series of circular mirrors, akin to the optical setup of the presently under-construction Giant Magellan Telescope . With seven perfect circles instead of 18+ tiled hexagons, it has the light-gathering power of the area of all seven circles combined, but the resolution of the diameter across which the primary mirrors are mounted. With this design: all of the stray light problems from a JWST-like design are eliminated, the already-developed foldable primary mirror technology could still be utilized, the picometer-level stability technology being developed across mirror segments would still apply, and instead of a single secondary mirror and/or a single coronagraph, each of the seven segments could get their own. As a bonus, there would be no wires required to cross the primary mirror optics, as the secondary mirror(s) could be held in place with wires that went in-between the gaps in the circular segments: precisely why the Giant Magellan Telescope will be the first world-class observatory without diffraction spikes on its stars. The 25-meter Giant Magellan Telescope is currently under construction, and will be the greatest new ground-based observatory on Earth. The spider arms, seen holding the secondary mirror in place, are specially designed so that their line-of-sight falls directly between the narrow gaps in the GMT mirrors, creating a view of the Universe without sharp corners to its mirrors or diffraction spikes around its stars. As one of the two US Extremely Large Telescopes proposed by astronomers and currently in development, it is an essential part of bringing about a new generation in cutting-edge ground-based astronomy facilities. Credit : Giant Magellan Telescope/GMTO Corporation With the right design and implementation, and the technology maturation pathway laid out by NASA’s astrophysics division, we could be looking at a Habitable Worlds Observatory: that launches as early as the late 2030s/early 2040s, that’s on-budget and on-time, that possesses the necessary architecture to achieve its observational goals without needing a starshade, that’s fully refuellable and whose instruments are fully serviceable and replaceable, that could have a starshade upgrade added to it at any point in the future, and that quite possibly images enough “Earth-like” planets to discover at least one (and maybe even more than one) exoplanet that’s actually inhabited. The big question that needs to go into the design of this telescope is the trade-off between how many Earth-like candidates it can directly image versus how large and costly the telescope is going to be. While the 6-to-7 meter range seems like the sweet spot, the nightmare scenario is that we build this observatory just a little too small and cost-conservatively to find what we’re ultimately seeking: an inhabited alien planet. We’d hardly regret it if we built one that was large enough that we sampled enough of the Universe to find more than one inhabited planet! We must remember that in the search for life beyond Earth, we are playing a lottery with unknown odds. Each Earth-like planet that we image and characterize represents a ticket: a ticket in a lottery where the odds of all of the prizes are unknown. Our chances of success depend entirely on which tickets are winners and whether we buy enough of them. The hard part is we won’t know if we have meaningful constraints on what those odds actually are until after the findings from Habitable Worlds Observatory come in, and so it’s up to us to build it in such a way that our odds of at least one success are as great as possible. If we do, we might finally have the answer to “Are we alone in the Universe?” Just maybe, we’ll know for certain that the answer is, “No, there are others.” This article was first published in February of 2023. It was updated in November of 2026. This article NASA’s next flagship to answer the biggest question: “Are we alone?” is featured on Big Think . Space & Astrophysics

doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02137-4.title: Methane outburst driven by magma–sediment interactions at Fentale Volcano detected by satellite
doi:10.1038/s41561-026-02137-4.summary: Abstract Magmatic intrusions into sedimentary rocks can release carbon-based greenhouse gases, dominantly methane, and have been linked to rapid changes in past climate. However, modern volcanic systems typically emit very little methane, meaning that appropriate analogues are lacking. Here we report satellite measurements of an outburst of methane and carbon dioxide from a restless but non-erupting volcano in the East African Rift. Following a mega-dyke intrusion in 2025, Fentale Volcano (Ethiopia) released at least 38.2 ± 3.9 kt CH 4 over 3 months and at least 2.9 ± 1.0 MtCO 2 . The peak methane emission rate of 157 ± 41 t h −1 is comparable to major industrial blowouts and approximately four orders of magnitude higher than methane emission rates from other volcanic systems. The emissions coincided with localized ground subsidence and thermal anomalies within Fentale’s caldera. We propose that the intrusion disrupted an impermeable cap beneath which methane, derived from hydrocarbon-rich sediments, was trapped. This single outburst is small compared with annual emissions from natural and anthropogenic sources, but demonstrates an unrecognized source of episodic methane emissions, providing insight into greenhouse gas release from magmatic–sedimentary systems.

doi:10.1126/science.aeg4265.title: Atmospheric organic nitrogen is a major nutrient source to global oceans
doi:10.1126/science.aeg4265.summary: Atmospheric nitrogen (N) deposition is a critical nutrient source for marine ecosystems, but its organic nitrogen (ON) component remains poorly quantified. We measured ON in marine aerosols collected during 21 research cruises transecting multiple ocean basins and both hemispheric high latitudes. We used these observations to constrain and evaluate an atmospheric chemistry model with updated ON sources and sinks, enabling global mapping of ON deposition. The model estimated annual ON deposition to oceans at 12.8 (4.0 to 22.7) teragrams of nitrogen per year (Tg N year −1 ), contributing 27% (11 to 40%) of total N deposition. Marine emissions supply 3.9 (0.7 to 6.9) Tg N year −1 (30%) of deposited ON, while terrestrial sources contribute 8.9 (3.3 to 15.7) Tg N year −1 (70%). In N-limited regions such as the central Atlantic and Indonesian seas, ON accounts for ~50% of total N deposition.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16545-2026.title: Saharan dust transport and boundary layer entrainment over western Europe: multi-instrument observations and convection-permitting model evaluation
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16545-2026.summary: Saharan dust transport and boundary layer entrainment over western Europe: multi-instrument observations and convection-permitting model evaluation Hengheng Zhang, Gholam Ali Hoshyaripour, Heike Vogel, Frank Wagner, Thomas Leisner, Jochen Förstner, Prabhakar Shrestha, and Harald Saathoff Atmos. Chem. Phys., 26, 16583–16597, https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-26-16583-2026, 2026 We implement a blowing-snow sea salt aerosol parameterization in the TM5 atmospheric chemistry transport model and the EC-Earth3 climate model, evaluating it against observations from the Multidisciplinary drifting Observatory for the Study of Arctic Climate (MOSAiC) expedition and Arctic stations. doi:10.5194/acp-26-16599-2026.title: Environmental moisture and stability controls on raindrop size distribution within convective clouds under sheared conditions
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16599-2026.summary: Environmental moisture and stability controls on raindrop size distribution within convective clouds under sheared conditions Takashi Unuma Atmos. Chem. Phys., 26, 16599–16614, https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-26-16599-2026, 2026 The microphysical features of convective clouds were examined, reflecting environmental conditions in idealised setups. Larger temperature lapse rates produced larger raindrops, and increased lower-tropospheric moisture produced more small raindrops, both increasing rainfall intensity. Weaker wind shear reduces raindrop evaporation under humid conditions and reduces vertical variations in size distribution whilst keeping its shape, thereby increasing rainfall amounts.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16571-2026.title: An overlooked kinetic relaxation in the formation of sesquiterpene-derived criegee intermediates
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16571-2026.summary: An overlooked kinetic relaxation in the formation of sesquiterpene-derived criegee intermediates Hengjia Ou, Yao Li, Yuqing Sha, Hui Zhou, Jingkun Jiang, and Kunpeng Chen Atmos. Chem. Phys., 26, 16571–16582, https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-26-16571-2026, 2026 We studied the kinetic relaxation in the formation of Criegee intermediates (CIs) from sesquiterpene ozonolysis. We found that the formation rate constant of sesquiterpene-derived CIs is initially unstable but gradually approaches a plateau that equals the rate constant of sesquiterpene ozonolysis. This kinetic relaxation may enable new reaction channels, such as radical reactions with primary ozonides (POZs), which could alter the fate of atmospheric sesquiterpenes.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16465-2026.title: A potential emergent constraint on cloud liquid water path adjustments to aerosol–cloud interactions
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16465-2026.summary: A potential emergent constraint on cloud liquid water path adjustments to aerosol–cloud interactions Johannes Mülmenstädt and Po-Lun Ma Atmos. Chem. Phys., 26, 16465–16476, https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-26-16465-2026, 2026 Aerosols emitted by human activities change the planetary energy budget by, among other mechanisms, changing how much liquid water is contained in clouds and thus their reflectance. Different lines of evidence (observations and models) disagree on the sign of the liquid water change even though they agree on the sign of the correlation between aerosols and liquid water in present-day internal variability. We show one way that observations can constrain models to resolve this disagreement.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16477-2026.title: Molecular composition of wintertime haze over the northern Indian Ocean suggests extensive atmospheric processing during transport
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16477-2026.summary: Molecular composition of wintertime haze over the northern Indian Ocean suggests extensive atmospheric processing during transport Karin Stegelius, Pauline Thompson, Pia Karbiener, Piotr Markuszewski, Andre S. H. Prevot, Sachchida N. Tripathi, Claudia Mohr, Liine Heikkinen, Krishnakant Budhavant, and Sophie L. Haslett Atmos. Chem. Phys., 26, 16477–16500, https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-26-16477-2026, 2026 High-time-resolution observations in the Maldives indicate that submicron aerosol over the northern Indian Ocean is primarily composed of inorganic sulfate and highly oxidised organic matter, indicative of aged continental outflow. The consistent composition across various air mass origins, alongside identification of sulfur-containing organics, underscores the influence of long-range transport and sulfate-driven secondary chemistry on regional aerosol characteristics and their climate impacts.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16521-2026.title: Insights into the chemical and physical drivers of surface ozone in the Trans-Himalaya
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16521-2026.summary: Insights into the chemical and physical drivers of surface ozone in the Trans-Himalaya Imran A. Girach, Mehul R. Pandya, Tabish Ansari, Sonam Angmo, Subrat Sharma, Bipasha Paul Shukla, Aditya Vaishya, Lokesh Kumar Sahu, Tim Butler, and Narendra Ojha Atmos. Chem. Phys., 26, 16521–16543, https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-26-16521-2026, 2026 We investigated variabilities in free-tropospheric ozone (O3) over the Trans-Himalaya, one of the most climate-sensitive regions. Daytime O3 buildup, a unique feature not observed over high-altitude mountains, is mainly governed by photochemistry and entrainment. Manmade NOx emitted outside South Asia is a larger contributor to O3. Seasonal cycle, shaped largely by stratospheric inputs and biogenic emissions of precursors, peaks in June, unlike April-May over the Himalaya and Gangetic regions.

doi:10.5194/acp-26-16501-2026.title: Measurement report: Tethered balloon observations of vertically resolved aerosol size distributions during the U.S. DOE ARM CoURAGE and BNF campaigns
doi:10.5194/acp-26-16501-2026.summary: Measurement report: Tethered balloon observations of vertically resolved aerosol size distributions during the U.S. DOE ARM CoURAGE and BNF campaigns Yuhang Guo, Chongai Kuang, Darielle Dexheimer, Peter DeCarlo, Manish Shrivastava, Benjamin Nault, Ogochukwu Enekwizu, Yang Wang, Jingbo Mao, Gan Luo, Fangqun Yu, and Jie Zhang Atmos. Chem. Phys., 26, 16501–16519, https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-26-16501-2026, 2026 Aerosol particle size distributions can vary greatly with height, but these vertical changes are rarely measured directly. Using a tethered balloon, we measured particle size distributions from the ground to about 1.2 kilometers in two contrasting environments. We found that atmospheric mixing strongly shapes their vertical structure, storage overnight, and redistribution the next day. These observations improve our understanding of how aerosol populations evolve in the lower atmosphere.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei1245.title: Predictive model for nanoparticle incorporation into crystals reveals essential role of interfacial solution structure
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei1245.summary: Control of interfacial phenomena remains limited by incomplete understanding of molecular-scale solution structure at solid-liquid interfaces. We address this challenge by developing and validating a comprehensive analytical model for nanoparticle incorporation during crystallization. Using atomic force microscopy (AFM) probes surface functionalized to be “particle proxies” combined with three-dimensional AFM and force spectroscopy, we measure nanoparticle-calcite crystal binding energies and kinetic barriers associated with interfacial hydration layers. These measurements, together with diffusivities, parameterize a predictive model that is corroborated using surface-functionalized fluorescent silica nanoparticles incorporated into calcite. We show that surface chemistry governs incorporation by reshaping the energy landscape, with amine groups particularly favoring incorporation. Applying this approach to nanoparticles with different topologies further supports our finding that kinetic barriers play a pivotal role in incorporation processes. This synthesis science framework links interfacial solution structure, particle dynamics, and crystallization kinetics, identifying kinetic barriers as a key design principle for engineering bioinspired nanocomposites beyond empirical approaches.

doi:10.5194/ar-4-589-2026.title: Isomer-resolved online analysis of organic aerosols using ion mobility mass spectrometry
doi:10.5194/ar-4-589-2026.summary: Secondary organic aerosol (SOA) makes up much of the particulate matter in the troposphere and impacts global climate and human health, although uncertainties regarding the sources and properties of SOA limit our understanding of these effects. New analytical techniques are required to better characterize the molecular composition of SOA, including methods that can identify isomeric compounds that may have different contributions to SOA properties, such as hygroscopicity or volatility. We present a method for isomer-resolved analysis of SOA using a commercially available chemical ionization ion-mobility time-of-flight mass spectrometer (CI-IMS-TOF) and a Vaporization Inlet for Aerosols (VIA). The compatibility of the VIA and the CI-IMS-TOF was assessed through the analysis of 10 carboxylic acid standards across a large temperature range (30–170 °C). Ion drift times were found to be stable to within 0.075 % of their initial values after drift time calibration. The VIA-CI-IMS-TOF was also used to collect real-time ion mobility and mass spectra of SOA constituents during an α -pinene ozonolysis chamber experiment. Several reaction products were identified in the SOA using synthetic standards, including structural isomers of C 8 H 12 O 4 and C 9 H 14 O 4 . Temporal evolution of reaction products was used to assess formation timescales and to determine the generation of oxidation for individual isomers. Both iodide and bromide reagent ions were used in the VIA-CI-IMS-TOF to achieve a more comprehensive analysis of SOA. This study demonstrates the performance of the VIA-CI-IMS-TOF for online, isomer-resolved analysis of organic aerosol and its potential for improving the current understanding of SOA composition.

doi:10.3847/psj/aeb2e8.title: Analyzing Post-asteroid-impact Downstream-flooding Hazards via GeoClaw Flood Modeling
doi:10.3847/psj/aeb2e8.summary: Abstract While large asteroid impacts are relatively uncommon on Earth, it is essential that we prepare for the possibility of an impact that could affect a region or the entire globe. Our level of planning in preparation and mitigation relies on our understanding of both immediate and delayed hazards. This work focuses on potential delayed flooding risk post-asteroid-impact by adopting a hazard timeline similar to the more common and well-documented wildfire–flood sequence. A hypothetical asteroid impact event derived from the 2023 Planetary Defense Conference (PDC) risk corridor is examined as a case study to develop a preliminary downstream-risk data pipeline. This method employs GeoClaw, a physics-based fluid-flow model that solves the shallow-water equations, to simulate the effects from postimpact precipitation caused by the initial impact’s thermal radiation. The flood-simulation output is compared to population data, leading to estimates of overall hazard exposure and loss of life for varying scenarios. Trends in these estimates provide insight into potential downstream-risk severity, the influence of various parameters, and future planetary defense strategies. In this study, downstream flooding hazards have been found to be nonnegligible and therefore relevant for further research.

url:https://www.universetoday.com/articl.title: Sound Waves From Sunspots Launch Fiery Plasma Jets Across the Sun
