doi:10.1038/s41612-026-01579-2.title: Resolution-adaptive generative ensemble prediction with integrated global-to-regional modelling on unstructured meshes
doi:10.1038/s41612-026-01579-2.summary: Abstract Integrated global-to-regional ensemble prediction represents an important frontier in Earth system science, yet its realization is hindered by the prohibitive computational cost of running large ensembles on the associated unstructured variable-resolution meshes. Here we introduce HiRe-EFM, a generative deep learning model designed for integrated global-to-regional large-ensemble weather prediction. To address the dual challenges of geometric complexity and multi-scale information flow, HiRe-EFM employs a geometrically consistent mapping onto hierarchical meshes, implements adaptive cross-scale fusion, and incorporates localized enhancement to restore details in refined regions. Benchmarked against a state-of-the-art baseline on a global variable-resolution simulation dataset, HiRe-EFM improves global CRPS by 12.8% while maintaining well-calibrated ensemble dispersion. Crucially, the improvement rises to 16.1% within high-resolution target areas, demonstrating HiRe-EFM exploits the advantages of global variable-resolution simulations. By accelerating global ensemble forecasting by over three orders of magnitude, this study provides a viable pathway for integrated global-to-regional large-ensemble weather prediction.

doi:10.1038/s41550-026-03010-5.title: The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front
doi:10.1038/s41550-026-03010-5.summary: Abstract The Milky Way is commonly depicted as having four main spiral arms, including the Norma–outer arm, and a central stellar bar whose properties remain debated. Masers associated with young high-mass stars have been used to trace a segment of the ‘Norma arm’ extending from one end of the Galaxy’s central stellar bar. Recent work suggests that these masers may reside along a spiral arm or occupy the dominant x 1 stellar orbits that give the bar its shape. Here we use a new generation of N -body, hydrodynamic simulations to argue that these million-year-old masers instead trace the Galactic bar’s quadrant I shock front or, equivalently, its dust lane. This implies that the bar dust lane is star-forming, shedding new light on our understanding of star formation processes in the Milky Way. By associating the masers with the simulated shock front, we determine the parameters of the bar to be: a ≈ 4.3 ± 0.2 kpc, b ≈ 2.3 ± 0.2 kpc, ϕ = $${{20}_{-2}^{+5}}^{\circ }$$ 20 - 2 + 5 ∘ and Ω p ≲ 40 km s −1 kpc −1 , representing the semimajor and semiminor half-lengths of the bar, the inclination angle and the pattern speed, respectively. This raises questions about the Milky Way’s spiral structure and suggests that the Galactic bar is long, slow and star-forming.

doi:10.1126/science.aeb1122.title: Widespread marine mammal and seabird reductions are unlikely to benefit salmon due to indirect ecosystem effects
doi:10.1126/science.aeb1122.summary: Pacific salmon are depleted due to anthropogenic impacts, and populations have failed to recover despite management interventions. Predation on salmon by pinnipeds and seabirds has been suggested as a barrier to recovery, leading to calls for predator culls by some. However, no studies have evaluated the whole-ecosystem impact of removing these predators nor estimated the direct and indirect effects of these culls on salmon. We use an end-to-end ecosystem model to assess the efficacy of widespread culls in marine environments. We find that culls are unlikely to benefit salmon due to the indirect food web effects of predator reduction and the low biomass of top predator groups. Instead, more abundant fish predators, northward-expanding competitors, and temperature-sensitive prey have larger effects on salmon in the ocean.

doi:10.1126/science.aee2641.title: Balancing redox-mediated cytotoxicity and catalysis in natural product biosynthesis
doi:10.1126/science.aee2641.summary: Redox-mediated chemistry is central to both the biosynthesis and cytotoxicity of many natural products, yet how microbes balance these processes remains poorly understood. Here, we uncover a conserved mechanism that coordinates three redox-mediated processes in secondary metabolite biosynthesis: self-protection, prevention of substrate degradation, and late-stage biosynthesis. Using the antitumor antibiotic doxorubicin as a model system, we show that the vicinal oxygen chelate (VOC) protein DnrV prevents reactive oxygen species formation and substrate degradation while promoting P450 catalysis. We expand this paradigm to a conserved family of VOC-fold proteins, redox-associated cytotoxin-binding proteins (REACT), found across bacteria, fungi, and plants. REACT represents a multifunctional protein class that balances antibiotic assembly, self-protection, and prevention of metabolite destruction, providing a foundational understanding of production of redox-active natural products.

doi:10.1126/science.aei7840.title: Telemetric calorimetry for wireless continuous reaction profiling
doi:10.1126/science.aei7840.summary: Real-time monitoring of chemical reactions is often achieved with specialized instrumentation along with custom-designed reactors or intrusive sampling. In this study, we introduce reaction telemetry, a wireless analytical strategy that enables remote, nonintrusive monitoring directly within operating reaction vessels. This approach uses light-powered microelectronic devices that communicate optically and function as autonomous sensing elements. We demonstrate continuous calorimetric measurements across diverse chemical reactions relevant to pharmaceutical and fine chemical synthesis, including photochemical and electrochemical systems, providing access to reaction kinetics under native operating conditions with subsecond temporal resolution. The resulting measurements will support catalyst evaluation, safety assessment, and mechanistic investigation and will accelerate data-driven reaction discovery. By embedding analytical functionality directly within reaction vessels, reaction telemetry establishes a general framework for information-rich observation of chemical processes across research, development, and education.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2603924123.title: The debt burden of tropical cyclones and climate change
doi:10.1073/pnas.2603924123.summary: Addressing climate change through mitigation and adaptation is expected to require more than $6 trillion in global investment annually by 2035. Yet many countries face significant barriers to accessing this finance, including low or absent credit ratings, large debt burdens, and high borrowing costs. Climate change may further amplify these barriers, creating a “vicious cycle” in which mounting economic losses reduce the capacity of countries to invest in adaptation and mitigation. We provide evidence that the cost and availability of capital for many countries have already been shaped by both historical exposure to naturally-occurring tropical cyclones (TCs) and anthropogenic warming. Our empirical estimates suggest that, on average across TC-exposed countries, 20% of debt-to-GDP ratios are attributable to TCs from 1980 to 2019. Across all countries, GDP levels are on average 12% lower due to the combined impacts of baseline naturally-occurring TCs and anthropogenic warming. In a separate correlational machine-learning analysis, we estimate that these macroeconomic impacts are associated with an increased likelihood of hotter countries receiving credit ratings below investment grade ( < BBB–), as well as persistent credit risk premiums of at least 1 basis point in 64 countries and 5 basis points in highly exposed countries. We provide estimates for 181 countries, including many TC-affected and/or hot countries that do not have bond yield data. Future increases in temperature and TC activity may further worsen sovereign credit conditions, potentially undermining climate resilience and long-run development prospects.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2620401123.title: Diffusive and advective transport in structurally anisotropic fibrous hydrogels
doi:10.1073/pnas.2620401123.summary: Changes in fiber orientation in structurally anisotropic fibrous extracellular matrices govern transport, distribution, and accumulation of biologically active molecules and therapeutic nanoparticles in tissues. Fundamental studies of advection-driven transport in such matrices are challenging because changes in network anisotropy are generally coupled with variation in fiber dimensions, density, and surface chemistry. Here, a fibrous hydrogel was engineered in which the type and degree of fiber orientation were decoupled from these structural characteristics. Advection of charge-neutral nanoparticle probes under physiologically relevant pressure gradients was studied in a channel geometry that imposed spatially nonuniform flow across the fibrous network. The probe advection was quantified by the time of probe permeation through the gel along the fastest flow path and the time of probe distribution within the gel. We show that the permeation timescale was governed by advection along the pressure gradient, whereas the distribution timescale transitioned between advection- and diffusion-limited behavior depending on fiber orientation and probe dimension. The decoupling between these timescales became more pronounced with stronger alignment along the pressure gradient and with increasing probe dimension. Scaling analysis and a fluid dynamics simulation model further provided mechanistic insight into these experimental findings. Together, these results identify the key structural factors governing advection in anisotropic fibrous networks and provide a platform for future studies of the role of fiber orientation in tissues in regulating the transport, distribution, and dissemination of biologically active molecules, exosomes, and nanoparticle therapeutics under interstitial fluid flow.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2523162123.title: Overlooked biodiversity hotspots revealed by a pluralistic approach for quantifying amphibian biodiscovery needs
doi:10.1073/pnas.2523162123.summary: Undocumented and poorly known species spanning Linnean and Wallacean biodiversity shortfalls pose a major challenge to conservation due to the uncertainty they introduce. To address this, we developed a novel pluralistic approach that accounts for sampling gaps, spatial patterns, environmental associations, and varying conservation needs simultaneously, using amphibians as a case study. Using environment-based richness models and species accumulation curves (SACs), we identified areas with high biodiscovery needs for amphibians. These were concentrated primarily in humid tropical South America, sub-Saharan Africa, and East/Southeast Asia. While environmental models produced more reliable richness estimates than SACs overall, SAC-based estimates nonetheless added unique insights, especially in biodiverse, moderately well-sampled areas like Costa Rica and Panama. By integrating environmental models and SACs—thus leveraging combined strengths of previous approaches—our holistic scoring technique also proved consistent in estimating biodiscovery priorities across ecoregions, enabling robust recommendations for future sampling.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2616772123.title: Niche constraints drive differences between mycorrhizal fungal guilds in future range shifts
doi:10.1073/pnas.2616772123.summary: Mycorrhizal fungi are a diverse and ubiquitous group of plant symbionts whose distribution strongly influences ecosystem function across the globe. Yet, until now, we do not have quantitative data on the range sizes of different mycorrhizal fungal taxa, limiting our capacity to forecast future shifts in community composition and function. Here, we use 115,924 DNA sequence-derived observations to map the distribution of 651 common mycorrhizal fungal taxa and forecast future changes to their range sizes. We demonstrate that climate, plant cover, and soil factors, particularly mean annual temperature, net primary productivity, and soil organic carbon, exert major control over mycorrhizal fungal distributions. Based on these drivers, the ecological niches of mycorrhizal fungi consistently differ between arbuscular and ectomycorrhizal functional guilds. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungal taxa generally occupy a wider niche breadth than ectomycorrhizal fungi, occurring across larger ranges of climate, soil, plant cover, topography, and disturbance conditions. Our models also predict widespread decreases in the suitable range size of mycorrhizal fungal taxa under projected future global climates, with average ranges decreasing by 13.8% or ~2.2 million km 2 under high emissions scenarios (ssp5-8.5). This decrease in projected range size will be most pronounced for ectomycorrhizal fungi, strongly linked to constraints from their smaller overall niches. By generating a global atlas of common mycorrhizal fungi and their associated environmental niche, we establish a critical baseline for widely suspected declines in global fungal biodiversity.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2625362123.title: Galectin-3 links microglial neuroinflammation to Aβ aggregation and lysosomal processing
doi:10.1073/pnas.2625362123.summary: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet the molecular mechanisms linking microglial dysfunction to amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify galectin-3 (Gal3) as a regulator of plaque-associated microglial responses, linking Aβ aggregation, lysosomal function, and neuritic pathology. Using postmortem brain tissue from AD patients, we found that Gal3 + microglia preferentially associate with cored plaques and correlate with increased LAMP1 + dystrophic neurites. Gal3 was also detected in microglial lysosomal compartments, extramicroglial dystrophic structures, and in association with extracellular amyloid fibrils, suggesting roles in both intracellular and extracellular Aβ processing. In APP mice, Gal3 deficiency reduced plaque burden and neuritic dystrophy, increased plaque compaction, and enhanced TREM2 coverage around amyloid plaques. Mechanistically, in vitro microglial experiments showed that Gal3 modulates Aβ uptake and lysosomal processing, whereas lysosomal dysfunction promoted the accumulation of fibrillar Aβ from initially monomeric species, particularly in Gal3-deficient cells. Cell-free assays demonstrated that Gal3 preferentially binds fibrillar Aβ, inhibits secondary nucleation, and alters fibril morphology, while Gal3-modified fibrillar Aβ reduces N2a neuronal cell number. Finally, in silico structural analyses identified candidate Gal3 interactors enriched in leucine-rich-repeat and immunoglobulin-like proteins, supporting a role for this lectin in immune receptor regulation. Complementary in vivo transcriptomic profiling showed that Gal3 deletion suppresses type I interferon and microglial neurodegenerative transcriptional signatures. Together, these findings position Gal3 at the interface between Aβ remodeling, lysosomal homeostasis, and plaque-associated microglial responses in AD.

doi:10.1073/pnas.2619331123.title: Linear plasmids mediate antimicrobial resistance gene transfer between environmental bacteria and hospital-adapted enterococci
doi:10.1073/pnas.2619331123.summary: As animal hosts adapted to land, Enterococcus species diverged from a common ancestor shared with Vagococcus species by acquiring genes essential for survival and transmission in the exposed arid environment. In addition to their intrinsic ruggedness, human-associated enterococci now frequently exhibit multidrug resistance, largely driven by the accumulation of antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) on mobile genetic elements (MGEs). However, the source of these resistance elements, their diversity in natural reservoirs, and their risks remain unclear. To investigate clinically relevant ARGs and their associated MGEs in a wastewater-impacted environment, we examined environmental vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE) recovered from a polluted urban river in Hanoi, Vietnam. Whole-genome sequencing of VRE isolates revealed multidrug-resistance pELF-type linear plasmids harboring a fluoroquinolone resistance gene ( qrtA ) encoding a major facilitator superfamily transporter. The qrtA gene appears to have originated on Vagococcus -related chromosomes and may have been mobilized by IS 1216E -associated MGEs. Vagococcus genomes show strong associations between ARGs, IS 1216E, and plasmids related to those in enterococci, and conjugation experiments demonstrated that pELF-type linear plasmids can transfer between Enterococcus and Vagococcus without major fitness costs. Comparative analysis of pELF-type linear plasmids, together with database mining, identified qrtA -positive clinical isolates from geographically separated regions in Asia and Europe, indicating that qrtA is not confined to a single local setting. These findings highlight the need for coordinated international One Health surveillance of ARG and MGE dynamics, including emerging determinants such as qrtA , together with interventions to limit their spread.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeg5378.title: PEG-free tunable poly(2-oxazoline) lipids modulate mRNA-LNP biodistribution and expression in vivo
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeg5378.summary: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have transformed drug delivery, enabling the stabilization and efficient intracellular delivery of nucleic acids. Current LNP platforms, including those used in clinical COVID-19 vaccines, rely on polyethylene glycol (PEG) to stabilize the nanoparticle. However, anti-PEG antibodies are ubiquitous in the population and are a major cause of anaphylaxis and reduced therapeutic efficacy by accelerating the blood clearance of PEGylated products. Here, we report the development of poly(2-oxazoline) (POx) lipids as alternatives. POx polymers are poorly immunogenic and mitigate accelerated blood clearance. Upon varying polymer hydrophilicity and molecular weight, we screened transfection efficiency in multiple cell lines and evaluated top candidates in vivo. Our findings demonstrate that POx-lipids incorporating short hydrophilic oxazoline chains enhance target transfection while mitigating liver expression. These POx-lipids boost expression in key extrahepatic tissues, including lymph nodes and spleen. This marks a notable advancement toward replacing PEG in LNP therapies and provides a clear path to optimizing POx-lipids for targeted vaccine and therapeutic applications.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei1820.title: Dual-modality photoacoustic and optical coherence tomography imaging simultaneously tracks transplanted stem cells and their viability
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei1820.summary: Monitoring transplanted cell viability in vivo, noninvasively remains a considerable challenge. By using multiwavelength photoacoustic microscopy powered by a reactive oxygen species (ROS)–responsive contrast agent, we can relatively and semiquantitatively assess and longitudinally monitor the viability of human-induced pluripotent stem cell–derived retinal pigment epithelium (hiPSC-RPE) cells in vivo. The contrast agent comprises colloidal chain-like gold nanoparticle (CGNP) clusters conjugated with IR775c, a heptamethine cyanine dye that undergoes selective oxidative quenching under elevated ROS conditions associated with cellular death (CGNP-IR775c). Dual-wavelength photoacoustic microscopy at 620 and 775 nanometers provides self-calibrated ratiometric measurements that enable relative viability assessment, distinguishing healthy from nonviable cell populations. In vitro studies demonstrated that CGNP-IR775c exhibited biocompatibility and showed dose-dependent ROS sensitivity across physiologically relevant H 2 O 2 concentrations. hiPSC-RPE cells labeled by CGNP-IR775c were subretinally transplanted into living rabbit eyes and longitudinally monitored for 2 weeks, showing that laser-induced oxidative stress produced measurable photoacoustic signal changes that were consistent with the viability status of the transplanted cells. The imaging technology developed here provides a practical solution for noninvasive, longitudinal, and semiquantitative assessment of the transplanted cell viability in vivo, and may contribute to ophthalmology cell-based therapy in both preclinical and clinical settings.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei7767.title: Asymmetric interactions and feast-famine cycles drive chaos in microbial populations
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei7767.summary: Predicting the dynamics of ecological systems is a central challenge in biology. One factor that may limit predictability is ecological chaos. Theory has long suggested that even simple interactions can produce chaos, yet empirical demonstrations in living systems remain scarce. In a two-strain system of Escherichia coli , increasing the duration between resource replenishment reveals transitions from competitive exclusion to chaos, driven by asymmetric ecological interactions and periodic environmental forcing. Guided by these observations, we developed a dynamical systems framework grounded in empirical data that recapitulate the observed dynamics and predicts intermediate ecological states and transitions. Experimental validation of these predictions by implementing the corresponding conditions successfully reproduces the full range of predicted dynamical regimes. Because feast-famine cycles and asymmetric interactions are widespread in nature, our findings provide a model for uncovering the ecological and evolutionary significance of chaos, opening avenues to use resource fluctuation and interaction strength to quantify, monitor, and manipulate complex ecosystem behavior previously interpreted as stochasticity.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei7801.title: The importance of organics in hydrothermal environments: A synchrotron laboratory study
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aei7801.summary: The icy moon Enceladus has hydrothermal plumes that are of astrobiologic interest as they could provide conditions to sustain life or allow for its origin. To understand the geology of hydrothermal environments on icy moons, a carbonaceous asteroid simulant similar to the material Enceladus may have accreted from was subjected to conditions analogous to that of its seafloor. The sample environment used allowed high-resolution in situ synchrotron x-ray diffraction data to be collected during the experiment. Mineral reactions were observed as they occurred. Multiple mineral reactions had a large dependence on organic matter. Organics catalyzed the breakdown of aluminosilicates and dissolved pyrite. Melanophlogite and pyrrhotite were also formed as a result of organics being present. This study reveals that organics can have a large impact on mineral reactions and likely play an important role in the geology of hydrothermal vents on icy moons, which have an abundance of organics.

doi:10.1126/sciadv.aek9035.title: Resolving the black hole sphere of influence in a hyperluminous obscured quasar at redshift 4.6
doi:10.1126/sciadv.aek9035.summary: Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) imprint gravitational signatures on the matter within their sphere of influence (SoI). Nuclear gas dynamics can hence be used to accurately measure the mass of an SMBH, yet these measurements remain elusive in the early universe. We report the first dynamical measurement of an SMBH mass at z > 2, based on high–spatial resolution observations of the ionized-carbon 157.7-micrometer and carbon monoxide (12-11) 216.93-micrometer emission lines that resolve the SoI in an obscured quasar at z = 4.6. The radial profile of the velocity dispersion reveals a clear Keplerian rise, requiring the presence of an ∼6 × 10 9 –solar mass SMBH. We propose that heavily obscured quasars allow such tracers to survive in the inner regions and may be ideal targets for increasing dynamical SMBH mass estimates in the early universe.

doi:10.1029/2026je009973.title: Magnetic Field Pressure Imbalance at Mars and Heavy Ion Transport From Ionosphere to Magnetosheath
doi:10.1029/2026je009973.summary: Abstract In the absence of an intrinsic planetary magnetic field, the interaction of the solar wind with unmagnetized planets produces a plasma system with vertical scales comparable to an ion gyroradius. Such small spatial scales render the interface between the solar wind and planetary plasmas highly variable and structurally complex. The ionosphere–magnetosheath boundary plays a key role in mediating the transfer of energy and momentum from the solar wind to planetary ions, thereby influencing the long‐term atmospheric escape of the planet. Mars provides a natural laboratory for studying this interaction, where the boundary thickness can be as small as ∼20 km, which, combined with typical spacecraft velocities of ∼3 km/s, requires time resolutions of 5 s to adequately resolve boundary crossings. To date, MAVEN is the only mission capable of meeting these requirements, and it has accumulated sufficient observations to enable statistical investigations. Unlike previous studies, this work employs an epoch‐style analysis in which individual orbit segments crossing the ionosphere–magnetosheath interface are analyzed case by case and aligned relative to local plasma conditions, rather than binned in fixed planetocentric coordinates. This approach accounts for variability in boundary location and enables a statistical characterization of interface properties. Each crossing is characterized by plasma density gradients, magnetic field conditions, and the penetration of heavy planetary ions across the boundary. The epoch‐style analysis shows that magnetic pressure imbalances are associated with sharper density gradients, while enhanced heavy ions leakage occurs under weak magnetic field conditions, indicative of near‐radial magnetic field configurations.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06446.title: Integrating Lattice and Molecular Oxygen Pathways to Enhance Toluene Oxidation via Mn Substitution in Fe x Co3– x O4 Spinel
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06446.summary: Abstract Activation of lattice oxygen and molecular oxygen critically governs the catalytic degradation of volatile organic compounds (VOCs), driving substantial research into harmonizing the bonding state of oxygen atoms in transition-metal oxides to facilitate VOCs abatement. However, the underlying mechanism of oxygen activation via cation substitution in spinel remains to be explored owing to its significant flexibility in both tetrahedral and octahedral sites. Herein, a Mn-substituted FexCo3–xO4 spinel catalyst was developed for promoting oxidation of toluene (one of the typical aromatic VOCs), with the temperature of 90% toluene conversion decreasing by approximately 51 °C relative to the pristine one. Multiple characterizations and theoretical calculations revealed that Mn3+ substitution at octahedral Co3+ sites of FexCo3–xO4 modulated the metal–oxygen bonds within the Mn–O–Co structure for activating surface lattice oxygen, accompanied by the creation of abundant oxygen vacancies for O2 excitation. The combined results of temperature-programmed analyses, isotopic labeling experiments, and in situ spectroscopy showed that the adsorbed toluene could be synchronously oxidized by activated lattice oxygen and chemisorbed oxygen generated via O2 activation, thereby accomplishing the deep oxidation of toluene. This study clarifies the synergistic role of lattice and molecular oxygen in toluene oxidation and affords a potential catalyst for environmental remediation.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12709.title: Unveiling the Hidden Load: High Flux and Deposition Dynamics of Atmospheric Microplastics in the North China Plain
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12709.summary: Abstract Atmospheric microplastics (MPs) play an important role in the transport of MPs across diverse environmental media, yet their annual deposition dynamics across heterogeneous urban–cropland regions remain poorly understood. We conducted a one-year field campaign at three contrasting sites in the North China Plain (NCP): Beijing (BJ, urban), Tianjin (TJ, industrial/coastal), and Handan (HD, agricultural). Atmospheric bulk-deposition samples were characterized for particle deposition rates, size, morphology, and polymer composition, with observations evaluated using meteorological and land-cover information. Deposition rates were significantly higher in BJ than in TJ (p < 0.05) and HD (p < 0.001). Median (interquartile range) deposition rates were 34640 (18703–90472), 14367 (6000–25810), and 6990 (3903–11790) items m–2 d–1 in BJ, TJ, and HD, respectively. Small particles (20–50 μm) dominated particle abundance (80.7%), whereas fragments dominated particle morphology (90.4%). Backward trajectories indicated seasonal differences in potential air-mass transport pathways. Integrating particle mass estimates with land-cover data yielded order-of-magnitude estimates of annual atmospheric MP inputs of approximately 6 Gg to urban areas and 17 Gg to cropland in the northern NCP. These results reveal pronounced spatiotemporal variability in atmospheric MP deposition and highlight the dominance of small MP fragments across urban and cropland ecosystems.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07111.title: Purple Phototrophic Bacteria as a Novel Platform for Coenzyme Q10 Production from CO2, Syngas, and Sulfur Waste Byproducts
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07111.summary: Abstract The efficient conversion of CO2 and industrial waste streams into value-added products remains a critical challenge for sustainable microbial processes. Here, we present the first systematic demonstration of purple phototrophic bacteria (PPB) as platforms for the autotrophic valorization of CO2 and industrial off-gases or sulfur byproducts into valuable metabolites. Genome-guided screening combined with experimental validation identified strains capable of coupling photoautotrophic growth with the production of CoQ10 and carotenoid pigments. Among them, Rhodospirillum rubrum DSM 467 and DSM 107 exhibited the highest performance, maintaining stable CO2 and H2 consumption under semicontinuous operation and accumulating up to 9.6 ± 0.2 mgCoQ10 gbiomass–1 under CO2/ H2 conditions, comparable to engineered production systems. In addition, R. rubrum DSM 467 efficiently oxidized CO from syngas via the water–gas shift reaction, displaying hierarchical substrate utilization driven by energetic constraints. In contrast, Marichromatium purpuratum simultaneously oxidized H2 and thiosulfate (S2O32–), enabling parallel electron input into the photosynthetic electron transport chain and enhanced growth. Overall, these results establish PPB as robust and metabolically flexible biocatalysts for converting CO2 and industrial waste streams into high-value chemicals with direct applications in the pharmaceutical and nutraceutical industries.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.5c16364.title: Advancing Environmental Justice Research within and beyond Science and Engineering
doi:10.1021/acs.est.5c16364.summary: Abstract Scientists and engineers have historically approached questions of environmental justice (EJ) differently from social scientists and humanists, from how they formulate problem scope to how they propose solutions. While scientists and engineers have assessed distributional injustices extensively, there are opportunities for deeper interdisciplinary collaboration with other EJ schools of thought. In this Perspective, we first present an EJ schematic for a science and engineering audience, where we trace epistemologies within EJ schools to show how EJ scholars conceptualize knowledge, how this relates to their methods, and how they present and publish work. We survey the EJ literature─mainly work related to the United States─across disciplines to determine major tensions within EJ and between EJ, science, and engineering scholarship. We also discuss possibilities for enabling interdisciplinary collaboration for scientists and engineers working on EJ-related questions by analyzing epistemological compatibilities. Next, we highlight opportunities to facilitate collaboration through an illustrative interdisciplinary case study. We conclude with takeaways for scientists and engineers moving forward, alongside some of the challenges accompanying interdisciplinary EJ research.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06287.title: Direct Evidence for Carbon Monoxide-to-Dioxin Conversion via Fly-Ash-Catalyzed Sequential Reactions in Incineration Flue Gas
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06287.summary: Abstract The formation of polychlorinated dibenzo-p-dioxins and dibenzofurans (PCDD/Fs) in industrial thermal processes is traditionally attributed to solid carbon precursors via de novo synthesis. Carbon monoxide (CO), despite serving as an operational indicator of incomplete combustion, has not been directly implicated as a molecular carbon source for dioxin generation. Here, we provide definitive experimental and mechanistic evidence that CO can be catalytically converted into dioxins and dioxin-like compounds through a sequential reaction network mediated by fly ash. Using fixed-bed reactors packed with real fly ash, we isolate CO, H2O, and HCl as minimal reactants to reconstruct flue-gas chemistry. Transition metal species (Cu, Fe) in fly ash catalyze CO conversion via a coupled water–gas shift and Fischer–Tropsch-type process, generating a wide spectrum of aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons. Concurrently, fly ash mediates HCl oxidation to active Cl2, enabling chlorination of these intermediates into chlorobenzenes and chlorophenols, which subsequently evolve into polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), polychlorinated naphthalenes (PCNs), and ultimately PCDD/Fs. Notably, Cl4–8DD/F congeners account for >90% of the formed PCDD/Fs, consistent with de novo synthesis signatures. This work establishes a new mechanistic paradigm for dioxin generation and highlights CO emission control as a critical lever for mitigating toxic pollutant generation.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12991.title: Evaluating Emergency Emission Controls During an Unprecedented Regional Haze Event Using Causal Machine Learning
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12991.summary: Abstract Emergency emission controls are widely implemented to mitigate severe haze, yet their effectiveness is difficult to disentangle from meteorological variability and concurrent changes in activities. Here, we develop a three-step evaluation approach integrating air quality meteorological normalization, augmented synthetic control, and machine-learning prediction to causally quantify intervention-attributable changes in local emission strength and ambient pollutant concentrations. Applied to Shijiazhuang’s unprecedented 45-day “Sharp Sword to Cut Haze” campaign in 2016, the approach revealed that local emission strengths of PM2.5, PM10, SO2, NO2, and CO were reduced by 4.3%, 4.8%, 15.8%, 5.8%, and 15.3%, respectively. Corresponding concentrations fell by 42.1 (14.8%), 47.4 (12.4%), 13.8 (16.6%), 15.8 (15.5%) μg·m–3, and 0.9 mg·m–3 (19.6%). Observation-based PM2.5 source apportionment results independently supported these estimates: contributions from vehicle emissions, steelmaking, and coal combustion were 4.1%, 11.0%, and 21.7% lower, respectively, than during the corresponding period in 2017. Despite stringent controls, PM2.5 averaged 243.2 μg·m–3 during the intervention period. Thus, stringent local controls substantially reduced emissions, but regional transport and unfavorable meteorology partly offset the resulting air quality benefits, highlighting the need for coordinated regional mitigation.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c04589.title: Economic Potential of Nuclear Power in the Transportation Sector: Analysis of E-Fuels as An Alternative Fuel for Total Cost of Ownership and Vehicle Emissions
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c04589.summary: Abstract Advanced nuclear reactors could expand U.S. nuclear energy beyond electricity generation into transportation by supplying heat and power for hydrogen and synthetic hydrocarbon fuel production. We evaluated nuclear-enabled hydrogen for fuel cell electric vehicles (FCEVs) and nuclear-derived electro-fuels (e-fuels) for internal combustion engine vehicles (ICEVs) and hybrid vehicles across selected light-, medium-, and heavy-duty classes. Economic performance was assessed using total cost of ownership (TCO), and environmental performance was evaluated using life-cycle emissions. We then estimated carbon abatement costs for alternative fuel/vehicle pathways relative to conventional gasoline and diesel systems. Our findings indicate that conventional ICEVs fueled by gasoline or diesel generally remain the lowest-cost options in 2035. For small sport utility vehicles (SUVs), however, hybrid vehicles using nuclear-based e-fuels and battery electric vehicles (BEVs) with home charging increase TCO modestly relative to gasoline vehicles, while e-fuels achieve the lowest emissions among the alternatives. In long-haul trucking, hydrogen and e-fuels show potential, with marginal TCO increases relative to conventional systems and relatively low abatement costs. Although hydrogen and e-fuels produced with advanced nuclear reactors remain relatively expensive, continued advances in reactors, electrolysis, and fuel synthesis, together with scale economies, could improve competitiveness, diversify transportation fuel options, and reduce emissions.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c05850.title: Convergent Biogenic Magnetite Formation from Diverse Iron (Oxyhydr)oxide Precursors Drives Cr(VI) Reduction via an Environmental Battery Mechanism
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c05850.summary: Abstract Iron (oxyhydr)oxides mediate electron flux across coupled biogeochemical cycles in anoxic environments, yet whether their biogenic transformation feeds back to reshape interfacial electron transfer efficiency remains unresolved. Here, five structurally distinct iron (oxyhydr)oxide precursors (ferrihydrite, goethite, magnetite, wüstite, and hematite) were exposed to anaerobic sulfur-oxidizing bioreactors under Cr(VI) stress, and their transformation trajectories were tracked using synchrotron EXAFS spectroscopy, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, DFT calculations, and metagenomic profiling. Mineral bioavailability decreased in the order ferrihydrite > goethite > magnetite > wüstite > hematite, a hierarchy governed by lattice iron-leaching energetics quantified via DFT (Efev from −8.96 eV for ferrihydrite to 5.76 eV for hematite). Despite this wide disparity in precursor lability, all biotransformation trajectories converged on magnetite as the thermodynamically stable end point. In the ferrihydrite system, biogenic magnetite reached 60% of the final solid phase and operated as an in situ “environmental battery” (storing and releasing electrons through reversible Fe(II)/Fe(III) lattice cycling), lowering interfacial charge transfer resistance and producing a 4.77-fold higher pseudo-first-order Cr(VI) reduction rate constant than the mineral-free biotic control (C-S). Metagenomic analysis revealed mineral-specific restructuring of the microbial community toward a tightly coupled sulfur–iron redox network. These results reframe precursor mineralogy from a determinant of intrinsic reactivity to a kinetic regulator of biogenic electron-buffer formation, providing a mechanistic basis for mineral-informed bioremediation design.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07569.title: Phage-Based Biofilm Control in Engineered Water Environments
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07569.summary: Abstract Biofilms represent a predominant bacterial lifestyle and contribute to the ecological stability and biochemical functioning in water systems. Paradoxically, excessive biofilm formation threatens water security and public health by causing biofouling, harboring pathogens, and facilitating the transmission of antimicrobial resistance. Phage treatment offers a promising strategy for the targeted regulation of biofilm microecology without generating harmful disinfection byproducts. However, its performance in environmental settings can be constrained by spatiotemporal heterogeneity, suboptimal phage exposure, and the evolution of phage resistance in bacteria, creating additional challenges for engineering applications. Here, we synthesize phage-based biofilm control as a multilevel intervention paradigm organized by biological bottlenecks. We examine strategies that improve transport and host access, enhance targeting and productive lysis, induce biofilm disruption through prophage activation, and perturb biofilm communities through keystone-centered interactions. We then align these intervention principles with distinct biofilm scenarios and operational constraints in engineered water environments. Emerging technologies are evaluated according to their roles in target identification, validation under application-relevant conditions, and treatment monitoring. Finally, we propose a closed-loop framework encompassing system diagnosis, intervention design and validation, monitored deployment, and adaptive management. Overall, this Review provides an integrated roadmap for advancing scalable and sustainable phage-based biofilm control in engineered water environments.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c03752.title: River Plastic Retention and Export across Europe
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c03752.summary: Abstract Rivers play a central role in the global distribution of plastic pollution. Despite recent research showing that the majority of plastic is not transported to the sea, most plastic transport models have not explicitly included plastic retention in rivers. We propose a new model to quantify micro- and macroplastic retention on land and in rivers, and export toward the sea. Of the 3.55 Mt year–1 of plastics emitted to the environment, only 0.1% of microplastics and 0.5% of macroplastics are exported from the river outlet. This results in 16.9 (15.7–35.1) kt year–1 of microplastic and 3.2 (1.4–12.1) kt year–1 macroplastic export. Rivers store plastic, retaining 159.0 (147.8–330.6) kt year–1 of microplastics (5.3%) and 67.4 (29.7–255.4) kt year–1 of macroplastics (2.5%), while the greatest proportion of plastic remains on land. Although large basin size and high plastic emission to land characterize high absolute micro- and macroplastic retention and export, large basin size is a weaker predictor for high plastic retention and export per capita. By aggregating ranks for plastic export and retention, we provide a new and comprehensive outlook on the most polluting rivers of Europe. This work provides crucial baseline estimates for plastic pollution in light of missing plastic reduction quotas to guide future prioritization and assessment of mitigation actions.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c13075.title: Chasing Bubbles: Toward a Standardized Approach for Quantifying Methane Ebullition Using Bubble Traps in Streams and Rivers
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c13075.summary: Abstract Ebullition transports large quantities of the potent greenhouse gas methane (CH4) from stream sediments into the atmosphere. However, the use of different sampling designs complicates comparisons of CH4 emissions estimates between studies. Here, we present the first systematic review of sampling designs used in the past for assessing fluvial CH4 ebullition rates. In addition, we conducted field experiments to estimate the optimal number of bubble traps and the length of the sampling period, and to assess uncertainties in determining CH4 content in the emitted bubbles. Our results demonstrate considerable spatial variability in bubble fluxes (0–4.8 L m–2 d–1) and CH4 content in the bubbles (0.01–67%), necessitating a larger number of bubble traps than typically deployed in streams. Using fewer traps leads to greater deviations in CH4 ebullition estimates than shorter deployment times. Therefore, the robust sampling design should account for strong small-scale heterogeneity in streams through an adequate number of bubble traps and link bubble fluxes to trap-specific gas content. It should also consider the risk of CH4 concentration decreases in accumulated bubbles over a few days, primarily due to redissolution, followed by oxidation and leakage.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c02846.title: Heavy-Duty Diesel Vehicle Deterioration: Impact of Vehicle Age and Emission Control Technology on NO x Emissions
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c02846.summary: Abstract This study examines the effect of aging and deterioration on NOx emissions from heavy-duty diesel trucks (HDDTs) with different emission control technologies, including Engine Control only, exhaust gas recirculation (EGR), and selective catalytic reduction (SCR). In-use tailpipe emissions were measured from 12,023 HDDTs from 13 roadside measurement campaigns conducted in California and Utah between 2008 and 2024. Vehicle registration records and the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) engine certification database were used to identify engine NOx control technology. At younger ages, SCR-equipped HDDTs generally emitted significantly less NOx than non-SCR-equipped HDDTs. However, after several years of aging, NOx emissions from SCR-equipped HDDTs were comparable to or exceeded those from non-SCR-equipped HDDTs across locations, engine manufacturers, and engine model years. Although cumulative lifetime emissions from SCR-equipped HDDTs remained lower than non-SCR HDDTs, the reduction in lifetime NOx emissions was substantially smaller than estimated by EPA’s MOtor Vehicle Emission Simulator (MOVES). MOVES predicts an 80% reduction in lifetime NOx emissions from SCR-equipped HDDTs, whereas our estimate is approximately 32%. These findings may indicate that the long-term benefits of SCR for reducing HDDT NOx emissions are smaller than expected and highlight the need for continued emissions monitoring of in-use HDDTs.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08647.title: Winter and Summer Differences in Oxylipin Responses to Ambient Particles: Roles of Sizes and Constituents
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08647.summary: Abstract Ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) has been associated with increased mortality risk, but whether it is more harmful on colder or warmer days is unclear. Here, we investigate seasonal variations in PM2.5 mass, sizes, constituents, and their association with oxylipin changes in humans. In a panel study of 123 adults in Beijing, we measured 27 PM2.5 metrics and five circulating lipoxygenase-derived oxylipins (i.e., leukotriene B4 [LTB4], 5-, 8-, 12-, and 15-hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid [HETE]) across winter and summer. PM2.5 exposure was associated with peak oxylipin increases at lag 0–1 days. Across particle size fractions and constituents, oxylipin increases ranged from 3.3% to 114.2%, with the most robust associations for ultrafine particles, accumulation mode particles, organic carbon, and chloride. Furthermore, an exposure-response relationship between UFP and oxylipins was observed only in summer. An IQR increase in UFP was associated with oxylipin changes of 12.9–97.7% in summer and −7.7 to 18.8% in winter. Conversely, oxylipin increases associated with accumulation mode particles and organic carbon were greater in winter. These findings suggest that the sizes and constituents of PM2.5 may partially explain the seasonal difference in the health effect of PM2.5 exposure, helping identify components associated with stronger biomarker responses in specific seasons.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c03200.title: Electrification, Lightweighting, and Materials Supply: A Dynamic Life Cycle Assessment of the U.S. Light-Duty Vehicle Fleet
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c03200.summary: Abstract Electrification and lightweighting are reshaping vehicle designs and materials demand, with uncertain net effects on life cycle greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Most existing fleet studies treat material choices, materials markets, and vehicle adoption separately, without capturing feedbacks between design, supply chains, and consumer behavior. This study develops an integrated system dynamics–life cycle assessment (SD–LCA) framework to explore these interactions for the U.S. light-duty vehicle fleet from 2000 to 2060. The model extends an established powertrain diffusion framework by endogenizing vehicle body material selection, battery capacity evolution, and materials market responses, linking these dynamics to a bottom-up life cycle assessment of fleet GHG emissions. Scenario analysis shows that increasing aluminum use in lightweight gasoline vehicles improves their utility and market share, largely offsetting use-phase GHG savings and yielding only modest reductions in total fleet emissions. In contrast, faster battery electric vehicle adoption raises cradle-to-gate emissions but more than compensates through lower use-phase emissions, reducing total fleet GHGs. Shifts in vehicle material demand also generate transient imbalances in steel and aluminum markets, temporarily lowering recycled fraction and increasing cradle-to-gate emissions. The SD–LCA framework demonstrates how feedbacks between vehicle design, materials supply, and consumer adoption shape fleet decarbonization pathways.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10536.title: Relative Humidity Modulates Nitration and Ring Fragmentation during Heterogeneous Oxidation of Catechol by Nitrate Radicals
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10536.summary: Abstract Catechol is an important biomass-burning-derived phenolic compound and a precursor to secondary organic aerosols (SOAs). Although nitrate radicals (NO3) are recognized as major nighttime oxidants, the influence of the aerosol water content on heterogeneous NO3 oxidation of phenolic compounds remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the impact of relative humidity (RH = 0–90%) on the heterogeneous oxidation of catechol thin films by nitrate radicals generated from the reaction of O3 and NO2. Product formation was characterized using Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, UV–visible spectroscopy, electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (ESI-MS), ultrahigh-pressure liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (UHPLC–MS), and ion chromatography–mass spectrometry (IC–MS). Under dry conditions, oxidation favored nitration and oligomerization pathways, producing mono-, di-, and trinitrocatechols together with catechol dimers and trimers. These products exhibited enhanced absorption in the 300–500 nm region, characteristic of brown carbon chromophores. Increasing RH progressively suppressed the relative nitration capacity of the NO3/N2O5 system while promoting oxidative ring-opening reactions, leading to the formation of dicarboxylic acids, including cis,cis-muconic acid, 2,3-dihydroxymaleic acid, and oxalic acid. Product distributions revealed a transition from functionalization-dominated chemistry at low RH to fragmentation-dominated chemistry at high RH. These results indicate that RH strongly controls nighttime nitrate radical oxidation of biomass-burning phenolics by shifting product formation from light-absorbing nitroaromatic brown carbon toward highly oxygenated fragmentation products. The findings provide new mechanistic insights into the role of aerosol water in governing the chemical aging and optical evolution of biomass-burning aerosols.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12080.title: From Molecular Topography to Ozone Pollution: Species Sources and Photochemical Kinetics of Individual Organic Peroxyl Radicals
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12080.summary: Abstract Ground-level ozone (O3) poses significant threats to global public health and climate change. Organic peroxyl radicals (RO2) serve as crucial intermediates in atmospheric O3 formation. Although individual RO2 species exhibit distinct reactivities, the quantification and source attribution of individual RO2 species remain poorly understood. Here, we address the challenge by integrating high-resolution field observations with fundamental theoretical kinetics within a novel hybrid receptor-kinetic modeling framework. The concentration and composition of RO2 species exhibit significant seasonal and diurnal dependencies. In summer, the 19 RO2 pool was characterized by a substantial contribution from biogenic sources (29%), particularly isoprene-derived species (ISOPOBO2). Conversely, the wintertime RO2 composition shifts, dramatically dominated by industrial emissions (41%), notably ethylene-derived species (HOCH2CH2O2). Source apportionment via the RO2+NO pathway further demonstrates that O3 photochemical formation potentials align closely with the kinetics of RO2 production. A data-driven machine learning model effectively captures the contribution of individual RO2 species to O3 formation in summer, but it shows significant deviations from kinetic simulations in winter. The framework establishes a dynamic framework to support daytime O3 mitigation by quantifying the high-time-resolution RO2 radical pool from field VOCs measurements.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c13861.title: Environmentally Persistent Free Radicals on Aged Polyamide Microplastics Drive Neurotoxicity in Eisenia fetida via a Glutamate-Centered Cascade
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c13861.summary: Abstract Nitrogen-containing microplastics (N-MPs) are widespread in soil and often exhibit distinct environmental behaviors and effects owing to their unique elemental composition and molecular structure. However, their toxicity to soil organisms remains poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, the toxicity of pristine and aged polyamides (PA) was evaluated in earthworms (Eisenia fetida), a representative soil invertebrate. At 0.01% (w/w), aged PA increased the magnitude of body-weight loss, MDA levels, and AChE activity by 24.4%, 11.6%, and 24.1%, respectively, relative to pristine PA-MPs. Greater accumulation of aged PA-MPs was accompanied by enhanced oxidative damage and neurotoxicity. Integrated multiomics, quantitative real-time PCR, and biomarker analyses revealed that oxidative stress-mediated membrane damage promoted glutamate accumulation, receptor overactivation, Ca2+ overload, synaptic injury, and ultimately neurotoxicity. Pharmacological interventions and transmission electron microscopy of the ventral nerve cord provided functional and morphological support for this cascade. Radical quenching and comparative leachate bioassays further supported the important contribution of environmentally persistent free radicals in aged PA-MPs to neuronal damage. These findings define a mechanistic pathway for aged microplastic-induced neurotoxicity and provide a basis for assessing the ecological risks of aged N-MPs in soils.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07341.title: A Perspective on the Development of Novel In Situ Remediation of Contaminated Sediments Using Black Carbon
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07341.summary: Abstract The field of contaminated sediment remediation was disrupted two decades ago by the emergence of a new way to reduce risk in situ through the amendment of black carbon sorbents─activated carbon and specialized biochars. This required a paradigm shift from a focus on reducing pollutant mass to reducing exposure through bioavailability control. Sorbent amendment technology has advanced from laboratory and pilot field demonstrations to full-scale applications at many sites and has recently been incorporated in USEPA records of decision at Superfund sites. This perspective summarizes critical points in advancing the new technology: 1) accurate problem definition recognizing that sediment pollutant mass reduction does not necessarily lead to risk reduction, 2) breakthroughs in bioavailability science and unraveling the role of native black carbon in sediments, 3) demonstration of pollutant bioavailability reduction with strong sorption, 4) quantitative descriptions of the process, 5) addressing the challenges of mercury, 6) understanding unintended consequences, and 7) development of freely dissolved concentrations as a key bioavailability metric with regulatory and stakeholder engagement. The lessons learned in this journey from early science through technological maturity can help inform other technologies that are in development to address evolving threats to the environment.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10880.title: Near-Complete Decomposition of Soil Microplastics over Transient Electrical Heating and Associated Benefits
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10880.summary: Abstract Soil serves as a significant sink for microplastics, posing considerable risks to both the ecological and human health. The diverse composition and dynamic transformation of microplastics present major challenges for remediation as conventional strategies often fail to achieve efficient and complete decomposition. In this study, biochar was applied to microplastic-contaminated soil as a conductive material to initiate transient electric heating under a low-power input. This approach facilitated near-complete decomposition of soil microplastics (>95.0%) across the tested soil and microplastic types while preventing soil hardening. Specifically, electric heating enhanced interactions between soil microplastics and the biochar conductor, leading to the formation of highly aromatic carbon (HAC). The resulting HAC not only improved soil microecology but also supported the growth of pak choi (Brassica campestris L. ssp.). The newly formed HAC was found to upregulate the expression of auxin-responsive gene families, including Aux/IAA and GH3, in the roots. HAC enriched tryptamine in the rhizosphere, and tryptamine abundance was positively correlated with the relative abundance of Sphingomonas, a genus with a reported capacity to convert tryptamine-derived intermediates toward indole-3-acetic acid (IAA) biosynthesis. These findings demonstrate that transient electric heating offers a sustainable strategy for decomposing diverse soil microplastics and that the remediated soil remains safe and conducive for agricultural production.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c14976.title: Mechanistic Understanding of Breath-Borne Bacterial Inactivation Kinetics in Oxidant-Rich and Natural Air
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c14976.summary: Abstract Bioaerosols play a central role in respiratory infection transmission, but how atmospheric oxidants affect their viability, especially in human respiratory fluids, remains unexplored. Here, we investigated the inactivation of five bacterial species with distinct cell envelope architectures (Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Bacillus subtilis, Staphylococcus aureus, and Mycobacterium smegmatis) suspended in human exhaled breath condensate (EBC) droplets exposed to gas-phase hydroxyl radicals (•OH) produced by ultraviolet irradiation of H2O2. Compared with the other three exposure conditions, the •OH-generating (H2O2+UV) treatment caused the greatest viability loss, with 4-h survival ranging from 24.3% (E. coli) to 63.0% (M. smegmatis). Gram-negative bacteria were sensitive to both H2O2 and •OH, whereas Gram-positive species resisted H2O2 but were inactivated by •OH. M. smegmatis showed the highest tolerance. Inactivation accelerated in smaller droplets, and the size-dependent kinetics were characterized using Weibull and first-order models incorporating surface-area-to-volume ratio. Morphological, biochemical, and metabolomic analyses indicated that the observed inactivation differences were associated with bacterial envelope types and surface characteristics. •OH preferentially degrades outer membrane glycolipids in Gram-negative bacteria and oxidizes cytoplasmic membrane lipids in Gram-positive bacteria, while all species shared a core signature of nucleic acid oxidative damage. These findings provide a molecular understanding of bacterial inactivation kinetics in human EBC droplets and may inform the assessment of bioaerosol transmission risks.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08811.title: Microplastics Are Prevalent in Striped Bass and Shiner Surfperch Tissues across San Francisco Bay, California
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08811.summary: Abstract The ingestion of microplastics by fish is widely documented, but the drivers of contamination and the movement of particles within organisms are still not well understood. We investigated microplastic contamination in sport fish caught from San Francisco Bay in California, USA. We compared microplastic contamination in striped bass (Morone saxatilis) and shiner surfperch (Cymatogaster aggregata). We observed an average of 5.9 ± 5.6 (Std Dev) microplastics per fish, with significantly higher overall contamination in striped bass but higher concentrations (microplastics/gram of tissue) in shiner surfperch. For each, we considered contamination relevant to their consumption by recreational anglers. For striped bass, where only the fillet is typically ingested, we found that contamination among tissues differed significantly (on average 3.8 ± 3.1 microplastics/fish fillets). Shiner surfperch, which are typically consumed whole, had an average body burden of 9.1 ± 1.2 microplastics/fish. Contamination varied significantly (p-value < 0.0001) among sampling locations for shiner surfperch, with the highest amounts observed near urban centers (no significant spatial pattern was observed for striped bass). Our findings show microplastics in tissues beyond the gastrointestinal tract, posing concerns for fish health and suggesting that fish caught from San Francisco Bay are a pathway for human consumption of microplastics.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11441.title: Observation-Based Emission Estimates of the Potent Greenhouse Gas HFC-23 for Article 5 and Non-Article 5 Country Groups under the Montreal Protocol
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11441.summary: Abstract The Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol requires parties to destroy, to the extent practicable, HFC-23 generated as a byproduct during the production of controlled hydrochlorofluorocarbons and hydrofluorocarbons. Global total HFC-23 emissions estimated from reported abatement and known sources (bottom-up) agreed with those inferred from atmospheric observations (top-down) before 2015, but have been substantially lower since then. Here, we show that during 2011–2013, bottom-up estimates of global total HFC-23 emissions were right for the wrong reasons: bottom-up estimates for the non-Article 5 (mainly developed) country group were lower than top-down estimates (1.7 ± 0.2 vs 3.1 ± 0.5 Gg yr–1 on average), while those for the Article 5 (mainly developing) country group were higher (11.8 ± 0.4 vs 9.7 ± 1.0 Gg yr–1), resulting in a cancellation at the global scale. We further show that during 2015–2023, while the underestimation of global bottom-up emissions was dominated by the Article 5 country group, the non-Article 5 country group also contributed in 2023 [bottom-up (byproduct emissions reported to UNEP plus other known sources) vs top-down: 0.5 ± 0.2 vs 1.3 ± 0.6 Gg yr–1]. Our results underscore improvement of emission accounting and mitigation for both country groups under the Kigali Amendment.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c02757.title: Event-Scale Deposition of Atmospheric Microplastics in Snowfall of the Sierra Nevada in North America
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c02757.summary: Abstract Atmospheric deposition of microplastics (MPs) at an event-scale resolution can be measured in snowfall events, as snow scavenges atmospheric MPs and the snowpack serves as a repository for MP accumulation. We monitored MP deposition in freshly fallen snow, the snowpack, and dry deposition over the course of 6 months in the Sierra Nevada of North America. Average microplastic concentrations in fresh snow ranged from 11.8 to 37.5 p/L at remote sites, which were significantly less than the 68.3 to 92.9 p/L MP concentrations found at the anthropogenically impacted site. Average bulk deposition rates were estimated to be 267 to 3190 p/m2/day at remote sites, significantly lower than the 3242 to 7480 p/m2/day at the anthropogenically impacted site. HYSPLIT back-trajectory modeling characterized the potential regional transport of MPs from upwind regions that were predominantly agricultural and suburban areas, as well as localized anthropogenic activities that could significantly affect MP deposition rates in snowfall. This study introduces high-throughput FTIR analysis methods with a highlight on fiber spectroscopy, demonstrates the value of estimating MP fluxes at the meteorological event scale, reports MP deposition rates in a critical water resource, and provides a basis for future long-term atmospheric MP monitoring.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11475.title: Biochar Application Enhances Photochemical Reactivity of Dissolved Organic Matter to Stimulate CO2 Emissions in Paddy Water
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11475.summary: Abstract Dissolved organic matter (DOM) plays a pivotal role in regulating photochemical reactivity and carbon turnover in flooded paddy systems. While biochar (BC) is recognized as a promising strategy for soil carbon preservation, its impact on DOM evolution and photochemical carbon cycle in paddy water remains unknown. Here, we demonstrated that BC amendment continuously enhanced the photogeneration of hydroxyl radicals (•OH) and low-energy excited triplet-state DOM (3DOM*-L) in paddy water, increasing CO2 emissions by an average of 35.5% while playing a minor role in CH4 formation over a 34-day incubation. The enhanced photoactivity was associated with the enrichment of the photoactive molecular pool characterized by highly aromatic compounds and polyphenols with higher aromaticity, unsaturation, and oxygenated degrees. The proposed mechanisms in enriching photoactive DOM of paddy water depended on soil types, i.e., BC facilitated the biotic reprocessing of inert, highly recalcitrant aromatics into metabolites associated with photoactivity in sandy soil, whereas abiotic processes, including BC-induced dissolved black carbon release and mineral-associated organic carbon desorption, likely played more important roles in loam soil. Enhanced anaerobic fermentation further supplied photolabile substrates for amplifying mineralization. Extrapolation estimations suggested that BC-enhanced photochemistry may release an additional 3.56–15.47 Tg CO2 yr–1 globally, potentially offsetting ∼0.7–7.0% of BC’s CO2 mitigation potential. The findings revealed a previously unrecognized photochemical pathway of BC-involved carbon loss across the soil-water continuum, with implications for evaluating the net climate benefit of biochar as a carbon management strategy.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06201.title: Microplastic-Derived Dissolved Organic Matter Regulates Reactive Bromine Species Formation by Modulating the Photochemistry of Seawater Dissolved Organic Matter
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06201.summary: Abstract Microplastic-derived dissolved organic matter (MP-DOM) is emerging as a non-negligible organic input to marine systems, yet how its interactions with seawater DOM (S-DOM) regulate the photochemical formation of reactive bromine species (RBS) remains unclear. In this study, the RBS formation potential of poly(vinyl chloride) (PVC)-derived MP-DOM, S-DOM, and their mixed systems was systematically investigated under simulated solar irradiation. MP-DOM input exerted a nonlinear ratio-dependent regulatory effect on S-DOM-mediated RBS formation. At relatively low MP-DOM proportions (5–20%), the formation rate constant of 4-bromo-3,5-dimethyl-1H-pyrazole (Br-DMPZ), which represents the RBS formation potential, increased relative to S-DOM alone, reaching a maximum enhancement of 47.4% at 20% MP-DOM under seawater halide ion conditions (540 mM Cl– + 0.8 mM Br–). This enhancement was associated with increased quinone-/carbonyl-related redox-active structures, electron exchange capacity, and tannin-like components, which could facilitate photoinduced charge separation, electron transfer, and Br– oxidation. In contrast, higher MP-DOM proportions (40–50%) promoted hydrophobic lipid-like mixed assemblies, enhancing excited-state quenching and suppressing electron transfer and RBS photogeneration. These findings demonstrate that MP-DOM is not an inert byproduct of microplastic aging but rather an important regulatory factor in S-DOM-mediated halogen photochemistry in plastic-impacted marine waters.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c02655.title: Influence of Urban Form, Weather and Population on Outdoor Airborne Infection Risk: Implications in Greater London for SARS-CoV-2
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c02655.summary: Abstract Although airborne infectious disease transmission outdoors is possible, particularly in densely built urban areas with limited ventilation, the role of urban morphology and neighborhood climate heterogeneity in modulating the risk remains poorly quantified. We couple an urban climate model (SUEWS) and a modified Wells-Riley framework to develop a transferable neighborhood-scale approach for mapping outdoor airborne infection risk across morphologically diverse neighborhoods, factoring in urban form, population distribution and meteorologically driven viral infectivity decay. We demonstrate this framework by applying it to SARS-CoV-2 in Greater London. Considering outdoor urban ventilation alone, estimated risk follows a diurnal cycle and peaks at night. Including population distribution, daytime risk in busy commercial centers is up to 7.23 times higher than nighttime. Infectivity decay from ultraviolet B (UVB) exposure reduces risk by 35–45% in less dense areas and up to 99% in high built-density neighborhoods. Despite this mitigation, the highest risks persist in high-rise, high-workplace-density districts (e.g., City of London and Westminster), while lower-rise areas (e.g., Lambeth and Croydon) exhibit reductions exceeding 90%. For SARS-CoV-2, these findings demonstrate strong intraurban heterogeneity in outdoor airborne infection risk in Greater London. More broadly, the transferable framework supports high-resolution mapping to inform targeted, place-based public health interventions.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12903.title: Substantial Emerging Impact of Amine-Based Carbon Capture on Atmospheric Particle Formation under Carbon Neutrality
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12903.summary: Abstract Carbon capture (CC) is indispensable to carbon neutrality, and amine-based absorption using monoethanolamine (MEA) is among the most mature CC technologies. MEA can enhance atmospheric new particle formation (NPF), the primary source of atmospheric particles. However, the atmospheric impacts of MEA escaping from future large-scale CC deployment remain unknown. Here, we develop a three-dimensional model that represents MEA sources, sinks, and H2SO4-MEA nucleation based on quantum chemical and cluster dynamics calculations, to evaluate atmospheric MEA and its impacts from CC deployment at China’s coal-fired power plants under carbon-neutrality scenarios. By 2060, even moderate CC deployment raises atmospheric MEA concentrations to tens of pptv, exceeding dimethylamine (DMA), the canonical urban NPF agent. H2SO4-MEA nucleation consequently overtakes H2SO4-DMA nucleation across extensive CC-deployment regions (∼1 million km2) and is more than 10 times stronger within the CC-intensive core (∼0.2 million km2), raising particle number concentrations by 50–187% and exposing ∼430 million people to levels exceeding the WHO high-exposure benchmark. The associated rise in ultrafine particles is estimated to cause ∼34,800 additional deaths across China in 2060. We reveal that CC deployment may deliver climate benefits while inadvertently worsening particulate pollution and public-health burdens, warranting proactive and early preventive action.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09034.title: Solar Activation of Peroxymonosulfate by Chromophoric Dissolved Organic Matter Enables Predictable Micropollutant Attenuation in Real Waters
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09034.summary: Abstract Solar-driven activation of peroxymonosulfate (PMS) is a promising advanced oxidation process for water and wastewater treatment; however, the kinetics of emerging contaminant removal in real water matrices remain poorly understood. In this study, we investigated PMS photosensitization in three environmentally relevant water matrices and evaluated its role in the abatement of 42 pharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs). Under simulated solar irradiation, CDOM promoted PMS transformation and generated multiple photochemically produced reactive intermediates (PPRIs). A multiple-probe chemical method was employed to quantify the cumulative exposure doses of HO•, SO4•–, Cl2•–, CO3•–, and 1O2. Across the tested matrices, PPRI exposure doses followed the order CO3•– > 1O2 > Cl2•– ∼ SO4•– > HO•. The measured PPRI exposure doses, together with second-order rate constants, reasonably predicted PPCP removal in the solar/PMS/CDOM system. For several phenolic and aniline-containing PPCPs, DOM-mediated inhibition was observed and was attributed to reductive back-reaction of one-electron oxidation intermediates; incorporating inhibition factors improved the agreement between calculated and experimental removal efficiencies. Furthermore, four commonly detected PPCPs, sucralose, metformin, caffeine, and carbamazepine, were first identified as practical indicator compounds for estimating PPRI exposure without adding external probe chemicals. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for predicting PPCP attenuation during solar/PMS treatment in CDOM-rich waters and highlight the importance of secondary radicals in real aquatic matrices.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10425.title: Novel NIR-II Imaging Reveals Gut-First, Brain-Later Inorganic Mercury Signals with Structural Injury in Zebrafish
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10425.summary: Abstract Mercury (Hg) neurotoxicity has generally been assessed by organic methylmercury, whereas inorganic mercury [Hg(II)] is often considered less likely to cause direct brain exposure. Conventional approaches cannot resolve the in vivo spatiotemporal distribution of Hg(II) across tissues. In this study, we first developed an Hg(II)-responsive aggregation-induced emission sensor for second near-infrared (NIR-II) fluorescence imaging, which was then employed to track Hg(II) signals in live zebrafish. The sensor produced enhanced NIR-II signals in the presence of Hg(II), allowing low-background, noninvasive, and real-time imaging. We observed that Hg(II)-responsive sensor signals first appeared in the intestinal region and later increased in the brain region, revealing an intestine-first and brain-later temporal pattern in living zebrafish. During a 48-h continuous exposure followed by depuration, brain-region Hg(II)-responsive sensor fluorescence increased with exposure concentration and time and remained detectable during the depuration phase. Expansion microscopy further showed that low-dose Hg(II) exposure reduced the brain cell density and average cell size, and disrupted the local tissue organization. These results provided in vivo evidence of Hg(II)-responsive sensor in the brain region and its association with structural brain injury during development. Thus, inorganic Hg should also be considered in the assessments of developmental brain exposure and neural structural injury.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06036.title: Mapping the Carbon Footprint of Organic Chemicals in Commerce
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06036.summary: Abstract The chemical industry is a major contributor to global CO2 emissions, accounting for ∼10% of total greenhouse gases, underscoring the need for a sustainability transition. However, public carbon footprint data exists for only hundreds of the more than 100,000 chemicals in commerce, limiting effective action. To address this, we collect high-quality primary chemical carbon footprint data and refine a machine learning model to estimate the carbon footprint of 94,697 chemicals in commerce across 26 national and regional chemical inventories. Our analysis reveals clear molecular structure–carbon footprint relationships that may guide future molecular design: carbon footprints are strongly linked to molecular frameworks, the number of ring structures, and types of heteroatoms. Newly commercialized chemicals tend to have higher carbon footprints than older chemicals, emphasizing the urgent need to embed “sustainable-by-design” principles into chemical innovation from the outset. This study provides a database of chemical carbon footprints and actionable insights for the sustainable design and use of chemicals, supporting the environmental decision-making of chemical producers, consumers, and policymakers.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07419.title: Electron Transfer at Microbe–Mineral Interfaces: From Molecular Mechanisms to Ecosystem-Scale Biogeochemical Cycling and Remediation
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07419.summary: Abstract Microbe–mineral electron transfer (MMET) drives key microbial processes and biogeochemical cycling, but linking these microscopic interactions to ecosystem-scale dynamics remains a major challenge. MMET couples intracellular metabolism to extracellular mineral transformations. The resulting changes in mineral redox state and reactivity can, in turn, influence microbial energy conservation and metabolism. MMET flux could therefore provide a quantitative link between nanometer-scale electron exchange and larger-scale biogeochemical processes. In energy-limited and contaminated environments, electroactive microorganisms may transfer electrons to or acquire electrons from redox-active minerals, depending on their metabolic capabilities and local redox conditions. These interactions can support energy conservation, mitigate toxic stress, and generate localized zones of high biogeochemical activity. As their effects accumulate across space and time, microscale electron transfer may influence ecosystem-scale elemental cycling, microbial community succession, organic carbon stabilization, and contaminant fate. Building on established modeling approaches, we suggest that integrating individual-based models (IBMs) with genome-scale metabolic models (GSMMs) could translate spatially heterogeneous, genome-informed microbial responses into collective MMET fluxes across scales while accounting for key thermodynamic and kinetic constraints. More broadly, progress requires characterizing electroactive microbial diversity and mechanisms, engineering microbe–mineral interfaces through computational design and synthetic biology, and translating MMET principles into scalable environmental applications.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c03165.title: Subsoil versus Topsoil Straw Addition Shifts Microbial Carbon Allocation for Enhanced Carbon Sequestration and Emission Mitigation
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c03165.summary: Abstract Subsoils (>20 cm) represent an underutilized sink for soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration because C inputs in subsoil are typically limited. To clarify how organic inputs regulate subsoil SOC accrual and C emissions in rice paddies, we combined a 2-year field experiment with 13C-labeled straw incubation and validated the results with a global meta-analysis. Results showed that compared with no addition and topsoil straw addition, subsoil straw addition increased SOC stocks by 10.5% and 2.2%, respectively, primarily via enhanced mineral-associated organic C (MAOC) formation at 0–30 cm. The 270-day incubation revealed that subsoil addition accelerated microbial conversion of straw C into amino sugars, evidenced by 13C-phospholipid fatty acids, promoting MAOC formation. Relative to topsoil addition, subsoil addition reduced CH4 emissions by 15.3%, driven by improved root growth and enhanced CH4 oxidation, and decreased CO2 emissions by lowering topsoil C availability and peroxidase activity.
