Meta-analysis confirmed that C emissions decrease progressively with increasing incorporation depth, and machine-learning models indicate that deeper incorporation (>20 cm) mitigates global C emissions by half under future climate change. Overall, compared with topsoil addition, subsoil addition represents a win–win strategy that simultaneously enhances SOC sequestration and reduces C emissions, with potential applicability beyond paddy systems.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c05777.title: Unveiling Seven-Decade Disparities of Methane Emissions across China
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c05777.summary: Abstract China’s century-long economic transition generated substantial methane emissions, yet the trajectory and factors of this evolution remain poorly quantified. A systematic understanding is essential for reconciling China’s economic growth with emission mitigation targets and for informing Global South nations. Using a bottom-up estimate of subnational methane emissions (1949–2022), we uncover a fundamental shift from agriculture-dominated to industry-dominated methane emissions in China. Nationwide emissions peaked in 2012, declining 3.8% by 2022, yet provincial disparities widened by 48%. While superficially reflecting heterogeneous fossil fuel use, these disparities are attributable to a shift in explanatory dominance from purely economic to dual economic-policy factors, particularly carbon policies. The long-term stability in agricultural sectors reflects nationwide efforts to food security, which maintains a baseline level of production across provinces. Recent regional decoupling masks the disproportion between emissions and economic gains. Western provinces (e.g., Shanxi, Ningxia, Guizhou) continue to exhibit high-emission but low-return economic profiles. The average of their methane emissions per GDP was 4.8 times that of eastern regions in 2022, with extremes reaching 150-fold differences. For equitable mitigation, future focus should shift from “who emits” to “why emits”, establishing a scientific basis for fair compensation between resource-dependent and resource-consuming regions.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10023.title: Influence of COVID-19 Lockdown on Atmospheric Nitrate Sources and Chemistry in the Northeastern US
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10023.summary: Abstract The outbreak of COVID-19 and subsequent lockdowns caused widespread restrictions on human activities. This presented a unique opportunity to track atmospheric chemistry changes under rapid emission reductions. Using stable nitrogen (δ15N) and triple oxygen isotopes (δ18O and Δ17O) of particulate nitrate (pNO3) collected from 2019 to 2020 in the northeastern US, combined with 0-D box-model simulations, we investigate the response of atmospheric nitrate chemistry during the COVID-19 lockdown period (March 2020) in the northeastern US. Triple oxygen isotope measurements indicate that emission reductions altered the relative contributions of NOx oxidation pathways, with a shift toward the NO2 + OH pathway and a reduced contribution from N2O5 hydrolysis. This shift was consistent with the modeled increase in OH concentrations and the observed and modeled decrease in O3 during the COVID-19 lockdown, which limited N2O5 formation and subsequent heterogeneous nitrate formation. Moreover, nitrogen isotope-constrained sensitivity analysis suggests that a reduction of approximately 40(±10)% in transportation NOx emissions relative to the annual emission inventory estimates may be required to reproduce the observed decrease in δ15N(pNO3) during the COVID-19 period. These findings highlight the utility of isotopes to detail the complex interactions between emission reductions, atmospheric oxidation chemistry, and secondary aerosol formation. Understanding these interactions is critical for effectively determining air pollution mitigation strategies and testing air-quality models, particularly under rapidly evolving emission conditions associated with energy transitions and policy interventions.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11456.title: Nanoconfinement Decouples Calcium-Enhanced Phosphate Capture from Calcium Phosphate Crystal Maturation
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11456.summary: Abstract Calcium phosphate (Ca–P) scaling, which is ubiquitous in nature and in water systems, has been shown to interfere with the capture of phosphate by ferric oxide-based sorbents, thereby deteriorating their decontamination performance in repeated cycles. Here, we show that a specifically designed gel-type nanocomposite, namely HFO@N201, enables Ca-enhanced phosphate sequestration while restricting Ca–P scaling via nanoconfinement. Increasing the initial Ca2+ concentration from 0 to 160 mg/L improved phosphate uptake from ∼4.5 to ∼6.2 mg/g in the first cycle. After 20 adsorption-regeneration cycles, phosphate uptake remained at ∼6.4 mg/g in the Ca-containing system, twice that of ∼3.2 mg/g in the Ca-free system. In fixed-bed tests, the presence of Ca2+ enhanced the working capacity from ∼1350 to ∼1800 bed volumes, which could be observed again in the subsequent cycle. Asynchronous release of Fe, P, and Ca during acidic elution of P-loaded HFO@N201 indicates heterogeneous and nonstoichiometric Ca-associated phosphate retention rather than formation of a mature bulk Ca–P phase. XRD, TEM, EXAFS, and Mössbauer spectroscopy further show that the retained Ca–P species remained weakly ordered and that the nanosized ferrihydrite-like Fe phase persisted during cyclic operation. Thermodynamic analysis, classical nucleation theory, and molecular dynamics simulations further support that the nanoconfinement structure of HFO@N201 (∼2 nm) creates a low-mobility hydration environment that restricts solvent exchange, ion rearrangement, and long-range ordering, thereby stabilizing Ca–P species in a weakly ordered interfacial state. Our work demonstrates nanoconfinement as a strategy to exploit Ca-enhanced phosphate capture while reducing Ca–P scaling in regenerable sorbents.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c13254.title: Deriving Organism-Relevant Nanoparticle Safety Exposure Limits from In Vitro Toxicity Data
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c13254.summary: Abstract Establishing human safety limits of engineered nanoparticles remains a challenge. In vitro assays have become a major toxicity data resource, driven by the demand for new approach methodologies (NAMs) that reduce animal testing. However, robust tools that bridge in vitro data with in vivo outcomes are still lacking. Here, we present an integrated computational framework using physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling to derive organism-level BMD10-based dose estimates directly from in vitro liver toxicity data. For 4 nondissolvable nanoparticles (TiO2, SiO2, Au, and graphene oxide), we curated in vitro toxicity data sets spanning 7 liver-relevant cell systems (5 human and 2 mouse) across 24 assays and estimated in vitro effect thresholds using the benchmark dose for a 10% response (BMD10). Mouse in vitro BMD10 values were then reverse-translated into predicted BMD10IVIVE values using a validated mouse PBPK model and benchmarked against available mouse-derived in vivo effect threshold (BMD10eq) data to ensure consistency. The resulting nanoparticle-specific BMD10IVIVE ranges showed qualitative concordance with animal-derived reference doses, supporting the biological plausibility of these screening-level dose estimates. We further applied the same workflow to human liver cell systems to derive human-relevant BMD10-based points of departure. This approach establishes a scalable and prospective animal-free workflow for human nanoparticle risk assessments, overcoming a critical translational gap.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08900.title: Pesky Metals: Historical Perspective, Advances, and Challenges for Remediation of Problematic Metal Contaminants
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08900.summary: Abstract Persistent and problematic toxic metal and metalloid pollutants (in particular, As, Hg, Pb, Cd, and Cr) have long been challenging and expensive remediation targets in contaminated surface and subsurface environments. Since the advent of environmental regulations and cleanup in the late 20th century, much progress has been made to address sites of legacy metal pollution and limit new contamination. Despite this, metal pollution remains a global problem, particularly in soils and sediments, with many large legacy sites inadequately remediated, metal contamination widespread in developed and developing nations, and new pollution occurring from informal and often illegal extraction and recycling processes. In this perspective, we highlight advances and challenges in science and technology, and key economic and social factors, that have influenced remediation of these “pesky” metals over the last ∼50 years. Through this lens, we consider emerging challenges and opportunities associated with legacy and critical metals, climate resilience, and sustainability.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06868.title: A Framework for Time-Explicit Life Cycle Optimization
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06868.summary: Abstract Life cycle optimization (LCO) selects optimal processes and supply chains from a set of alternatives given environmental constraints and objectives, supporting the design of sustainable systems and their transitions. However, current approaches rely on static assumptions, overlooking two interacting temporal dimensions: temporal distribution (flows are spread over time) and temporal evolution (processes and supply chains change over time). Because distribution and evolution jointly dictate the magnitude of a flow at a given time, both must be considered simultaneously to accurately optimize against cumulative environmental impacts and time-specific environmental constraints. We present a framework for time-explicit LCO that captures these interdependencies to determine optimal transition pathways. The framework tracks flow timing relative to process installation and dynamically determines flow magnitudes from time-specific process parameters and background supply chains. A case study on integrated methanol and pig iron production demonstrates how time-explicit LCO enables optimization against time-resolved environmental impacts and constraints, revealing mitigation strategies inaccessible to static approaches: prioritizing early high-efficiency technology installation to idle older processes as operational savings outweigh embodied impacts of stranded assets, and avoiding transient resource bottlenecks through diversification. To facilitate widespread application, we provide the open-source Python package optimex, enabling practitioners to design transition pathways that rigorously respect environmental limits.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09991.title: Industrial Solid Wastes Recycling from Steel and Power Sectors Delivers Climate and Net Societal Benefits
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09991.summary: Abstract Sectoral decarbonization can substantially reshape the quantity and composition of industrial solid waste and its associated resource recovery potential, yet how these changes evolve along decarbonization pathways remains poorly understood. Here, we develop a sectoral transition framework linking future waste generation, recycling technologies, life cycle environmental impacts, and societal benefits. We focus on the steel and power sectors, which represent major industrial solid waste sources and distinct decarbonization pathways across six major producing regions from 2025 to 2050. By 2050, steel sector wastes remain at 0.61–0.78 Gt, whereas power sector wastes decline from 1.11 Gt in 2025 to 0.17–0.50 Gt. Under four scenarios, cumulative mitigation ranges from 25.68 to 53.39 Gt CO2-eq, with discounted net societal benefits of USD 11.24–23.81 trillion. Steel sector benefits are sensitive to recycling technology shares, whereas power sector benefits are more strongly shaped by transition-driven changes in the waste generation and composition. These findings highlight the importance of integrating evolving waste flows and technology choices into long-term decarbonization and circular economy strategies.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06512.title: Small Modular Electrochemical Containers for Decarbonization of AI Data Centers
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06512.summary: Abstract The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) is increasing data-center electricity demand and reinforcing the near-term role of fossil-fuel power generation. Decarbonizing this infrastructure requires carbon capture systems that are efficient, compact, modular, and compatible with space-constrained data centers. Here, we evaluate Small Modular Electrochemical Containers (SMECs) as a deployment-oriented application of a two-stage, membraneless electrochemically mediated amine regeneration (EMAR) process. The design integrates CO2 absorption and electrochemical desorption within one gas-diffusion-electrode cell, eliminating absorber columns and ion-exchange membranes. Single-cell experiments were conducted under simulated natural-gas and coal-derived flue gas. Polarization mapping identified optimized operating conditions, which were then used in a 300-cycle, 50-h accelerated stability test with periodic polarity switching. The cell maintained repeatable voltage and CO2 absorption/desorption profiles, with absorption and desorption efficiencies of ∼90% under optimized conditions. The energetics ranged from 50–85 kJe/molCO2, and GC/IC analyses showed no detectable gaseous or liquid side products. The paper further includes theoretical modeling of SOx and NOx effects on the absorbent. In a case study for a 360 MW data-center power plant, the TEA showed that fewer than 20 SMEC units could achieve near-complete decarbonization, increasing the levelized electricity cost from about \$58/MWh to \$74/MWh.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06457.title: Unraveling the Differentiated Roles of Reactive Chlorine in Regulating Atmospheric Oxidation and Secondary Formation
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06457.summary: Abstract Reactive chlorine species significantly perturb atmospheric oxidation, yet systematic observations of multiple chlorine species and comprehensive assessments of their distinct photochemical roles remain limited. Here, we present concurrent field measurements of four reactive chlorine species (ClNO2, Cl2, HOCl, and NCl3) in a coastal urban atmosphere. Cl2 photolysis dominated Cl• production (40.2%), whereas HOCl photolysis served as a dual source of Cl• and OH•, a mechanism previously overlooked, and most effectively elevated ROx• levels. Temporally, ClNO2 photolysis enhanced early morning oxidation, Cl2 prevailed around noon, and HOCl dominated the afternoon radical budgets, while NCl3 photolysis contributed minimally throughout the diurnal cycle. Incorporating chlorine-induced volatile organic compounds (VOC) consumption in the box model amplified O3 and PAN production by up to 43.4 and 43.8%, respectively, without altering the VOC-limited regime. Our findings underscored that regulating coastal atmospheric oxidation required a species-specific, time-resolved treatment of chlorine chemistry, with direct implications for air quality management.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09700.title: Fog Intensity and Droplet Size-Resolved Aqueous Secondary Organic Aerosol (aqSOA) Formation in Polluted Winter Fog: New Insights from a Combined Observational and Modeling Study
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09700.summary: Abstract Fog is a chemically active aqueous medium in which dissolved organic gases and particles are converted into highly oxidized aqueous secondary organic aerosol (aqSOA). Its magnitude is difficult to constrain, and most published estimates rely on models. We analyzed size-resolved fogwater collected over two winters at Kanpur, India, by offline high-resolution aerosol mass spectrometry and apportioned by positive matrix factorization (PMF). Three highly oxidized factors (O/C 0.95–1.19) were summed as an aqSOA proxy. Combining this proxy with colocated liquid water content and water-soluble organic carbon yielded 3.1–8.4 μg m–3 aqSOA across seven events. The droplet aqSOA accounts for a median of about 7% of ambient SOA and 5% of ambient OA, reaching 13% of SOA in the densest fogs. Fine droplets carried the largest aqSOA share (43–84%), driven by higher concentrations of dissolved Fe and Cu and longer residence times. Ambient OA was less oxidized during dense than light fog (O/C 0.52 versus 0.61). Returning aqSOA after dissipation gave direct-radiative-effect increments of −0.048 W m–2 (dense) and −0.032 W m–2 (light). These size- and intensity-resolved observational constraints quantify fog–aerosol interactions and their air quality consequences in a heavily polluted region.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c14170.title: The End of Uniformity: Spatial, Climatic, and Toxicological Redefinitions of Air Quality

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12256.title: Resuspension of Micro- and Nanoplastics Trapped in Coastal Sediments: Insights into Their Cross-Interface Transport and Environmental Fate in Transitional Zones
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12256.summary: Abstract Changes in environmental conditions may drive the transfer of micro- and nanoplastics (MNPs) between sediment layers and overlying waters, yet their resuspension behavior in coastal transitional waters and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study comprehensively investigated the resuspension dynamics of MNPs from sediments with different properties, as well as the effects of aquatic environmental conditions, including salinity, sediment water content, and hydrodynamics, on MNP resuspension. Sediment grain size and mineralogical composition played a dominant role in governing MNP resuspension. Differences in resuspension behavior between microplastic and nanoplastic particles were identified. MNP resuspension showed a nonlinear response to salinity, with increasing salinity generally suppressing resuspension. Resuspension was highly sensitive to salinity changes within the low-salinity range. A U-shaped pattern was observed in PSNP resuspension, with the resuspension rate initially decreasing as sediment water content declined and then increasing as sediments became drier. Positive correlations between MNP resuspension and fluid shear rate were observed, while sediment-trapped MNPs exhibited distinct sensitivities to hydrodynamic disturbances between freshwater and marine conditions. Trapped MNPs were more susceptible to hydrodynamic disturbance under freshwater conditions. These findings offer valuable insights into MNP resuspension and advance understanding of their vertical transport and overall environmental fate in coastal regions.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12276.title: In Situ Reconstruction-Directed Electrocatalyst Design Enables Low-Energy Anodic Oxidation for Water Purification
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12276.summary: Abstract Anodic oxidation reactions (AORs) hold promise for degrading persistent organic pollutants, yet practical deployment is constrained by inadequate anode stability and sluggish kinetics under low-bias operation. Prussian blue analogues (PBAs) feature cyanide-bridged metal frameworks with efficient intermetallic electron transfer, yet their surfaces inevitably undergo uncontrolled reconstruction during electrolysis, producing outcomes that range from beneficial activation to detrimental degradation. Here, we reported a first-ever paradigm shift from suppressing reconstruction to actively directing it, demonstrating that the intrinsic instability of FeMn PBA could be harnessed as a design lever. Through an in situ self-reconstruction process, we discovered that the morphology and surface coordination environment were spontaneously reorganized into FeMn nanoflowers grown on carbon paper (FeMn@CP), a configuration never before achieved from this precursor. This reconstruction-guided pathway uniquely yielded a 201-fold increase in electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) over pristine FeMn PBA, alongside markedly enhanced electrochemical stability, synergistic gains not attainable by conventional stabilization strategies. Capitalizing on this reconstructed architecture, FeMn@CP achieved efficient phenolic pollutant degradation at low bias, with robust reusability, broad matrix adaptability, and substantially reduced effluent toxicity. Continuous-flow experiments further verified its sustained performance under practical conditions. This study unveils, for the first time, that catalyst reconstruction, when rationally exploited, serves as a decisive and generalizable strategy to concurrently boost AOR activity and stability, opening an unexplored avenue for designing next-generation electrocatalytic water purification systems.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10715.title: Liquid Crystal Monomers in Paired Indoor Dust and Urine: Compound-Specific Enrichment Patterns and External–Internal Exposure Profiles
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10715.summary: Abstract Liquid crystal monomers (LCMs) are extensively used in liquid crystal display devices, yet the relationship between household contamination and human internal exposure remains unclear. We investigated fluorinated and nonfluorinated LCMs (FLCMs and NFLCMs) in paired indoor dust and urine samples. Widespread occurrence of LCMs was observed in 58 paired indoor dust and first-morning urine samples collected in Suizhou, with 48 of 49 LCMs detected in dust and 40 in urine. Median concentrations of ∑49LCMs were 255 ng/g in dust and 26.9 ng/mL in urine. FLCMs were predominant in dust, whereas NFLCMs contributed more to urinary burden. The dominant compounds differed markedly between dust and urine. Among these, only 2,3-difluoro-1-methoxy-4-[4-(4-propylcyclohexyl)cyclohexyl]benzene (DMPCB) showed a significant positive dust-urine correlation (r = 0.409, p < 0.01). Relative-enrichment analysis revealed compound-specific shifts, with several NFLCMs relatively enriched in urine and several FLCMs in dust. The median estimated daily intake of ∑49LCMs via dust ingestion was 0.110 ng/kg bw/day, far below levels reported for e-waste recycling areas. Although hazard quotients (HQs) for all 39 LCMs with available toxicity benchmarks were several orders of magnitude below 1, incomplete toxicity reference data remain a major source of uncertainty in risk characterization. Overall, the findings indicate widespread mixed exposure to LCMs and suggest that urinary LCM profiles may reflect contributions from multiple exposure pathways and compound-specific toxicokinetic processes in addition to household dust.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12532.title: Molecular Insights into a Precursor–Chlorine Trade-Off Governing Divergent Formation Pathways of PCDD/Fs and Emerging Cl-PAHs in Waste Cocombustion of Cellulose, PET, and PVC
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12532.summary: Abstract Co-combustion of industrial and municipal solid waste (ISW/MSW) is widely practiced, yet PCDD/Fs and emerging chlorinated polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (Cl-PAHs) formation under mixed-feedstock conditions remains poorly understood. Here, cellulose, polyethylene terephthalate (PET), and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) were combusted individually and cocombusted with MSW to elucidate how feedstock chemistry regulates chlorinated pollutant formation. Comprehensive mass-spectrometric profiling of target pollutants, aromatic precursors, and the top 50 combustion intermediates, combined with DFT calculations, revealed a precursor–chlorine trade-off governing pollutant formation. PET preferentially generated oxygenated aromatic intermediates, particularly dibenzofuran; PVC supplied the most PAHs and reactive chlorine, and cellulose primarily contributed carbon skeletons. Accordingly, two distinct pathways were proposed: dibenzofuran-centered, chlorination-limited formation of PCDD/Fs and stepwise aromatic growth followed by site-selective chlorination of Cl-PAHs. The higher HOMO energies of two representative PAHs, anthracene and phenanthrene, relative to dibenzofuran indicated their greater susceptibility to electrophilic chlorination. Consequently, Cl-PAHs exceeded PCDD/Fs by 1–3 orders of magnitude and accounted for 83.4% of estimated TEQ. Increasing chlorine availability alleviated the kinetic constraint on dibenzofuran chlorination, causing an approximately 42-fold increase in PCDD/F emissions at 20% PVC blending. These findings establish a molecular basis for feedstock-chemistry-guided management and broaden emission-control priorities from regulated PCDD/Fs to emerging Cl-PAHs.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08752.title: Modeling Decadal Organosulfates in Particulate Matter to Improve Estimations of Aerosol Hygroscopicity in the United States
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08752.summary: Abstract Organosulfates (OSs) can comprise a substantial fraction of secondary organic aerosol and exhibit significantly different hygroscopicity than inorganic sulfates, yet their spatiotemporal prevalence and climatic impacts remain poorly constrained because speciated measurements are sparse and common chemical transport models do not explicitly represent OS formation. This study develops a flexible and robust modeling framework to quantify isoprene-derived OS (iOS) concentrations and OS impacts on aerosol hygroscopicity (κ) across the contiguous United States (U.S.) for summers spanning 2013–2022. Using the Community Multiscale Air Quality (CMAQ) model with updated iOS chemistry, simulations reproduce Interagency Monitoring of Protected Visual Environments (IMPROVE) network-derived organosulfur and inorganic sulfate and agree with speciated iOS measurements from filter analyses. OS concentrations are elevated in the eastern U.S., with summertime mean values up to 0.51 μg m–3. OS formation produces a net 5.6% decrease in κ (direct OS contribution, +2.8%; indirect, −8.4% via sulfate reduction). We apply an interpretable machine-learning surrogate to identify predictive features associated with OS variability and enable efficient estimation without rerunning CMAQ. These results provide the first observation-validated, high-spatial-coverage OS reconstruction and nationwide quantification of OS-driven κ changes, underscoring the importance of representing OS formation and expanded observations to improve aerosol-cloud radiative effect assessments.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09617.title: Fingerprints of Airborne Plastics in Urban PM2.5: Applications and Implications
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09617.summary: Abstract To better identify emission sources of airborne plastics, we employed nine plastic-associated chemicals (PlsACs) in 240 daily PM2.5 samples collected in Singapore during 2018–2020. A unique PlsAC, tris(2,4-ditert-butylphenyl) phosphate (I168O), is most abundant, accounting for 90% of the total quantified PlsACs and identifying at least 40% more PM2.5 linked to respirable airborne PlsACs. A newly resolved source of plastic production, use, and burning (PlasticPub) accounts for the highest fraction (37%) of the quantified PlsACs among the seven apportioned PM2.5 sources. Nearly all di-iso-butyl phthalate (DIBP) and more than half of di-n-butyl phthalate (DNBP) are attributed to two factors of Background and Marine aerosols, indicating their potential worldwide transport. More than 90% of diethyl phthalate (DEP) is associated with transported peat forest (PF) burning smoke, demonstrating involvement of anthropogenic activities. Following PlasticPub, Traffic & road dust is the second predominant source responsible for >20% of the near-range PlsACs and featured with a DNBP/di-2-ethylhexyl phthalate (DEHP) concentration ratio of 2.2. The DNBP/DEHP concentration ratio higher than 1 can indicate nonexhaust emissions from on-road traffic due to abrasion of tires, brakes, and road markings. The average enrichment ratio of quantified PlsACs within PM2.5 (ng PlsACs per μg PM2.5) for each resolved source provides a basis for assessing strategies to cocontrol airborne plastics and PM2.5.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10305.title: Coupled Geophysical and Technoeconomic Industrial Growth Constraints on Geological Carbon Storage Scale-Up: Application to UK Offshore Resources
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10305.summary: Abstract Geological carbon dioxide storage is central to meeting many national climate change commitments, but large-scale deployment may be limited by both techno-economic rates of growth and physics-based processes imposed by subsurface geology. We develop a modeling framework for the assessment of feasible CO2 storage scale-up trajectories that unifies constraints arising from industrial rates of growth, dynamic injection rate limits from reservoir pressurization, and static maximum cumulative storage resource. We employ logistic and Gompertz models to represent policy-compliant deployment trajectories, parametrized by the total cumulative storage resource. We then use a simplified physics model to estimate the resulting regional subsurface pressurization along these trajectories. Growth curves where reservoir pressurization exceeds safe limits are updated by reducing the static storage resource until residing in the safe deployment range. The result is both a growth trajectory and static storage resource achievable subject to injectivity limits. Applying the framework to the United Kingdom (UK), we find that offshore storage resources are sufficient to accommodate all government midcentury deployment rate scenarios up to 175 Mt yr–1. Cumulative storage of up to 78 Gt, representing a reference estimate of the UK storage resource base used in national planning, can be achieved under Gompertz growth trajectories. The more aggressive logistic trajectories are constrained by reservoir pressure, limiting the achievable resource base to 69 Gt. The framework is transferable to other regions to assess the feasibility of policy-driven CO2 storage pathways under coupled industrial growth and geophysical constraints, informing national decarbonization planning and global integrated assessment models.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c02821.title: Atmospheric Aging Modifies the Toxicological Profile of Biomass Burning Particles in Epithelial Lung Cells
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c02821.summary: Abstract Wildfire activity and associated smoke emissions are increasing globally, leading to widespread exposure to biomass burning particulate matter (PM). Although people are mainly exposed to aged wildfire smoke rather than fresh emissions, the effects of atmospheric aging on wildfire particulate toxicity remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated how atmospheric processing (“aging”) modifies biological effects of biomass burning particles (BBPs) generated under controlled flaming and smoldering combustion conditions. BB emissions were produced in the Photochemical Large Aerosol Chamber (PHOTO-LAC) and aged under alternating photochemical and dark conditions. Fresh and aged BBP extracts were subsequently sampled and tested in human bronchial epithelial cells (BEAS-2B). We assessed cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, oxidative DNA damage, genome-wide transcriptional responses, and inflammatory and extracellular matrix-related protein expression. Atmospheric aging substantially altered BBP toxicity in a combustion-dependent manner. Aged BBP enhanced intracellular reactive oxygen species formation and oxidative DNA damage, particularly for smoldering emissions, while cytotoxicity remained largely unchanged. In contrast, inflammatory and matrix-remodeling responses were attenuated with aging in smoldering particles but remained stable for flaming BBP. These findings demonstrate that atmospheric aging can simultaneously amplify oxidative and genotoxic stress while dampening inflammatory signaling, underscoring the need to incorporate aging state into health risk assessments of wildfire smoke exposure.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07034.title: Water Footprint and Scarcity Risks of Low-Carbon Fuels
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07034.summary: Abstract Production of ammonia, methanol, and hydrogen is key to decarbonizing hard-to-electrify sectors but is also water-intensive. However, the water implications of scaling these energy carriers under low-carbon pathways remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate direct water consumption with facility-level geospatial analysis and hydrological modeling to quantify water-scarcity exposure across each production facility in North America. Low-carbon production routes require more direct and indirect water consumption than conventional pathways, with electrolytic hydrogen and e-methanol increasing water-intensity by up to 5-fold in regions with limited renewable availability─a trade-off further amplified by supply chain effects, particularly for solar PV-based electricity and direct air capture-based CO2 feedstocks. Water scarcity already affects about 58% of methanol production in Mexico, 2% of ammonia production in the U.S., and 5% and 27% of refinery production in the U.S. and Mexico, respectively. Under midcentury climate scenarios, exposure increases in both magnitude and spatial extent. Although irrigation accounts for over 80% of local water consumption in various fuel production facilities, municipalities and manufacturing often exert the greatest pressure on low-carbon fuel production, depending on the product and country.. These results demonstrate that technology choice, system design, and facility siting are as important as hydrology considerations in determining water risks. Incorporating water availability in low-carbon fuel projects is therefore essential to ensure that decarbonization pathways are scalable, operationally resilient, and truly sustainable.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11481.title: Global Steel Decarbonization under Policy, Technology, and Resource Constraints: A Process-Unit Agent-Based Model
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11481.summary: Abstract Deep decarbonization of steel requires low-emission technologies to be deployed through a long-lived and heterogeneous asset fleet without disrupting steel supply. We developed a country-resolved agent-based model that follows global steel process units annually from 2023 to 2060. Units choose among continued operation, renewal, retrofit, conversion, retirement, and new construction, subject to construction time, linked upstream capacity, national production pathways, and annual supplies of scrap, hydrogen, natural gas, and pellets. Four scenarios distinguish stronger climate policy from improved technology and resource availability. Global process-chain CO2 emissions decline by 67–79% by 2060, reaching 0.476–0.737 Gt. The integrated case achieves the lowest emissions, but the two-component interventions do not independently outperform the reference case. Stronger policy changes when assets enter a finite transition queue, whereas technology and material conditions determine whether replacement routes can be built and operated at that time. By 2060, Scrap-EAF supplies 74–80% of crude steel, but residual unabated blast furnaces and coal-based direct reduction keep national steel pathways above their allocated levels in many countries. Deep decarbonization, therefore, depends on coordinating asset turnover, construction, and complementary material systems, rather than on technology availability or carbon-price pressure alone.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10592.title: Constructing Prospective Multiregional Input-Output Tables via Scenario-Constrained Optimization for Future Environmental Footprint Assessment
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10592.summary: Abstract Prospective multiregional input-output (MRIO) tables that integrate scenarios from integrated assessment models (IAMs) support forward-looking environmental footprint analysis, but the trade-off between historical structural fidelity and scenario compliance has not been quantified. We constructed 12 prospective MRIO tables from EXIOBASE 2019 and the IMAGE SSP2 scenario for 2035, including a Leontief-based projection and 11 optimization-based projections under different combinations of scenario constraints on GDP, value added, sector outputs, as well as energy and agriculture consumption. Among the constraints, those on energy and agriculture consumption were satisfied at the highest cost in coefficient deviations from the Leontief-based projection and shifted the corresponding transaction flows most significantly. Regional shares of the global carbon footprint remained stable, but sectoral attribution within each region was substantially reshuffled, and the identification of high-growth consumption hotspots was sensitive to scenario compliance level. Some hotspots persisted at all levels of compliance. The consumption-based carbon footprint driven by China’s final energy demand grew the fastest and emerged as a major new hotspot in 2035. The footprint of livestock consumption showed persistent high growth in multiple regions and India and the Rest of Asia rose in environmental significance through their industrial sectors.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11772.title: Targeted Coupling of Electrogenerated Reactive Oxygen Species for Deep Pollutant Mineralization
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11772.summary: Abstract Electrochemical oxidation technology holds great promise for wastewater treatment. However, the inherent limitations of single-component reactive oxygen species (ROS) and their low yield impede thorough mineralization of organic pollutants and elevate energy consumption. Herein, we develop a directed ROS coupling oxidation (DRCO) system, which employs a Ni–Sb–SnO2 anode that leverages Ni(III)/Ni(II) redox cycling for highly selective OH generation, coupled with a CrMn@C anode for 1O2 production, significantly enhancing the coexisting ROS yield. By leveraging the electron-withdrawing and donating synergistic effect of •OH and 1O2, the DRCO system removes 61.2–78.5% total organic carbon (TOC) for diverse organics within 20 min. The observed kinetic constants are 1.4–52.6 times higher than those of systems that use •OH or 1O2 alone. Furthermore, the DRCO system achieves 85.4% TOC removal for actual pharmaceutical wastewater and sustains operational stability over a 120 h continuous flow period. Compared to commercial anodes, the DRCO system reduces energy consumption by 72% (to 12.02 kW·h·kgTOC–1) while effectively suppressing the accumulation of toxic intermediate products. This work demonstrates that high-selectivity •OH generation and the elucidated dual-ROS synergistic mechanism jointly offer a viable strategy toward efficient and energy-conscious electrochemical water purification.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c05158.title: Climate-Driven Sink-to-Source Transitions for Microplastics in Terrestrial Systems
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c05158.summary: Abstract Microplastics (MPs) are increasingly recognized as pervasive contaminants in terrestrial environments, where soils act as major dynamic reservoirs that retain particles but can also release them through hydrological, erosional, and atmospheric pathways. Climate change is altering the physical, hydrological, and biogeochemical controls that govern the MP retention-release balance. This review develops a climate-driven sink-to-source transition framework in which terrestrial systems shift episodically from retention-dominated to export-active states. We synthesize evidence that changes in freeze–thaw regimes and drought-rewetting reorganize pore networks and preferential flow; extreme rainfall and runoff can exceed hydrological retention and redistribute MPs vertically and laterally; and warming and salinization reconfigure interfacial interactions, polymer aging, aggregation behavior, and microbially mediated transport processes. Atmospheric entrainment and snowpack-snowmelt pathways further connect terrestrial MP reservoirs with other environmental compartments. Across these climate drivers, MP mobility depends on the coupled evolution of pore architecture, water flux, particle properties, and biogeochemical conditions rather than on any single forcing factor. By integrating laboratory studies, field observations, and emerging modeling perspectives, this review provides a mechanistic foundation for predicting terrestrial MP redistribution and associated environmental risks under ongoing climate change.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08309.title: Implementation Gap in Global Power Capacity Expansion to meet Paris Agreement Climate Targets
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08309.summary: Abstract Meeting the Paris Agreement’s climate targets demands an unprecedented expansion of renewable energy. Despite global commitments, significant implementation gaps persist due to economic, policy, and technical uncertainties. Here, we develop a Global Power Capacity Dynamics Framework, integrating facility-level data, machine learning and transition modeling to assess the feasibility of global power expansion. Analyzing 215,849 power plant units across five status modes (operating, planned, canceled, standby, retired), the framework explicitly incorporates the likelihood of planned capacity realization and the conversion of existing fossil assets. We find that by 2030, only 51% [40%–61%] of announced planned capacity is expected to become operational, while 26% [19%–36%] is likely to be canceled, with fossil fuel projects, especially coal, facing a cancellation rate of about 35%. Global operational capacity is projected to reach 9727 GW [9626–9848], including 178 GW [159–198] of existing fossil units requiring conversion or replacement (e.g., coal-to-gas, fossil-to-biomass). Although renewables dominate the planned pipeline, they are projected to constitute only 52% of the global energy mix by 2030, well below levels needed to meet climate goals. Regional disparities are pronounced: Asia, despite its relatively low cancellation rate, faces the world’s largest implementation gap, requiring an additional 2488 GW of solar and contending with 523 GW of stranded coal capacity to remain on a 1.5 °C pathway. This study provides the first probabilistic, facility-level assessment of global power capacity trajectories, revealing critical shortfalls in planned deployment and underscoring the urgency of aligning capacity expansion with climate targets.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07345.title: Environmental Mechanochemistry: From Force-Induced Reactivity to Aqueous Reaction Platforms
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07345.summary: Abstract Mechanochemistry is increasingly used in environmental research, but is still commonly treated as a material synthesis or pretreatment step rather than a mode of driving reactions that directly affects pathways relevant to pollution control and resource recovery. This Perspective argues that its environmental significance is most evident when force not only changes material properties before use, but also alters how reactions proceed during operation. We compare how force becomes chemically effective in inorganic and organic systems and classify environmental applications according to its primary role. Using zerovalent iron (ZVI) as a representative example, we show that mechanochemistry can simultaneously alleviate multiple bottlenecks in ZVI preparation, storage, and application. Earlier studies have shown that force can regulate ZVI lattice structure, surface state, and interfacial charge transfer. The wet-milling mechanochemical reactor (MCR) extends these effects into aqueous operation by applying force during rather than before reaction. This intensifies solid–liquid contact, accelerates heterogeneous kinetics, and, in some systems, shifts target transformation from surface-confined pathways toward subsurface redistribution and lattice-associated capture. Future advances should identify systems in which force can strengthen reactions sufficiently to open pathways that conventional treatment processes do not readily access.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09917.title: Mitochondrial-Endocrine Axis Dysfunction Mediates Diet-Dependent Susceptibility to Nanoplastic Ovarian Toxicity and PCOS Risk
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09917.summary: Abstract Nanoplastics (NPs) pollution represents an emerging threat to reproductive health, yet how dietary habits modulate this toxicity remains largely unexplored. Here, mice were assigned to a control (CD), high-fat (HFD), or high-fiber (HFib) diet and received oral doses of deuterated polystyrene nanoparticles at 0, 5, or 25 mg/kg/day over an eight-week period. Ovarian NP accumulation was dose-dependent under CD, reaching 23.33 ± 5.39 μg/g tissue at the highest dose. HFD markedly elevated this burden to 96.87 ± 13.44 μg/g, whereas HFib significantly reduced it to 7.77 ± 1.32 μg/g. Functionally, HFD synergized with NPs to disrupt estrous cyclicity (only 13% regular cycles), suppress anti-Müllerian hormone by 74%, and increase follicular atresia rate, while HFib maintained near-normal ovarian physiology. Transcriptomics identified steroid hormone biosynthesis and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) as core pathways convergently dysregulated by NPs across all diets. Mechanistically, HFD amplified NP-induced ovarian oxidative stress, inflammation, and mitochondrial OXPHOS impairment, culminating in hyperandrogenism and profound estradiol deficiency. Conversely, HFib preserved aromatase expression and mitochondrial respiratory capacity, thereby restoring steroidogenic homeostasis. Mendelian randomization further linked human orthologues of these dysregulated genes, including UQCR10 and COX4I1 encoding mitochondrial complex III and IV subunits, to elevated polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) risk, highlighting the central role of OXPHOS disruption. These findings establish a diet-NP interaction pattern with implications for reproductive health guidance in populations.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11530.title: Market-Average Data Can Misrepresent Supply Chain Environmental Impacts and Their Uncertainty
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11530.summary: Abstract Market-average data sets are often used in life cycle assessment and carbon accounting when the production route of a procured good is unknown. The uncertainty this introduces is commonly characterized using generic pedigree matrix factors, which do not reflect how variability across production geographies and technologies differs between goods. Here, we develop a hybrid method that combines pedigree matrix uncertainty characterization within individual production routes with market-share-weighted Monte Carlo sampling between known production routes to represent uncertainty about which route supplied the good. We compare it with conventional market-average uncertainty analysis for 30 economically important goods. For climate impacts, conventional 5th–95th interpercentile intervals are narrower than route-weighted sampling intervals for 25 goods, at least 50% narrower for 14 goods, and up to 82% narrower. Conventional intervals exclude the central climate impact estimates of 44% of possible production routes. Route-weighted sampling captures these outcomes and reveals multimodality and impact-category-specific uncertainty profiles that conventional analysis does not. Variance decomposition distinguishes geographical and technological differences between routes from uncertainty within routes, helping prioritize supplier data collection. These differences show that conventional uncertainty estimates can mislead and may not capture how substantially initial estimates could change when supplier-specific data become available.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09860.title: UV328 Promotes Plastisphere Formation on Microplastics through Quorum-Sensing-Associated Signaling Interference
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09860.summary: Abstract Microplastics have created an expanding anthropogenic microbial niche known as the plastisphere, yet the mechanisms by which plastic additives influence these microbial assemblies remain poorly understood. Here, we show that UV328, a ubiquitous benzotriazole stabilizer recently listed in the Stockholm Convention, may be associated with quorum sensing signaling that accelerates plastisphere formation, biomass accumulation, and extracellular polymeric substance production on microplastics. In UV328-exposed polystyrene and polylactic acid plastisphere, the total expression levels of biofilm formation genes are upregulated by 1.38- to 2.94-fold compared to the control and quorum quenching manipulations. Molecular dynamics simulations predict that UV328 structurally mimics N-acyl-homoserine lactone (AHL) and may plausibly occupy ligand-binding domains of the quorum sensing receptor SdiA and CciR with favorable energetics. UV328 exposure was further associated with the upregulation of genes involved in bacterial chemotaxis, flagellar assembly, and central carbon metabolism. This physiological reprogramming alters community assembly trajectories and leads to a protein-rich plastisphere phenotype that was reversible by enzymatic quorum quenching, potentially supporting the involvement of AHL-sensitive processes. Our findings suggest that UV328 can alter plastisphere development through signaling-associated ecological processes, raising the possibility that microplastics may function as chemically active interfaces and highlighting microbial signaling interference as an overlooked dimension of the ecological risks associated with plastic additives in aquatic ecosystems.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10138.title: Interfacial Triplet-Energy Funneling Directs Energy-Transfer-Mediated Singlet Oxygen Generation for Deep Toluene Mineralization
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10138.summary: Abstract Photocatalytic oxidation is a promising strategy for volatile organic compounds (VOCs) abatement, but incomplete mineralization and carbonaceous intermediate accumulation remain major challenges, especially when conventional charge-transfer pathways generate nonselective radical reactive oxygen species. Selective activation of molecular oxygen toward singlet oxygen (1O2) offers a potential route to controlled oxidation, yet efficient energy-transfer-mediated 1O2 generation in solid-state photocatalysts remains difficult to achieve. Herein, a strongly coupled In(OH)3/ZnGa2O4 heterojunction with an electronic structure consistent with an S-scheme configuration is constructed to investigate interfacial excited-state regulation. Spectroscopic measurements indicate modified excited-state relaxation and a reduced effective singlet–triplet energy separation, which may favor singlet-to-triplet conversion. Combined spectroscopic analyses, quenching experiments, and density functional theory calculations support a proposed interfacial triplet-energy-funneling pathway involving ZnGa2O4-related/interfacial triplet-related states and subsequent energy transfer to adsorbed O2 for 1O2 generation. As a result, the optimized In(OH)3/ZnGa2O4 photocatalyst achieves 98.3% toluene removal and 92.4% mineralization in a continuous-flow gas-phase reactor, together with excellent cycling stability and humidity tolerance. Mechanistic results further suggest that a pathway involving 1O2 contributes to methyl oxidation and the subsequent conversion of oxygenated intermediates, potentially limiting carbonaceous residue accumulation. This work provides an excited-state-engineering strategy for selective molecular oxygen activation and offers a promising route toward efficient, durable, and deeply mineralizing photocatalytic VOCs abatement.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10647.title: Soil Mineral Coatings on Biodegradable Microplastics: Formation and Control of Enzymatic Degradation
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c10647.summary: Abstract In agriculture, biodegradable plastics weather and fragment into microplastics that inevitably acquire mineral coatings. However, the impact of mineral coatings on microplastic degradation remains poorly understood. We examined coating formation and enzymatic degradation of pristine and photoaged poly(butylene adipate-co-terephthalate) microplastics (PBAT-MPs) in loessial soil and red soil under drought, moist, alternate wetting-drying, and flooded regimes during 64 days. Soil type, moisture, and photoaging governed coating accumulation. Loessial soil produced greater Al and Fe loading on PBAT-MPs than red soil, while unsaturated regimes increased Al and Fe by 394%–1109% relative to flooding (p < 0.05). Synchrotron micro-X-ray fluorescence combined with absorption near-edge structure spectroscopy analyses showed heterogeneous elemental distributions and mineral speciation on PBAT-MPs that resembled those of the source soils. Unexpectedly, loessial-soil coatings increased PBAT-MPs’ terephthalic acid and adipic acid release by 9.1%–17.4% and reduced residual PBAT mass by 6.5%–23.5% (p < 0.05). Kinetic analyses showed that although mineral coatings slowed enzyme adsorption via diffusion limitations, localized leaching of Ca2+ from the coatings enhanced cutinase activity and outweighed this physical constraint. These findings demonstrate that mineral coatings can regulate the enzymatic degradation of PBAT, providing new insights into the environmental fate of biodegradable microplastics in agricultural soils.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c04082.title: Molecular Interactions between Styrene Oligomers and Human Serum Albumin: A Multiscale Computational Study of a Plastic-Derived Environmental Contaminant
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c04082.summary: Abstract Micro- and nanoplastics are pervasive environmental pollutants known to accumulate in human organs. While the hazards of larger plastic particles are under intense investigation, the toxicological impact of molecular-level plastic oligomers with dimensions around 1 nm is a critical and underexplored area. This study provides a comprehensive molecular-level in silico characterization of the binding interactions between styrene oligomers (1–7 units) and HSA, characterizing their molecular basis and its potential relevance to HSA’s ligand transport function. A multilevel computational approach was employed, integrating molecular docking, MD simulations, DFT, MM/PBSA binding free energy calculations, and ProLIF interaction fingerprinting. FA1 accommodated 82–95% of the most favorable docking poses for oligomers containing three to seven styrene units and exhibited the lowest docking scores, reaching −11.9 kcal·mol–1, compared with −6.4 kcal·mol–1 for the monomer. MD simulations confirmed the structural stability of oligomer-HSA complexes, further supported by dynamic cross-correlation, principal component, and solvent-accessible surface area analyses. Quantum biochemistry analyses further confirmed FA1 as the most energetically favorable binding pocket, with an average interaction energy of −117.47 kcal·mol–1 compared with −73.96 kcal·mol–1 for FA6, a hierarchy independently reproduced by MM/PBSA calculations (R = 0.82). For the hexamer and heptamer, FA1 exhibited energetic advantages of 27.39 and 21.84 kcal·mol–1, respectively. These findings indicate that HSA binds styrene oligomers with high stability and affinity at FA1, providing a molecular basis for further investigation of their potential relevance to ligand transport and systemic exposure to plastic-derived contaminants.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11308.title: Source or Sink: Bioanalytical and Chemical Profiling of New and Field-Weathered Plastics
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c11308.summary: Abstract Plastics contain complex mixtures of chemicals that can leach into the aquatic environment. Conversely, the high sorption capacity of certain polymers renders plastics passive samplers for environmental pollutants from ambient waters. We evaluated whether effects from chemicals that are extractable or leachable from plastics from the North Pacific Ocean are dominated by plastic-associated or sorbed environmental compounds. First, bioanalytical profiling of chemical mixtures from solvent extracts of field-weathered marine plastics in cell-based bioassays was compared to that of chemicals from solvent extracts of newly purchased counterparts of the field plastics. Second, the new plastics were artificially UV-weathered and solvent-extracted, and the leachate waters were enriched with solid-phase extraction and dosed into a test battery of four in vitro bioassays where activation of the arylhydrocarbon receptor, oxidative stress response, and/or cytotoxicity were most responsive. Finally, chemical screening was performed using high-resolution mass spectrometry with subsequent mixture effect modeling to identify toxicity drivers. The results showed a multifaceted picture: Newly purchased high-durability outdoor products caused higher effects before weathering, whereas food packaging tended to show increased effects after field weathering. The analyzed chemicals could partially explain the observed effects (<0.1–98%). Our study underlines the relevance of field weathering for marine plastics and their potential to leach chemicals of concern into the environment.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07119.title: Light-Induced Formation of Volatile Organic Compounds from Bleach Cleaning in Indoor Environments
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07119.summary: Abstract Surface bleach cleaning is a common indoor activity that releases abundant strong oxidants, including hypochlorous acid (HOCl) and chlorine gas (Cl2), which can significantly influence indoor chemistry. While bleach-driven chemical transformations are recognized, the specific role of illumination remains poorly understood. This study combines field measurements and laboratory flow tube experiments to investigate volatile organic compound (VOC) formation from reactions between bleach emissions and surface-sorbed species, e.g., kitchen-derived organic films, under illuminated conditions. In real-world indoor settings, we observed that bleach cleaning under light predominantly generates oxygenated VOCs (OVOCs), accounting for ∼92% of total emissions. Saturated carbonyls contributed the most (∼82%), such as C6H12O, C9H18O, and C2H4O. Flow tube experiments using surrogate compounds and kitchen-collected surface films confirmed that OVOCs are generated via heterogeneous reactions between surface-bound organics (e.g., fatty acids, amides, amino acids) and radicals produced from photolysis of bleach-derived oxidants. VOC production was found to depend on surface accumulation and aging, with more accumulated and aged surfaces producing greater quantities and more diverse products. These findings provide important insights into VOC production from indoor surface chemistry initiated by bleach cleaning under typical indoor lighting conditions, advancing our understanding of volatile byproduct formation from indoor bleach photochemistry.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06663.title: Evaluating Individual Infection Risk: The Interplay between Air Mixing Intensities and Occupant Dynamics
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06663.summary: Abstract Aerosol transmission remains a critical route for the spread of respiratory infectious diseases, yet real-time exposure mapping in complex public spaces is computationally demanding. This study presents a robust and adaptable framework for estimating dynamic individual exposure (i.e., viral dose) by integrating high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics (CFD) with computer vision (CV) analysis. By overlaying validated steady-state viral aerosol plumes onto dynamic human interaction data, we evaluated the interplay between airflow patterns and human behaviors under two distinct air change rates (ACH: 25 h–1 and 3 h–1). Each scenario was simulated both with and without MERV-13 filtration. Applications in both a stochastic-movement hotel meeting room and a stationary-occupant office demonstrate that while high turbulence due to high ACH limits the spatial extent of plumes, sustained close proximity in structured settings can result in disproportionately high viral doses for specific individuals. MERV-13 filtration effectively reduced exposure within high-concentration zones. We propose a Reynolds number (Re)-based modeling guideline: steady-state CFD-CV for moderate mixing (900 ≤ Re ≤ 2300), a well-mixed assumption for high mixing (Re > 2300), and transient CFD-CV for low mixing (500 ≤ Re < 900) during breathing and speaking, and steady-state CFD-CV for coughing and sneezing regardless of Re value. This framework supports real-time monitoring and targeted interventions, providing a data-driven foundation for indoor occupant safety.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c15380.title: Mild Oxidant Regulation of *H Coverage Promotes Electrocatalytic Nitrate Reduction to N2 in Low-Conductivity Media
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c15380.summary: Abstract Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction reaction (NO3RR) has attracted growing interest for converting nitrate (NO3–) into ammonium (NH4+), yet NH4+ production from dilute, low-conductivity waters is constrained by high energy consumption, limited NO3– availability, and costly product recovery. Steering NO3RR directly toward benign N2 therefore represents a more practical route, but this pathway is often suppressed by excessive surface *H coverage, which drives the overhydrogenation of nitrogen intermediates to NH4+. Here, we report a mild oxidant-assisted coelectrolysis strategy that regulates interfacial *H coverage and promotes NO3–-to-N2 conversion in a Cu nanoparticle-decorated Ni cathode membrane electrochemical reactor. This reactor separates a highly conductive electrochemical chamber from a NO3–-containing chemical chamber, enabling NO3– reduction in low-conductivity media while maintaining a less negative cathodic potential. Mild oxidants, including H2O2, O2, CH3COOOH, and KIO4, consumed excess *H and redirected the reaction pathway toward N–N coupling. With H2O2 as a representative oxidant, N2 selectivity increased from 13.47% without H2O2 to 87.25% at 100 mM H2O2. Mechanistic analyses revealed that H2O2 decreases interfacial *H abundance, which suppresses NH4+ formation and facilitates the dimerization of nitrogen-containing intermediates. Verification in real low-conductivity groundwater further supports this strategy as a mechanistic basis for designing selective, low-energy electrochemical denitrification systems for low-conductivity NO3–-contaminated media.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08882.title: Size- and Time-Resolved Emission Rates of Particulate Matter Mass, Chemical Constituents, and Oxidative Potential from Indoor Sources
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08882.summary: Abstract We quantified the time- and size-resolved emission rates of particulate matter (PM) mass, its chemical constituents, and OP (via dithiothreitol assay) from six indoor sources in a test chamber (two types of incense, candle, toaster, humidifier, and cigarette). Both the chemical composition and mass-normalized OP (OPm) varied little temporally. However, both the chemical composition and OPm varied with particle size from <0.25 to 10 μm, with quasi-ultrafine particles (Q-UFPs < 0.25 μm) showing the highest OPm. The particle size distribution of the PM emitted from these sources was mostly unimodal, with both PM10 mass and OP emission rate concentrated in the Q-UFP size range. Given the abundance of Q-UFPs in the emitted PM with their high intrinsic OP, we find that 37 ± 3% of the emitted PM10 mass and OP from these sources has the potential to deposit in the respiratory tract, 45 ± 2% of which deposits in the alveolar region. An exploratory exposure assessment suggests that for an equal dose of PM10 mass and OP originating from these indoor sources vs ambient PM, the emissions from the tested indoor sources will likely result in a 76 ± 10% higher dose of alveolar-deposited mass and OP. Collectively, these results emphasize the need to better quantify the size-resolved toxicological properties of PM from myriad indoor emission sources to reliably estimate the resulting health risks.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12154.title: Wastewater Treatment Plants as Anchor Infrastructure for Geothermal Energy in Cold Regions
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c12154.summary: Abstract Thermal constraints in cold regions suppress biological treatment, increase energy demand, and elevate greenhouse gas emissions of existing wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs), and remain a major barrier to the deployment of adequate sanitation infrastructure in many cold-region communities. Where geothermal resources exist, low-enthalpy hydrothermal heat is well matched to this energy gap. Yet, WWTPs are underrecognized anchors for broader geothermal deployment, providing a continuous, weather-independent thermal offtake through which subsurface CAPEX can be amortized. We reframe geothermal-WWTP integration as a system-level enabler that benefits both parts. Using three cascaded configurations for a full-scale WWTP, a rapid techno-economic analysis identifies three trends: energy and carbon savings/revenues alone are insufficient under realistic policy stacks, whereas crediting the upgrade-deferral value of geothermally enhanced treatment makes the project economically favorable across most policy scenarios. Globally, this triple intersection encompasses ∼11,600 catalogued WWTPs serving ∼280 million people, with a further estimate of ∼48 million people in the same regions beyond current service radii. The opportunity is greatest in cold, remote, and underserved communities, where local geothermal resources, treatment intensification, and community-scale demand together carry a case that no single driver could sustain alone.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08117.title: Fe(II) Speciation Regulates Microbial Metabolic Reprogramming and Phototrophic Fe(II) Mineralization in Rhodopseudomonas palustris SX2
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08117.summary: Abstract Phototrophic iron mineralization (PIM) is a keystone biogeochemical process linking anoxic iron redox transformations to carbon sequestration. Although PIM is widely documented, how Fe(II) speciation impacts cell physiology and thus causes divergent mineralization phenotypes remains poorly understood. In this study, we systematically investigated the physiological, mineralogical, and molecular responses of a newly isolated photoferrotroph, Rhodopseudomonas palustris SX2, exposed to uncomplexed Fe(II) [Fe(II) without OM] versus organically complexed Fe(II) [Fe(II)-OM] under anoxic and illuminated conditions. We demonstrate that distinct Fe(II) speciation drives divergent metabolic reprogramming for rapid metabolic adaptation and phototrophic biomineralization phenotypes. Fe(II) without OM triggered cell-surface encrustation and activated stress-mitigation and metal-efflux systems, whereas Fe(II)-OM stimulated the formation of discrete intracellular iron nanoparticles while upregulating photosynthetic light harvesting and autotrophic CO2 fixation. Furthermore, genetic knockout and complementation confirmed that the pioABC operon constitutes the indispensable electron conduit driving Fe(II) oxidation across both speciation regimes, with organic complexation significantly enhancing its transcriptional activation. Our findings reveal how metabolic adaptation driven by Fe(II) speciation dictates the spatial distribution of biogenic iron minerals and regulates the efficiency of coupled carbon sequestration in anoxic ecosystems.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c05233.title: Direct Upcycling of Rare Earth Hyperaccumulator Biomass into Luminescent CaS:Ce Phosphors
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c05233.summary: Abstract Rare earth elements (REEs) are essential to high-tech industries and sustainable development, but traditional mining poses significant environmental challenges. Phytomining, which uses hyperaccumulators to recover REEs from soils or low-grade mines, has emerged as a sustainable alternative; however, the high cost and low efficiency of extracting and purifying REEs from harvested biomass remain major barriers to its practical application. Here, we propose a novel in situ doping strategy to directly convert cerium (Ce)-enriched hyperaccumulator biomass into color-tunable CaS:Ce phosphors and value-added syngas, bypassing complex separation of Ca and REEs. The results show that Ce, Ca, and S could be selectively enriched from hyperaccumulator biomass to the resulting char through solvothermal pretreatment with sulfuric acid and ethanol. Subsequent steam gasification of the char produces Ce-doped CaS phosphors with broad, green-yellow emission and high photoluminescence quantum yields of 18.5–37.4%. Our approach reduces energy use by 33.6%, carbon emissions by 22.4%, and costs by \$2.62 kg–1 biomass, outperforming conventional REE recovery in both environmental and economic sustainability. This strategy provides an environmentally sustainable and economically viable route for high-value utilization of REE-rich biomass, addressing a critical bottleneck in phytomining and advancing its development as a green REE recovery technology.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08297.title: Pollutant Release and Transfer Registers (PRTRs) as a Cornerstone of Global Chemicals Management: Current Gaps and Future Directions
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c08297.summary: Abstract Pollutant Release and Transfer Register (PRTR) systems in different countries are key tools for global chemicals management and an important data source for measuring progress toward achieving Sustainable Development Goal 12 of sustainable consumption and production patterns. However, current implementations face several structural and functional limitations that hinder the broad applicability of the PRTR reporting data. These limitations can be categorized into two main aspects: within-system issues and between-system inconsistencies. Within systems, data gaps can result from limited monitoring of nonpoint sources, incomplete reporting, exemptions due to thresholds and confidentiality agreements, and other similar factors, while data inaccuracies can be caused by estimation errors, duplicated counts, and other related issues. Between systems, differences in chemical lists, threshold settings, emission source types, reporting methods, and other discrepancies can hinder data comparability and integration, limiting the effectiveness of global chemicals management. Addressing these issues, through unified pollutant lists, harmonized reporting methodologies, expanded source coverage, and improved data verification, can significantly strengthen the utility of PRTR systems, advancing an integrated and evidence-based global sound management of chemicals.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c04705.title: Global Potential of No-Tillage in Enhancing Soil Carbon and Reducing Greenhouse Gas Emissions While Sustaining Crop Yields
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c04705.summary: Abstract Pursuing the balance between environmental sustainability and agricultural productivity remains a critical challenge for achieving global sustainable development goals. No-tillage (NT), as a key measure of sustainable conservation and climate-smart agriculture, offers a promising approach to addressing this challenge. However, its comprehensive effects on soil carbon accumulation, greenhouse gas emissions, and crop yields remain unquantified at the global scale, limiting our ability to optimize both environmental and agronomic outcomes. Here, we conducted such a global synthesis by combining a meta-analysis of 8,303 paired observations from 1,371 studies with a random forest model to assess the influence of site conditions and management on NT effects. Our meta-analysis demonstrates integrated benefits of NT in enhancing soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks in 0–30 cm layer by 11.0% and mitigating greenhouse gas (the sum of CO2, CH4, and N2O in CO2-equivalent) emissions by 13.5%, without a significant impact on crop yields (−0.6% ± 1.5%). The integrated benefits are stronger in drier climates and coarser-textured soils, and they exhibit significant time-dependent patterns. Our prediction identifies 44% of global croplands as being optimal for NT’s integrated benefits, mainly in Africa, South Asia, and North America. Adopting NT in these areas would result in a 4.8% increase in major food-crop yields, a 15.2% increase in 0–30 cm SOC stocks, and a 6.4% reduction in global cropland emissions, respectively. These findings underscore the relevance of implementing NT in suitable regions by adopting it into Good Agricultural Practice Guidelines.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07060.title: Cross-Level Responses of Freshwater Zooplankton to Micro/Nanoplastics: A Meta-Analysis Integrating Individual- to Community-Level Evidence
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07060.summary: Abstract Despite the known threats of micro/nanoplastics (MNPs) to freshwater ecosystems, their risks to zooplankton remain poorly resolved because existing evidence is fragmented across biological levels. Consequently, associations between lower-level responses and population- and community-level outcomes remain unclear. Here, we synthesized 3042 research cases from controlled experiments worldwide covering 12 response categories. We found significant overall negative effects of MNPs in systems without predators, with predators, and with predator-conditioned medium. Although molecular-level evidence remains limited, a consistent hierarchical response pattern emerged under predator-absent conditions. We therefore propose a conceptual hierarchical effect pathway (HEP) framework integrating effect sizes and cross-level associations. Within this framework, MNPs exposure was associated with increased ingestion of MNPs, physiological damage, feeding impairment, and reduced activity and defense. These responses formed an upstream tier associated with life-history impairments, including impaired growth and development, reduced reproductive capacity, and reduced survival, although these associations do not establish temporal ordering or causation. Under predator-present conditions, negative population- and community-level effects were also observed. Effect magnitudes also varied with MNPs characteristics, exposure duration, and zooplankton group. Together, the HEP framework clarifies cross-level associations and helps identify informative endpoints and incorporate food-web context into risk assessment of MNPs.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07540.title: Investigations of New Particle Formation Mechanisms in North China Plain during the Spring Campaign Based on Observations and Simulations
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c07540.summary: Abstract New particle formation (NPF) plays a critical role in atmospheric aerosol loading, yet the mechanisms controlling NPF under high-pollution conditions remain poorly understood. Ground-based measurements and GEOS-Chem-APM simulations were combined to investigate the factors governing NPF in a typical industrial city over North China Plain. During the spring campaign (3 May-2 June 2016), 10 NPF days were identified, each preceded by nighttime northwesterly ventilation and occurring under dry daytime conditions. The model reproduced 6 of 10 observed NPF events, whereas the remaining 4 showed substantially weaker simulated nucleation. Well-simulated events were generally associated with low relative humidity (RH) and condensation sink (CS) environment. NH3 remained in large excess throughout the campaign. In our test, increasing H2SO4 by up to a factor of 3 substantially enhanced nucleation rate (J) but did not fully reproduce the observed particle evolution, while replacing modeled RH and aerosol surface area with observations only moderately adjusted J. The model underestimated growth rates by 51% and 75% on well-simulated and poorly simulated days. These results indicate that nighttime ventilation reduces surface area and CS of pre-existing aerosol loading, favoring NPF, while successful reproduction of observed NPF depends jointly on diverse precursor-driven nucleation, aerosol scavenging, and subsequent particle growth.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09067.title: Slippery Amphiphilic Antifouling Loose Nanofiltration Membrane with “Double-Defense” Functionalities for High-Salinity Organic Wastewater Sustainable Management
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c09067.summary: Abstract Loose nanofiltration (LNF) holds potential for sustainable management of high-salinity organic wastewater through precise organics/salts fractionation, but practical application is constrained by severe organic–inorganic combined fouling. Herein, we propose a “double-defense” antifouling strategy and develop a slippery amphiphilic LNF membrane via facile stepwise surface modification. A hydrophilic branched polyethylenimine (PEI) network was first cross-linked onto a polyamide (PA) substrate to form a fouling-resistant protection layer, followed by covalent grafting of liquid-like polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) brushes to confer a slippery, fouling-release surface. The PEI layer acts as a hydration and electrostatic barrier to repel organic-cation complexes and scale precursors, while the slippery PDMS layer with high mobility and low surface energy minimizes interfacial interactions and strengthens hydraulic shear responsiveness. During the concentration of authentic leachate membrane bioreactor (MBR) effluent, the optimized membrane showed superior antifouling performance: low flux decline ratio (FDR) of 41.6% and high flux recovery ratio (FRR) of 98.1%, outperforming a commercial PA membrane (FDR 91.2%, FRR 78.4%). It also delivered an organics/salts fractionation selectivity 7.8 times that of the commercial membrane, demonstrating multiple cycles stability. This rationally designed architecture offers a practical solution for challenging wastewater and is extensible to other PA-based membrane systems in environmental applications.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c01277.title: Nanoconfinement Drives Non-Monotonic Methane Density in Shale Nanopores: Direct Observation of Competitive Water–Gas Exchange
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c01277.summary: Abstract The efficiency of unconventional gas recovery is fundamentally governed by the nanoscale partitioning and competitive exchange between methane and water in shale reservoirs, yet direct experimental insight into their coupled behavior under in situ conditions (pressure and temperature) remains elusive. Here, we integrate a first-of-its-kind approach, combining contrast-matching ultra- and small-angle neutron scattering (USANS/SANS) at 50 MPa with vapor sorption, cryo-microscopy, and molecular simulations, to achieve unprecedented direct visualization of methane–water distribution across the multiscale pore–fracture network of the Longmaxi Shale. We report a fundamental revision to classical models, discovering that methane density exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on pore size, increasing with nanoconfinement but peaking sharply at ≈2 nm before declining in sub-2 nm pores. Mechanistically, water forms continuous films on hydrophilic quartz surfaces but aggregates into distinct clusters on organic kerogen. The stronger affinity of water for quartz and its increasing interaction with kerogen at higher saturations enable it to displace adsorbed methane competitively, thereby directly controlling local gas saturation. Furthermore, we reveal that microfractures are the dominant pathways for early water flowback and subsequent gas migration, with pore–fracture connectivity dictating fluid accessibility and phase exchange efficiency. These results establish a mechanistic link between interfacial nanophysics and macro-scale reservoir performance, providing a scientific foundation for optimizing hydraulic fracturing and maximizing resource recovery in deep sedimentary systems.

doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06129.title: Building-Stock Turnover Reshapes Mitigation Priorities in China’s Building Sector
doi:10.1021/acs.est.6c06129.summary: Abstract China’s building sector is pivotal to the 2060 carbon-neutrality ambition, yet prospective assessments often insufficiently capture regional heterogeneity and life-cycle emission dynamics. Here, we develop a provincial-level dynamic framework integrating material flow analysis, life-cycle assessment, and machine-learning-informed parameter trajectories to project emissions through 2060.
